script_events.coling::dc12cc52-6173-4721-b8be-42699b3c:
INT. RESEARCH LAB - DAY

A scientist enters the room and sits at a desk covered with papers about complex systems.

She opens a file that shows failed attempts to predict how systems change over time.

The equations on her screen refuse to give answers fast enough for real use.

She closes that file and opens another one about machine learning methods.

A graph appears showing neural networks that learned to copy system behavior from raw data.

She clicks through examples where the networks worked in training but failed on new cases.

Her colleague walks in and places a coffee cup on the desk.

They discuss why the models break down when conditions shift even slightly.

The scientist stands and walks to a whiteboard that has "curriculum learning" written at the top.

She draws a diagram showing easy examples feeding into harder ones during training.

Her colleague nods and points to a paper about robots that learned tasks this way.

The scientist picks up a marker and writes "dynamical systems" under the diagram.

She turns back to her computer and pulls up data from a physical experiment.

A new window opens with calculations about how much data the training needs.

She runs a test that measures prediction quality over long time spans.

The results show that structure matters more than she expected.

Her colleague suggests using entropy to rank which data samples are simple or complex.

The scientist creates a new training plan that starts with low entropy cases.

She launches the training process and watches the error rates drop steadily.

The model finishes and she tests it on conditions it has never seen before.

The predictions hold steady far longer than previous attempts.

She saves the results and opens a document to record what data choices made the difference.

Her colleague returns with a second coffee and sees the successful graphs on screen.

They begin writing notes about how to pick training data for other systems.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::2e921a31-8ffa-4c78-8c4d-ef7e7243:
INT. RESEARCH LAB - DAY

A team unveils a system they call DSNS. The machine pulls traits from chess games and loads them into memory. Then it grabs features from paintings and adds those too. Music files feed in next, followed by photos of faces.

The computer starts mixing these parts together. New patterns form on the screen. The system spits out fresh chess puzzles no one has seen before.

A researcher clicks print. Sheets of problems slide from the tray. She carries them down the hall to a testing room.

Another program boots up to judge the puzzles. This older model already knows what makes chess problems beautiful. Numbers appear beside each puzzle as the software scores them.

The team calls in human experts. The specialists sit at tables and study the generated problems. They mark their ratings on clipboards.

Results come back from both evaluations. The numbers look promising. Many puzzles reach decent quality levels.

One batch stands out. These problems came from tournament games between beginners, mixed with ordinary snapshots of people. The researcher pulls up the data. These combinations produced three-move problems that match or beat the ones made from expert compositions. The process ran faster too.

A scientist stares at the screen. She cannot explain why photos of strangers help create better chess content. The question goes on a list for future work.

The team runs more tests. They feed the system objects from other fields. Each domain offers items with measurable features. The machine converts everything to numbers and begins recombining again.

New outputs appear across different creative areas. The approach works beyond chess. Any field with objects that have numeric traits can plug into this method.

The lead researcher saves the session. The machine waits for its next task. Creative work shifts from human hands to computer processes, one generated object at a time.
script_events.coling::7876816d-0ac2-4404-b2bf-deeaa0b7:
INT. OBSERVATORY CONTROL ROOM - DAY

A scientist points at a screen showing a glowing line in space.

SCIENTIST
This line cools the gas between stars.

The screen changes to show different galaxies.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Each one glows differently.

Another scientist enters the room carrying data files.

SCIENTIST 2
We still don't know what makes it shine so bright.

The first scientist pulls up older images on a second monitor.

SCIENTIST
Past teams could only see big blurry patches.

SCIENTIST 2
Miles and miles got mixed together.

The first scientist zooms in on a new target.

SCIENTIST
Today we look closer than anyone has before.

The screen focuses on a single spiral arm.

SCIENTIST 2
We will learn where the glow comes from.

A third scientist walks in with a telescope schedule.

SCIENTIST 3
We will see if it tracks new stars being born.

The team activates the space telescope and data begins streaming in.

SCIENTIST
The telescope is scanning one arm of the nearest big galaxy.

New images appear showing the glowing line and oxygen.

SCIENTIST 2
Now we compare this to other maps.

The screen splits to show gas clouds and hydrogen light.

SCIENTIST 3
The glow matches the star birth regions perfectly.

The scientist adjusts the image sharpness.

SCIENTIST
When we blur them the same way they look identical.

SCIENTIST 2
But the gas clouds don't match as well.

A graph appears showing measurements rising across the arm.

SCIENTIST 3
The cooling rate jumps up near the young stars.

The numbers climb from low values to five times higher.

SCIENTIST
The ratio stays steady at two percent.

SCIENTIST 2
That's three times what others reported.

The first scientist pulls up comparison data from other studies.

SCIENTIST
But those studies included the galaxy centers.

SCIENTIST 3
Centers always glow less efficiently.

SCIENTIST 2
And they never isolated just one arm.

The team runs a modeling program.

SCIENTIST
The model gives us reasonable numbers for the conditions.

The screen displays the final parameters for the star forming regions.
script_events.coling::1a16d27a-89fc-4df9-8b4f-cf2532a8:
INT. PHYSICS LAB - DAY

Two scientists stand at a board. One draws a flat grid.

SCIENTIST 1
We start with a flat grid.

The other adds circles at each point.

SCIENTIST 2
Now we place atoms here.

Scientist 1 sketches arrows spinning clockwise.

SCIENTIST 1
These spin one way.

Scientist 2 draws arrows spinning the other direction on top.

SCIENTIST 2
These spin backward.

They step back. The board shows both layers.

SCIENTIST 1
They cancel out.

Scientist 2 taps the edge of the grid.

SCIENTIST 2
No special states appear at the border.

Scientist 1 walks to a computer and types.

SCIENTIST 1
But watch this.

A simulation shows a twist forming in the grid.

SCIENTIST 2
A defect.

Numbers appear at the twist point.

SCIENTIST 1
Charge collects there. Not a whole unit. A fraction.

Scientist 2 adds a new element to the simulation.

SCIENTIST 2
I thread a magnetic line through.

The grid begins to rotate slowly.

SCIENTIST 1
It spins. The system pumps rotation.

They freeze the simulation. Scientist 1 opens a new window.

SCIENTIST 2
Can we build this from simple parts?

Scientist 1 drags atom symbols onto a workspace.

SCIENTIST 1
Not at first.

Scientist 2 drags in more atoms.

SCIENTIST 2
But if we add extra pieces.

The model clicks together.

SCIENTIST 1
Now it works. We call this fragile.

Scientist 2 writes a formula mixing positive and negative terms.

SCIENTIST 2
We describe it as atoms added and subtracted.

They turn to face each other.

SCIENTIST 1
This example shows a pattern.

Scientist 2 pulls up a chart of other cases.

SCIENTIST 2
All systems without edge states follow this rule. They either break into atoms or stay fragile.

Scientist 1 circles a conclusion on the board.

SCIENTIST 1
Edge states exist only when atoms cannot organize into simple groups.

Scientist 2 erases the grid and draws a single point.

SCIENTIST 2
We shrink the problem down to zero dimensions.

Scientist 1 writes out a list.

SCIENTIST 1
This gives us every possible case.

Scientist 2 adds a note at the bottom.

SCIENTIST 2
Interactions between particles reduce these options.

They both nod.
script_events.coling::28a6b262-a893-4fcb-a538-fc9aa5ad:
INT. OBSERVATORY - DAY

A SCIENTIST stands at a screen. The screen shows a graph.

SCIENTIST
The peak appears in matter spread across space.

The graph shifts. Numbers change at the top.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
It reaches out to a distance marked three point five.

A second scientist enters the room. She carries a folder.

SCIENTIST 2
Sound waves moved through early space. They left this mark.

The first scientist nods. He types on a keyboard. New data fills the screen.

SCIENTIST
We measure the peak with stars grouped together. The error is one percent.

Scientist 2 opens her folder. She pulls out a paper.

SCIENTIST 2
We also use light from far objects. The error grows to one point six percent.

A third person walks in. He holds a tablet.

SCIENTIST 3
The shape of space changes how we see size.

He taps the tablet. A sphere appears on the main screen.

SCIENTIST 3 (CONT'D)
Things look different when they sit far away. We use that fact.

Scientist 1 pulls up five new data points. They glow on the screen.

SCIENTIST
These come from the sky survey. Five spots at different distances.

Scientist 2 writes on a board. She puts down two names.

SCIENTIST 2
We test two ideas about the universe. One is standard. One is new.

The scientists gather around the board. Numbers appear below each name.

SCIENTIST 3
The new idea wins on the first test. Seventy five against twenty five.

Scientist 1 adds more numbers.

SCIENTIST
The standard idea wins on the second test. Eighty against twenty.

Scientist 2 steps back from the board.

SCIENTIST 2
We combine both tests now.

The final numbers appear. They are close.

SCIENTIST 3
Neither idea wins clearly.

All three scientists look at the screen.

SCIENTIST
We cannot say the universe speeds up. Not from this alone.
script_events.coling::2b392f9b-db4c-468a-bf65-fc00202e:
INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

A MAN stands at a whiteboard and picks up a marker.

MAN
Russia's economy crashed when the Soviet Union fell apart.

He draws a downward line on the board.

MAN (CONT'D)
Then the US banned imports of ammunition and firearms.

He adds another line going down.

MAN (CONT'D)
These bans kept pushing the economy lower.

A WOMAN enters the room and sits.

MAN (CONT'D)
Putin faced two choices.

He holds up one finger.

MAN (CONT'D)
He could watch his country die bit by bit.

He holds up a second finger.

MAN (CONT'D)
Or he could take action to save it.

The woman leans forward.

MAN (CONT'D)
The old USSR grabbed power by taking over other countries.

He draws arrows on the board pointing outward.

MAN (CONT'D)
They seized what those nations owned.

He circles several spots on the map.

MAN (CONT'D)
This brought them wealth and strength.

A SECOND MAN walks in and stands by the door.

MAN (CONT'D)
Putin decided to invade Ukraine for the same reason.

He taps the board with his marker.

MAN (CONT'D)
He refused to let his country fade away.

The woman shakes her head.

MAN (CONT'D)
I would not make this choice myself.

He sets down the marker.

MAN (CONT'D)
But his position has two sides.

The second man crosses his arms.

MAN (CONT'D)
He wants to save his nation, which gives him some justification.

He pauses and looks at both listeners.

MAN (CONT'D)
Yet war for money should never happen in my view.

The woman stands up.

MAN (CONT'D)
So his action remains unjustifiable at the same time.

The second man opens the door and all three exit the room.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::f4961832-eeb4-41fc-8a64-82c30107:
INT. SMALL APARTMENT - NIGHT

A young man sits at a laptop. He types the first line of his post.

YOUNG MAN
I do like Cowboy Bebop.

He pauses. His finger hovers over the keyboard.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
The animation looks good. The music sounds good too.

He leans back in his chair. The chair creaks.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
The action works. Sometimes all three parts come together.

He stands up and walks to the window. Rain starts to fall outside.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
The finale made my jaw drop. But problems exist.

He returns to the desk. He sits down again.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
I cannot call it a masterpiece. It works as a gateway show only.

He cracks his knuckles. The sound echoes in the quiet room.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
The characters cause many problems. Spike is great. Jet is great too.

A cat jumps onto the desk. The young man pets it absently.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
They make up two fifths of the crew. Ein gets introduced as a data dog.

The cat walks across the keyboard. The young man pushes it away gently.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
His intelligence goes nowhere. He becomes just a pet after that.

He takes a sip from a cold cup of coffee. He grimaces at the taste.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
Faye exhibits the worst traits. She acts bossy and greedy.

He sets the cup down. Coffee spills slightly on the desk.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
She obsesses over her beauty. She needs rescue often.

He wipes the spill with his sleeve. The stain spreads on the fabric.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
She hinders the group more than she helps. Her clothing reveals too much for fanservice.

The cat meows loudly. The young man ignores it this time.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
Ed hits or misses. She walks between endearing and annoying.

Lightning flashes outside. Thunder follows three seconds later.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
She receives little development after her introduction. The villain Vicious is especially bad.

The power flickers but stays on. The laptop screen dims briefly.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
He has little character. He wants more power and nothing else.

The young man rubs his tired eyes. His vision blurs momentarily.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
The show explores his backstory. It never establishes his motivation though.

He yawns widely. The clock on the wall shows midnight.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
Vicious ends up as just an evil guy in black. He fights well enough to make Spike struggle.

The cat jumps off the desk. It disappears into the dark hallway.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
He represents the syndicate Spike ran from. Five episodes involve him directly.

The young man types faster now. His words flow more quickly.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
Those episodes do not feel as spectacular as intended. The episode quality varies dramatically.

He stops typing. He reads what he wrote.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
Only five episodes build the overall story. Some episodes are fantastic like Waltz for Venus.

He nods to himself. He continues his thought.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
Ganymede Elegy works too. But some episodes feel dull.

The rain outside grows heavier. Water streams down the window.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
Reddit, help me appreciate this show. Tell me what I miss.

He clicks submit. The page loads. His post appears online.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::3bec38ad-9c98-4004-95a3-5b24858e:
INT. UNIVERSITY LECTURE HALL - DAY

A young man sits in the back row. He opens his laptop. A notification pops up on the screen about election day.

He closes the notification without reading it.

A friend leans over from the next seat.

FRIEND
You registered to vote yet?

YOUNG MAN
Nah. Not planning to.

The friend shrugs and turns back to his notes.

INT. STUDENT CAFETERIA - LATER

The young man buys coffee. A poster hangs on the wall behind the counter. It reads "It's only democracy if you vote, idiot."

He rolls his eyes.

A woman at a nearby table stands up. She walks to his table.

WOMAN
Hey, are you voting this year?

YOUNG MAN
No.

WOMAN
You're destroying our country's future.

She walks away before he can respond.

He sits down and pulls out his phone.

EXT. CAMPUS QUAD - AFTERNOON

Students walk between buildings. Green Party volunteers set up a table. They hold signs about free bus passes.

A volunteer approaches the young man.

VOLUNTEER
We're offering free bus passes outside peak hours if you vote for us.

YOUNG MAN
That's bribery.

VOLUNTEER
It's policy.

The young man walks past without taking a flyer.

INT. LECTURE HALL - NEXT DAY

The young man enters and finds his seat. A flyer sits on his desk. He picks it up.

The flyer lists all the parties. Each policy has a color code. Green means good. Red means bad.

The right wing parties show mostly red. The left wing parties show mostly green.

He crumples the flyer. He tosses it in the recycling bin.

The professor enters and starts the lecture.

INT. FLAT - EVENING

The young man sits on his couch. His flatmate comes home.

FLATMATE
Did you see the news? They're saying this is the most important election in history.

YOUNG MAN
They say that every time.

FLATMATE
But climate change—

YOUNG MAN
When Helen Clark left and John Key came in, did anything change for you?

The flatmate pauses.

FLATMATE
I guess not really.

YOUNG MAN
Exactly. Nothing will change for me either.

The flatmate sits down next to him.

FLATMATE
But you should still vote.

YOUNG MAN
Why? I don't know anything about it. I'd just pick randomly.

FLATMATE
Then research it.

YOUNG MAN
That takes time. I don't care enough.

The flatmate stands up and walks to the kitchen.

INT. FLAT - NIGHT

The young man scrolls through social media. A post appears showing the earth decaying. The word "VOTE" covers half the image.

He keeps scrolling.

Another post appears. It says people who don't vote are lazy.

He puts his phone down.

His other flatmate enters the room.

FLATMATE TWO
You voting?

YOUNG MAN
No.

FLATMATE TWO
Fair enough. Want a beer?

The young man nods.

Flatmate Two goes to the fridge and returns with two bottles.

FLATMATE TWO
People get too worked up about this stuff.

YOUNG MAN
The electoral commission acts like everyone cares.

FLATMATE TWO
They're all political nerds. They don't get it.

The young man opens his beer.

YOUNG MAN
It's like forcing everyone to watch rugby.

FLATMATE TWO
Actually, the All Blacks losing would affect you more.

YOUNG MAN
Exactly my point.

They both drink.

The television turns on across the room. An ad plays encouraging people to vote.

FLATMATE TWO
See what I mean?

The young man changes the channel.

A different ad plays. This one also tells people to vote.

He turns the television off completely.

The room goes quiet.

FLATMATE TWO
You know what bugs me most?

YOUNG MAN
What?

FLATMATE TWO
They guilt people into voting. Then those people vote without knowing anything. Then politicians just manipulate them.

YOUNG MAN
That's worse than not voting at all.

FLATMATE TWO
Way worse.

They finish their beers in silence.

The young man stands up and walks to the window. He looks out at the street below.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::365ba259-c2eb-480e-84d9-eab251a4:
INT. ONLINE FORUM - DAY

A USER types at a desk. Words appear on screen.

USER (V.O.)
I don't see the problem here.

The USER clicks a video link. A clip plays showing the procedure.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
Nobody gets hurt from what I hear.

The USER pauses the video. They open a new tab.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
They can't drown if you do it right.

A testimonial page loads. The USER scrolls down.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
It messes with your head, not your body.

The USER watches another clip. A reporter volunteers for a demonstration.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
People even try it on purpose.

The screen shows historical torture devices. The USER clicks away quickly.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
Nobody would volunteer for thumb screws.

The USER opens an article about physical scars. Photos appear.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
Those things damage you for life.

The USER closes that tab. They return to the forum.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
This thing just plays with your mind.

The USER types a new sentence. Their hands pause over the keyboard.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
America wanted a clean method.

The USER resumes typing. Words fill the text box.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
They found one that works without marks.

The USER leans back in their chair. They stare at the screen.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
It feels real but stays fake.

The USER sits forward again. They add another paragraph.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
I never served in uniform myself.

A family photo sits on the desk. The USER glances at it.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
My relatives did though, both sides.

The USER picks up the photo. They set it back down.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
I learned plenty from them growing up.

The USER returns to typing. Their pace increases.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
Maybe I miss something obvious here.

The USER stops. They read over what they wrote.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
Bigger problems exist in this world.

The USER clicks submit. The post goes live.

USER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
The right wing never says this part.

A MODERATOR account appears below. A pinned message posts automatically.

MODERATOR (TEXT)
Welcome to our community space today.

The message expands. Rules appear in a list.

MODERATOR (TEXT) (CONT'D)
Please review our guidelines before participating.

New text generates. Instructions about reporting show up.

MODERATOR (TEXT) (CONT'D)
Flag rule breaks instead of downvoting them.

Another line appears. A reminder about voting posts.

MODERATOR (TEXT) (CONT'D)
Downvotes serve no purpose for changing minds.

A wiki link populates. Common topics fill the page.

MODERATOR (TEXT) (CONT'D)
Check our archives before starting new threads.

A contact button highlights. The cursor hovers over it.

MODERATOR (TEXT) (CONT'D)
Message us with any questions you have.

The post sits waiting. No replies appear yet.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::4b504a77-e4f6-447f-996a-b39d54b5:
INT. NEWS STUDIO - DAY

A news anchor sits at a desk and begins speaking.

NEWS ANCHOR
Yemen's Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi appears on television screens across the region.

INT. BROADCAST STUDIO - DAY

Al-Houthi leans forward into the camera.

AL-HOUTHI
Our fighters will stay in the main cities and government buildings. We will not leave.

He pounds his fist on the table.

AL-HOUTHI (CONT'D)
Anyone who thinks we will surrender is dreaming.

EXT. SANAA STREETS - DAY

Saudi jets roar overhead. Bombs explode in the distance.

INT. SAUDI MILITARY HEADQUARTERS - DAY

Saudi Brigadier General Ahmed Asiri walks to a map on the wall.

ASIRI
Our airstrikes have destroyed their central command. We hit their communications networks hard.

He circles several areas with a marker.

EXT. YEMENI CAPITAL - JANUARY (FLASHBACK)

Houthi fighters pour into Sanaa. They storm government buildings.

INT. PRESIDENTIAL PALACE - JANUARY (FLASHBACK)

President Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi flees through a back entrance.

INT. SAUDI COMMAND CENTER - DAY (PRESENT)

Asiri points to a screen showing strike data.

ASIRI
We have launched two thousand three hundred airstrikes since March twenty-six. Operation Decisive Storm continues.

EXT. REFUGEE CAMP - DAY

Aid workers carry bodies on stretchers. A doctor checks a clipboard.

DOCTOR
Over seven hundred dead since mid-March. The violence grows worse each day.

INT. HOUTHI STRONGHOLD - DAY

Al-Houthi addresses his commanders.

AL-HOUTHI
The Yemeni people stand with us. They will fight back against these attacks.

He walks to a window.

AL-HOUTHI (CONT'D)
Our children and women are dying. We will not listen to any voices or cries from our enemies.

EXT. MILITARY BASE - DAY

General AbdulRahman AlHalili removes his old insignia. He pins on new badges showing loyalty to Hadi.

AIDE
Sir, your ten thousand troops are ready to switch sides.

AlHalili nods and walks toward waiting vehicles.

INT. SAFE HOUSE - DAY

President Hadi meets with Saudi officials.

HADI
I am still the legitimate leader. I will return to Yemen soon.

He signs documents on the table.

EXT. COASTAL CITY - DAY

Boats arrive carrying desperate refugees. People wade through the water toward shore.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::17ad7e76-2fa1-4c9b-a42b-44a53287:
INT. DEBATE CLASSROOM - DAY

A STUDENT stands at a podium. He picks up a piece of paper.

STUDENT
I haven't made up my mind yet. But I'll argue against gay marriage today.

He sets the paper down and looks at the class.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
I chose this side for two reasons. First, I agree with it less, so I can practice making weak arguments. Second, the other side needs to prove their case.

He clicks a remote. A screen lights up behind him.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Watch this video. It's two minutes long.

The video plays. Students watch in silence. The video ends and the screen goes dark.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
That argument shows something. The people who want to change marriage must prove why.

He walks to the side of the podium.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
When someone says "Why not?" they dodge the question. They shift the burden away from themselves.

A student in the front row raises her hand. The speaker ignores her and continues.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
People say this is about equality. The Constitution gives everyone the same rights to life and liberty and happiness. But equality is a distraction here.

He picks up a marker and writes on the whiteboard.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Marriage is not a privilege. It's not a right that covers all relationships. Marriage exists because of procreation.

He underlines the word he just wrote.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Gay couples can love each other and commit to each other. But they cannot procreate by definition.

A student in the back shifts in her seat. Another student whispers something.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Some straight couples can't have kids either. Old couples get married. Infertile couples get married. But the video explains why that's different. Exceptions exist, but they don't change the definition. The norm doesn't get defined by what breaks the rule.

He caps the marker and sets it down.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
This isn't like women getting the vote. It's not like ending slavery. Those were real equality issues.

He walks back to the center.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
People ask a question. They say if two people love each other, why can't they marry?

He shakes his head.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Love has nothing to do with marriage criteria. Romantic love doesn't matter either. If love is your only rule, then incest becomes acceptable.

Several students gasp. One stands up and then sits back down.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Some will say incest is different. They bring up power imbalances. They mention genetic defects. But power problems happen in any relationship. Straight couples have them. Gay couples have them. Incestuous couples have them too.

He counts on his fingers.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Marriage law shouldn't be based on power dynamics. Also, incestuous couples don't need to have children. They can adopt instead. They might be infertile. They might even be gay themselves.

A teacher in the corner writes notes on a clipboard.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Maybe someone thinks incest should be allowed for marriage too. You can argue that if you want. But you have to prove it.

He points at the class.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Don't tell me "why would you care?" That argument means nothing. Just because something doesn't hurt anyone doesn't mean we change institutions randomly.

He walks to the other side of the room.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Even utilitarian logic fails here. Gay people can have long relationships without marriage. They can be romantic and sexual and fulfilled. Redefining marriage for one group's happiness is like giving in to lobbyists so they feel better.

A student raises both hands. The speaker waves him off.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Most arguments use emotion or popularity. The phrase "gay rights" makes it sound like we imprison them. The word "homophobe" was invented to shame opponents. This issue is popular now. Many opponents are religious fundamentalists who argue badly. But popularity doesn't make something right.

He returns to the podium.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Imagine a movement to legalize incestuous marriage. Imagine videos and websites glorifying those couples. If it became popular, people would support it.

He closes his folder.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Why is one sexual deviation more valid for marriage than another? I use that term with complete respect.

He sits down.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
My view changed. I was already mostly there when I started.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::ef2146c2-c9fe-4563-b26a-b39f1bb9:
INT. FAMILY HOME - DAY

A cake sits on the table. CHER LAIR stands next to it. Six boys and her husband STEPHEN stand around the room. A FRIEND holds a phone up to record.

Cher picks up a knife. She sets the blade against the frosting. The blade cuts down through the top layer. She pulls the knife toward her body. The slice separates from the rest of the cake.

Cher lifts the slice onto a plate. Pink sponge shows on the cut edge. Her mouth opens wide. She drops the plate. The plate hits the table with a bang.

Cher screams. The boys jump back. Stephen puts his hands on his head. The friend keeps the phone pointed at Cher.

Cher stumbles backward. Her legs give out. She falls to her knees on the floor. Her hands press against her face.

She gasps for air. She says the words oh my god. She says them again. She says them five more times. Her voice gets louder each time.

The boys start to clap. Stephen walks over to Cher. He puts his hand on her shoulder. She looks up at him with wet eyes.

A REPORTER appears in the room with a microphone. Cher stands up from the floor. She wipes her face with her hands.

The reporter asks Cher a question. Cher talks about baby number three. She talks about baby number four. She thought one would be a girl. Then baby five came. Then baby six arrived. She gave up hope after that.

The reporter walks away. A BAKER enters carrying flour on her apron. The baker explains she got the scan results on Monday. She made the chocolate cake with pink layers inside. The baker leaves through the front door.

Cher sits down in a chair. She talks to the camera about her worries. The house is full of boys. The girl will grow up surrounded by brothers. But Cher smiles when she mentions future plans.

She lists activities out loud. She will take her daughter to see Cinderella. They will get pedicures together. They will get manicures at the salon. They will shop for a prom dress years from now.

Stephen walks back into the frame. He announces the due date is in August. Cher shrugs because they have not picked a name yet.

The friend stops recording. She uploads the video to the internet. The view count climbs past one hundred thousand. Comments fill the screen below.

One person types that the video is awesome. Another person says the girl is lucky. Six brothers will protect her forever. More comments appear with congratulations messages.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::a1534ce8-2639-4c7c-b509-3d430b55:
INT. GEORGIA SOUTHERN UNIVERSITY - HANNER FIELDHOUSE - NIGHT

The rap trio Migos performs on stage. Students dance and cheer in the crowd. Two tour buses sit parked outside the arena in the lot.

Police officers arrive at the buses. They smell marijuana coming from the vehicles. The officers wait for the right moment to act.

Quavious Marshall raps into his microphone. Kirschnick Ball joins him for the next verse. Kiari Cephus moves across the stage with energy.

Outside, investigators approach the first bus. They open the doors and step inside. Flashlights sweep across the interior space.

An officer finds a gun under a seat. Another officer discovers bags of marijuana in a storage compartment. A third officer locates pills in a cabinet.

More officers search the second bus now. They pull out additional firearms from a hidden spot. They bag the drugs as evidence of crimes.

The concert continues inside the fieldhouse. Over a thousand students pack the venue. Nobody knows what happens outside yet.

The final song ends on stage. The crowd screams and applauds loudly. The three rappers wave to their fans.

Police officers enter the arena through side doors. They walk toward the stage with purpose. The band members notice them approaching now.

Officers escort Quavious Marshall off the stage first. They place handcuffs on Kirschnick Ball next. Kiari Cephus receives handcuffs last of all.

Students watch in confusion and shock. Some pull out phones to record video. The officers lead the rappers outside quickly.

Squad cars flash red and blue lights. The three band members sit in separate vehicles. About a dozen other people get arrested too.

EXT. POLICE STATION - DAY

The rappers appear before a judge. The judge reads the charges against them. Drug possession charges come first on the list.

The prosecutor mentions firearms in a school zone. The judge adds possession during a crime commission. The bail hearing moves to its conclusion.

The judge denies bond for all three. The rappers return to their cells immediately. Their tour must stop before it starts.

INT. EMPTY CONCERT VENUE - DAY

Workers clean up the KSU Convocation Center. The stage sits empty with no performers. Tickets for tonight get refunded to buyers.

Other venues in Wisconsin cancel their shows. Ohio and Michigan dates disappear from schedules. Pennsylvania and New York fans receive disappointment news.

The management team ignores phone calls completely. Emails from reporters go unanswered as well. The Versace and Fight Night hits play on radio stations still.
script_events.coling::23d0bd02-f2a0-4752-971c-cac75280:
INT. PARTY - NIGHT

PERSON1 stands near the bar. PERSON2 sits slumped in a chair.

PERSON1
Rocky, get up. Walk over to that woman by the window.

PERSON2 shakes his head.

PERSON2
She reads books. I can tell.

PERSON1 moves closer.

PERSON1
Then pick someone else. Anyone.

PERSON2 crosses his arms.

PERSON2
I need a wife who cooks my meals. That woman won't do it.

PERSON1 laughs.

PERSON1
The world changed. Women have jobs now.

PERSON2 leans back.

PERSON2
I meet plenty of old-fashioned girls. Just not here tonight.

PERSON1 raises an eyebrow.

PERSON1
What else do you want?

PERSON2 counts on his fingers.

PERSON2
She stays home. She cleans. She watches kids.

PERSON1 sits down across from him.

PERSON1
What will you do when you get home?

PERSON2 shrugs.

PERSON2
I eat dinner. I turn on the TV. I take out the trash once a week.

PERSON1 stands up fast.

PERSON1
You will die alone. A study came out last month. Forty percent of wives say their husbands do nothing at home.

PERSON2 waves his hand.

PERSON2
That's just who I am. Now tell me what you want.

PERSON1 walks to the window.

PERSON1
I want someone who talks to people. Who cares about them. Who doesn't judge them for being different.

PERSON2 rolls his eyes.

PERSON2
Good for you. I still think my way works better.

PERSON2 gets up from the chair.

PERSON2
I'm going home. I'll heat up a frozen dinner. Rusty will keep me company.

PERSON1 grabs his coat.

PERSON1
If I stay with you, I'll never meet anyone either.

PERSON2 walks toward the door.

PERSON1 calls after him.

PERSON1
Pet Rusty for me.

PERSON2 leaves. PERSON1 turns back to the party.
script_events.coling::49a2d576-81e8-4b16-889d-beb4a986:
INT. BRONX APARTMENT BUILDING LOBBY - NIGHT

Six teenagers stand in a circle passing a joint. Smoke drifts toward the ceiling.

A neighbor walks past and frowns at them.

EXT. STREET - NIGHT

The neighbor pulls out a phone and dials.

INT. POLICE STATION - NIGHT

A dispatcher takes the call and writes notes on a pad.

Two officers grab their hats and walk toward the door.

EXT. BRONX APARTMENT BUILDING - NIGHT

A patrol car pulls up to the curb. The headlights shut off.

INT. APARTMENT BUILDING LOBBY - NIGHT

The teenagers hear footsteps outside. One boy drops the joint and crushes it with his shoe.

The front door swings open. Two officers step inside.

The teenagers bolt toward the stairwell. Their shoes pound on the steps.

INT. STAIRWELL - NIGHT

HAKEEM KUTA, 17, races up the stairs with five friends behind him. The officers chase them, shouting commands to stop.

The group reaches the top floor. Hakeem pushes open the roof door.

EXT. ROOFTOP - NIGHT

The teenagers spill onto the roof. Wind whips their clothes.

Four of them leap across a gap to the next building. They land safely and keep running.

Hakeem and a 14-year-old boy reach a dividing wall. They stop and turn around.

The officers emerge from the door behind them. They advance slowly with hands raised.

Hakeem backs up against the wall. His friend stands beside him breathing hard.

Hakeem climbs over a three-foot wall without looking down first.

His foot finds nothing but air on the other side. He drops and his hands grab the ledge.

The 14-year-old lunges forward and seizes Hakeem's jacket. He pulls hard but Hakeem's weight drags him toward the edge.

Officer Edmundo Rivera runs forward and wraps both arms around the 14-year-old boy. He braces his legs and holds tight.

The jacket fabric rips in the boy's hands. Hakeem falls six stories down.

His body hits the pavement in the courtyard below. The sound echoes off the walls.

The officers run back to the stairwell and pound down the steps.

EXT. COURTYARD - NIGHT

The officers burst through a door and rush to where Hakeem lies motionless.

One officer kneels and checks for a pulse. The other radios for an ambulance.

Sirens wail in the distance growing louder.

INT. ST. BARNABAS HOSPITAL - NIGHT

Doctors wheel Hakeem through double doors. Machines beep around him.

INT. HOSPITAL WAITING ROOM - DAY

MUNIR KUTA, 42, sits with his head in his hands. A doctor enters and speaks quietly to him.

Munir begins to cry. The doctor places a hand on his shoulder.

EXT. APARTMENT BUILDING LOBBY - DAY

A detective picks up a small bag of marijuana from the floor. He seals it in an evidence pouch.

Another detective closes his notebook. No citation forms sit on the table.

The detective walks out the front door and the lobby stands empty again.
script_events.coling::724b2f69-4d19-4d08-9bbd-53e01537:
INT. POLICE STATION - DAY

A desk sergeant takes a phone call and writes down an address on Valentine Avenue.

EXT. BRONX APARTMENT BUILDING - NIGHT

Two police cars pull up to a six-story building in Mott Haven.

INT. APARTMENT BUILDING LOBBY - CONTINUOUS

Four officers enter through the front doors and spot six teenagers sitting on benches.

The teens jump up and sprint toward the stairwell.

The officers chase after them and begin climbing the stairs.

EXT. BUILDING ROOFTOP - CONTINUOUS

The teenagers burst through the rooftop door and scatter in different directions.

Three teens leap across a gap to an adjacent building and disappear.

Hakeem Kuta, seventeen years old, runs toward a corner with his fourteen-year-old friend beside him.

A dividing wall blocks their escape route and traps them.

The officers emerge onto the roof and move toward the two boys.

Kuta climbs over a three-foot wall without looking down first.

His feet find no surface on the other side and he begins to fall.

The younger boy grabs Kuta's jacket with both hands and holds tight.

Kuta dangles sixty feet above an alleyway between the buildings.

Officer Edmundo Rivera rushes forward and seizes the younger boy around the waist.

The fabric tears and slips through the boy's fingers.

Kuta drops through the air and hits the pavement six stories below.

The officers run back down the stairwell to reach the courtyard.

EXT. COURTYARD - CONTINUOUS

Kuta lies motionless on the ground with blood pooling beneath his head.

An ambulance arrives with sirens wailing and paramedics jump out.

They load Kuta onto a stretcher and speed away.

INT. ST. BARNABAS HOSPITAL - NIGHT

Doctors rush Kuta into an emergency room and begin working on him.

Machines beep and monitors display his vital signs.

A doctor places him on life support and connects multiple tubes.

INT. HOSPITAL WAITING ROOM - DAY

Munir Kuta, forty-two, sits in a chair with his head in his hands.

A nurse approaches and speaks quietly to him about his son's condition.

INT. HOSPITAL ROOM - SATURDAY MORNING

The monitors show flat lines at eleven o'clock.

A doctor disconnects the life support equipment and covers Kuta with a sheet.

INT. POLICE STATION - DAY

Spokesman Stephen Davis gives a statement to reporters about the incident.

He explains that officers found marijuana in the lobby after the fall.

He confirms that no summonses were written that night.

EXT. KUTA FAMILY HOME - DAY

Munir Kuta stands on his front steps and talks to news cameras.

He says his son was a junior at Bronx Envision Academy.

He states that Hakeem stayed away from trouble and never used drugs.

He wipes tears from his face and calls his boy a nice kid.

INT. POLICE HEADQUARTERS - DAY

An official tells the press that no arrests were planned that evening.

He says officers only wanted the group to stop smoking and leave the building.

EXT. VALENTINE AVENUE - DAY

The building stands quiet with yellow tape across the courtyard entrance.
script_events.coling::65648d18-be4d-475d-bcab-2fbcdb8a:
INT. ENGINEERING OFFICE - DAY

A PROFESSOR stands at a whiteboard. STUDENTS sit at desks with notebooks open.

PROFESSOR
The Atlantic Ocean stretches wider than the entire United States.

He draws a line across the board.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Storms roll in from the west.

A STUDENT raises her hand.

STUDENT
What about a bridge?

The Professor picks up a piece of chalk.

PROFESSOR
Salt water eats through concrete.

He writes the word CORROSION on the board.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Steel rusts even faster in ocean air.

A second student leans forward in his seat.

SECOND STUDENT
Could we sink posts into the seabed?

PROFESSOR
The ocean floor drops thousands of feet down.

He draws a vertical line downward.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Our posts would never reach bottom.

The first student flips a page in her notebook.

STUDENT
What about floating sections?

PROFESSOR
Waves would tear them apart.

He makes a ripping motion with his hands.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
The bridge would shake until it broke.

A third student speaks up from the back row.

THIRD STUDENT
People could drive across though.

PROFESSOR
The trip would take days.

He walks to a map on the wall.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Cars run out of gas.

The second student taps his pen on the desk.

SECOND STUDENT
We could build fuel stations.

PROFESSOR
Ships would need to bring fuel out.

He points to the middle of the ocean on the map.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
That costs more than flying.

The students write notes. One closes her notebook.

STUDENT
Then we dig a tunnel instead.

PROFESSOR
Water pressure increases with every foot of depth.

He draws arrows pointing down on the board.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Your ears pop when you swim to the pool bottom.

A student nods in recognition.

SECOND STUDENT
This would be worse.

PROFESSOR
Multiply that pain by ten thousand.

He underlines the number he writes.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
One crack appears in the wall.

The students lean back in their chairs.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Water blasts through like a laser beam.

THIRD STUDENT
The whole tunnel floods.

PROFESSOR
Everyone inside drowns within minutes.

The first student raises her hand again.

STUDENT
What about air to breathe?

PROFESSOR
Fans would need to push fresh air for thousands of miles.

He walks back to the whiteboard.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
The tunnel sections get built on land first.

A student sketches in his notebook.

SECOND STUDENT
Then workers lower them down.

PROFESSOR
The joints between sections create weak spots.

He taps the board where two lines meet.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Pressure finds every gap.

The third student shifts in his seat.

THIRD STUDENT
Cars still need fuel for the drive.

PROFESSOR
The same problem exists underground.

A student in the front row speaks for the first time.

FOURTH STUDENT
Has anyone tried to build this?

PROFESSOR
Engineers have drawn up plans.

He pulls a folder from his desk.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Politicians talk about it sometimes.

The students exchange glances.

STUDENT
Will it ever happen?

PROFESSOR
People in the eighteen hundreds thought space travel was impossible.

He opens the folder and shows diagrams.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
We reached the moon anyway.

SECOND STUDENT
So it could be done.

PROFESSOR
Technology improves every year.

The Professor closes the folder.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Someone would need to pay for it first.

THIRD STUDENT
Who would want to drive that far?

PROFESSOR
Planes cross the ocean in hours.

A student checks her watch.

STUDENT
A tunnel trip would take days.

PROFESSOR
No country would claim it either.

He points to international waters on the map.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
The ocean belongs to everyone.

SECOND STUDENT
And to no one.

The Professor sets down his chalk. The students close their notebooks. Class ends.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::37e384a6-d2b8-444e-ac7f-d4288c17:
INT. PARALYMPIC CLASSIFICATION OFFICE - DAY

A CLASSIFIER sits at a desk reviewing forms. An ATHLETE enters the room.

CLASSIFIER
We combine categories when we don't have enough riders. The cerebral palsy group races alongside the amputee group.

The Classifier stamps a form.

CLASSIFIER (CONT'D)
But we score each group separately. Most bike events do this to save time.

The Athlete nods and sits down.

CLASSIFIER (CONT'D)
The Paralympics uses many rules to keep competition fair. We don't have many disabled athletes to start with.

A SECOND ATHLETE wheels into the room in a wheelchair.

CLASSIFIER (CONT'D)
Each disability creates different problems. Amputees move faster than paralyzed athletes in wheelchair events because they weigh less.

The Second Athlete parks near the desk.

CLASSIFIER (CONT'D)
Sometimes we must let one type have an edge. Otherwise we can't hold the race at all.

The Classifier stands and walks to a chart on the wall.

CLASSIFIER (CONT'D)
The regular Olympics works the same way. Tall players win more games in basketball. Nobody tries to change that fact.

The Classifier points to different sections of the chart.

CLASSIFIER (CONT'D)
We sort athletes by what their body can do, not by their diagnosis. Cycling has four groups.

The Classifier taps the first section.

CLASSIFIER (CONT'D)
Upper body problems go here. One limb missing but both legs work goes there.

The Classifier moves down the chart.

CLASSIFIER (CONT'D)
One leg injury means you pedal with one leg only. Both legs affected makes the fourth group.

The First Athlete stands to look closer.

CLASSIFIER (CONT'D)
Cerebral palsy affecting legs puts you in that last group with anyone else who has two bad legs.

A DOCTOR enters carrying a clipboard.

DOCTOR
International classification requires a full exam. We test how the disability limits each athlete. This stops people from cheating their way into easier categories.

The Doctor begins the examination.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::5895f991-9d37-49fe-9f39-eeff324a:
INT. NATURE DOCUMENTARY STUDIO - DAY

A SCIENTIST stands before a screen showing an opossum.

SCIENTIST
The animal lies still on the ground.

The opossum's body goes limp.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Glands open under its skin.

Liquid oozes from the animal's fur.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
A foul smell spreads through the air.

A fox approaches and sniffs the carcass.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The predator backs away from the body.

The fox turns and walks into the brush.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Many hunters cannot digest rotten flesh.

The fox disappears behind a tree.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The predator moves on to find other prey.

The opossum opens one eye.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Animals lack the ability to understand deception.

A deer stands in a clearing, looking weak.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
A wolf spots the deer from a distance.

The wolf stops and watches the deer closely.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Signs of illness make the wolf hesitate.

The wolf sniffs the air and growls low.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Disease could pass from prey to hunter.

The wolf turns away and trots off.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The sick animal survives another day.

A man throws a punch in self-defense.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
His body floods with stress hormones.

The attacker falls to the floor motionless.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The threat ends and calm returns.

The man steps back and breathes hard.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
He cannot tell if death is real or fake.

A buffalo charges at a lion.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The lion drops and lies completely still.

The buffalo slows and stops its charge.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The urge to fight fades from the buffalo.

The buffalo walks away across the plain.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Movement triggers the instinct to attack.

A rabbit freezes in front of a bear.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The bear loses focus on the rabbit.

The bear wanders off toward the forest.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
A wolf pack circles a hiker who falls.

The wolves move closer to the body.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Their hunger does not fade with stillness.

The wolves bare their teeth and advance.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The meal begins.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::6ea6d618-d59e-455d-a265-490e1418:
INT. COMPUTER LAB - DAY

A TEACHER stands at a whiteboard. STUDENTS sit at desks with notebooks open.

TEACHER
A program can crash for many reasons. Let me show you the first one.

She draws a fraction on the board with zero as the bottom number.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
You learned in kindergarten that you cannot divide by zero. The answer does not exist.

A STUDENT raises his hand.

STUDENT
What happens if a program tries it?

TEACHER
The computer sends back an error message to the program.

She writes "ERROR" in red marker.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
If the program cannot deal with that message, it crashes right there.

The teacher erases the board and writes "ACCESS VIOLATION" at the top.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Every program gets permission to use certain memory locations only.

She draws boxes on the board and colors some green and some red.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The red boxes are forbidden territory.

A program tries to read from a red box in her diagram.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The computer sends another error message.

She adds another red "ERROR" notation.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Again, if the program cannot handle this, it crashes.

Two students, BILLY and SARAH, walk to the front. Billy holds a red block. Sarah holds a blue block.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Now watch these two. They will show you deadlock.

SARAH
I want your red block, Billy. Give it to me first, then I will hand you my blue block.

BILLY
No way. You give me your blue block first. Then I will give you my red block.

They stand frozen, staring at each other. Ten seconds pass.

TEACHER
They will wait forever like this. Neither one moves forward.

She claps her hands.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
When deadlock happens inside a program, everything freezes. You must kill the program and start over.

Billy and Sarah return to their seats. The teacher draws a ball being tossed between two stick figures.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Sometimes one part of a program throws an exception like tossing a ball.

She draws hands reaching to catch the ball.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Another part should catch that exception and fix the problem.

She draws the ball falling to the ground with no hands catching it.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
But if no part catches it, a dialog box appears on your screen.

She mimes clicking a mouse.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The program shuts down immediately after that.

A student raises her hand.

STUDENT 2
Why do programs have these problems?

TEACHER
Bugs cause all these crashes. Bugs are just mistakes in the code.

She walks to a different part of the board.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Some programs contain more bugs than others.

STUDENT 2
Why is that?

TEACHER
Maybe the programmers rushed through their work. Maybe they skipped important tests. Maybe the program grew too complex for them to predict every possible situation.

She sets down her marker.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Every bug is a place where the programmer did not think of something that could happen.

The bell rings. Students close their notebooks and stand up.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Next class we will learn how programmers find and fix these bugs.

The students file out of the room. The teacher erases the board.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::3dd39352-d471-4ab9-bd50-b7345fc1:
INT. TAX CONSULTANT'S OFFICE - DAY

A CLIENT sits across from a TAX CONSULTANT at a desk.

TAX CONSULTANT
What you're asking about is a wealth tax or capital tax.

The consultant opens a folder.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
These taxes target what you own, not what you earned this year.

The client leans forward.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Italy taxes people who own land in other countries.

The consultant pulls out a document.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Canada used to tax corporations based on their assets until about five to ten years ago.

The consultant flips to another page.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Switzerland taxes your total wealth if it goes above a set amount.

The client nods slowly.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
The US has one version called the Estate Tax.

The consultant writes a number on paper.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
It taxes everything you own when you die.

The client frowns.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
The threshold has jumped around a lot over the last twenty years.

The consultant circles the number.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Right now it sits around five million dollars.

The client relaxes slightly.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
These taxes will probably spread to more places.

The consultant closes the folder.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Don't panic when you see the initial price tag.

The client picks up a pen.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
A wealth tax could replace part of your income tax without raising your total bill.

The consultant draws two columns.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Say you owe ten thousand in income tax this year.

The consultant writes in the first column.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Next year a two thousand dollar capital tax gets added.

The consultant writes in the second column.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Your income tax drops to eight thousand.

The consultant taps both columns.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
You still pay the same total amount.

The client sets down the pen.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Whether these taxes work better is an economics question, not a personal finance one.

The consultant stands up.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Any money your savings earn gets taxed as income alongside your wages.

The consultant walks to the door.

TAX CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
A wealth tax would come on top of that income tax on your earnings.

The consultant opens the door for the client.
script_events.coling::a9b058a8-5ce8-448f-820a-6ffba640:
INT. CLASSROOM - DAY

A TEACHER stands at a whiteboard and draws a cone shape.

TEACHER
Vision works like a cone. It starts at your eye and spreads out.

She marks an angle between two lines.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The angle between these edges is the field of view.

A STUDENT raises his hand.

STUDENT
Pro gamers change that setting to see more.

The teacher nods and pulls up an image on the projector.

TEACHER
This game runs at forty-five degrees normally.

She clicks a button and the image shifts.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Now it jumps to sixty-five degrees.

The sides of the screen expand outward.

STUDENT
The trailers on the left and right appear now.

TEACHER
But look closer at those trailers.

The student leans forward.

STUDENT
They seem farther away than before.

TEACHER
The player hasn't moved at all.

She circles the trailers with a laser pointer.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
A wider angle makes distant things shrink faster.

Another STUDENT speaks up from the back.

SECOND STUDENT
So narrow angles do the opposite?

TEACHER
Exactly. Objects far away look bigger.

She switches to a photo of Earth and Moon.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The DSCOVR camera uses only zero point six one degrees.

The class murmurs in surprise.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
That tight focus pulls in light from far away.

SECOND STUDENT
The Moon and Earth look similar in size here.

TEACHER
Distance between them matters less with that narrow view.

She turns off the projector and faces the class.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Everyone hold your hand up to your face.

The students comply.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Your hand covers your monitor from where you sit.

She walks to the back of the room.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Now I step backward and my hand shrinks.

The students watch her move.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
At some point my hand and the monitor shrink together.

A THIRD STUDENT frowns.

THIRD STUDENT
Why does that happen?

TEACHER
My distance from both objects becomes much greater than the distance between them.

She returns to the front.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Angular size depends on how far you stand from things.

THIRD STUDENT
So the first Moon photo was taken close to it?

TEACHER
The Apollo camera was near the Moon and far from Earth.

She pulls up another image.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The DSCOVR satellite sits far from both bodies.

SECOND STUDENT
That's why they match their true size ratio?

TEACHER
The Earth does shrink in the second photo.

She zooms in on the comparison.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
But the Moon shrank much faster.

The first student raises his hand again.

STUDENT
Is it like a zoom lens?

TEACHER
The EPIC camera was designed to watch Earth from deep space.

She writes on the board.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Apollo cameras served general purposes instead.

SECOND STUDENT
What makes the zoom work?

TEACHER
Focal length controls how big the image forms on the sensor.

She draws a lens diagram.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Sensor size then determines the field of view.

THIRD STUDENT
And the pixels?

TEACHER
Pixel count sets the resolution of each image.

She erases part of the diagram.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Film cameras had resolution limits from their chemistry.

STUDENT
The lens adds its own limit too?

The teacher nods and caps her marker.

TEACHER
You can also crop a large image down.

She clicks to the final slide.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The DSCOVR image uses almost its complete original frame.

The bell rings and students gather their books.
script_events.coling::8eb96c1a-6193-4f0f-843b-4b91efbe:
INT. TRADING FLOOR - DAY

A TRADER sits at a desk. He opens an email. The email shows two options got exercised. He checks the time stamp. Both exercises happened today.

He picks up the phone. A BROKER answers.

TRADER
Can I lose money on both?

BROKER
Not on the same day. Exercises happen fast but assignments come later.

The Broker clicks a link on his screen. A webpage loads. It explains the assignment process.

BROKER (CONT'D)
The clearinghouse processes assignments after the market closes.

The clock on the wall shows four o'clock. The closing bell rings. The Trader hangs up and waits.

Night falls outside the window. His computer pings. Two assignment notices appear. He reads them both.

The first notice says someone put stock to him. The second notice says his stock got called away. He opens his position screen. It shows zero shares.

He opens his options screen. Both options disappeared.

He clicks on his cash balance. The number changes. Fifteen hundred dollars came in from selling stock. Thirteen hundred dollars went out to buy stock. His account shows two hundred dollars more than before.

He leans back. He bought at thirteen and sold at fifteen. The position forced him to buy at thirteen and sell at fifteen. Other people decided when.

His phone rings. A CLIENT speaks.

CLIENT
How do I lose money?

TRADER
One option gets exercised but not the other.

He types numbers on a calculator. If the stock drops below thirteen, nobody buys from him at fifteen. But someone sells to him at thirteen. If the stock rises above fifteen, nobody sells to him at thirteen. But someone buys from him at fifteen.

CLIENT
When do I make money?

TRADER
Neither gets exercised and you keep the premium. Or both get exercised and you keep the gap plus the premium.

The Trader stands and walks to the window. Early exercise rarely happens. It happens when options go deep in the money. Both going deep seems unlikely.

He checks historical data on his tablet. The stock moved fast yesterday. It crossed both strikes during the day. Expiration approaches tomorrow. Time value dropped to nearly nothing.
script_events.coling::59aec439-babf-4d21-b03b-4f331a96:
INT. BANK OFFICE - DAY

A CUSTOMER sits across from a BANK OFFICER at a desk.

BANK OFFICER
You need to call us first.

The Customer picks up a credit card statement and points to a line.

CUSTOMER
What happens when I send you money?

BANK OFFICER
We put the minimum toward your low rate debt. The rest goes to your high rate debt.

The Customer writes this down on a notepad.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
That's the law here. Other countries do it differently.

The Customer looks up from the notepad.

CUSTOMER
So you don't split it evenly?

BANK OFFICER
Not unless you ask. Never assume.

The Bank Officer pulls out a calculator and enters numbers.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
Say you owe six thousand dollars total.

The Customer leans forward to watch the screen.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
Five thousand sits at thirteen point five percent. One thousand sits at twenty two percent.

The Bank Officer presses more keys.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
You pay six hundred dollars this month.

The Customer nods and makes another note.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
We take five hundred off the purchase debt. We take one hundred off the cash advance.

The Bank Officer circles a figure on a paper.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
Your average rate works out to fifteen percent.

CUSTOMER
How did you get that number?

BANK OFFICER
I multiplied each rate by its balance. Then I added those together. Then I divided by the total you owe.

The Customer tries the math on the notepad and gets the same answer.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
We call that a weighted average.

The Customer puts down the pen.

CUSTOMER
What if you apply my payment to the low rate first?

BANK OFFICER
Then your average rate climbs each month.

The Customer frowns.

CUSTOMER
Why does it climb?

BANK OFFICER
The cheap debt shrinks but the expensive debt stays put.

The Bank Officer opens a laptop and types a web address.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
Your weighted average gives you a rough idea for now.

The screen shows an online calculator.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
But this site lets you enter two separate cards.

The Customer moves closer to see the screen better.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
You put in different amounts for each one.

The Bank Officer fills in two rows of data.

BANK OFFICER (CONT'D)
Now you can see when the expensive card gets paid off.

The Customer points to a date on the screen.

CUSTOMER
Will this match my real statement?

BANK OFFICER
It might be off by a small amount. You can live with that error or you can do the full math yourself by hand.

The Customer closes the notepad and stands up.
script_events.coling::9e189795-5152-41d4-9713-20ef5189:
INT. SMALL OFFICE - DAY

A CONSULTANT sits across from a CLIENT at a desk.

CONSULTANT
Wyoming works well for this kind of setup.

The Consultant slides a folder across the desk.

CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
The fees stay low and the state asks very little from you each year.

CLIENT
What about Delaware? Everyone talks about Delaware.

CONSULTANT
Delaware spends money on advertising. That's why people know the name.

The Consultant opens the folder and points to a list.

CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
But over fifty states and jurisdictions compete for your business now.

CLIENT
They all have different rules?

CONSULTANT
Each one has its own legislature. Those legislatures change the laws to pull in more companies.

The Consultant turns a page.

CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Delaware made headlines years ago. Then other states copied what Delaware did.

CLIENT
So Delaware lost its edge?

CONSULTANT
Those other states improved on the model. They offer better terms now.

The Client leans forward.

CLIENT
What about Delaware's special court?

CONSULTANT
The Chancery Court sets precedents. But judges in every state can cite those same cases.

The Consultant pulls out a rate sheet.

CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Wyoming charges less than Delaware for the same presence. The state collects less information about your business. And Wyoming has no corporate tax.

CLIENT
How do I handle the address requirement?

CONSULTANT
A registered agent solves that problem. They set up the paperwork for you.

The Consultant circles a number on the sheet.

CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
This runs between ninety-nine and two hundred dollars above what the state charges.

CLIENT
Does the LLC need a US address?

CONSULTANT
No legal requirement exists. But most registered agents let you use their address if you ask.

The Client nods and makes a note.

CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
Your business might need a bank account for trade. Some companies now accept payments without banks. But traditional commerce still runs through financial institutions.

CLIENT
Can I open an account from abroad?

CONSULTANT
That process gets complicated. The registered agent or a lawyer requests a Tax ID from the IRS first.

The Consultant stands and walks to a filing cabinet.

CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
The bank will want someone to visit in person. You'll need an employee or a nominee director based in the United States.

CLIENT
This person appears in the official documents?

The Consultant returns with another form.

CONSULTANT
The Operating Agreement lists them. The incorporation papers show their authority.

CLIENT
Then what happens?

CONSULTANT
They walk into any bank with your articles and agreement. The bank sees they can act for the entity. They open the account that day.

The Consultant sits back down.

CONSULTANT (CONT'D)
After that, this person resigns. The LLC keeps that resignation private.

CLIENT
And I can access the account?

CONSULTANT
You receive payments and connect to the global financial system. Multinational corporations create subsidiaries in multiple countries using this exact method.

The Client closes the folder.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::df393828-70be-448f-bbdb-11367e15:
INT. FINANCIAL ADVISOR'S OFFICE - DAY

A young CLIENT sits across from an ADVISOR at a desk.

ADVISOR
Stop looking at your credit score. Put the app away.

The CLIENT sets down their phone.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Write down what you earn and what you spend. Stick to that plan.

The ADVISOR slides a blank notebook across the desk.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Put money aside each month. Some for next week, some for next year.

The CLIENT opens the notebook and picks up a pen.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Pay every bill when it comes due. Never miss a date.

The CLIENT starts writing.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Borrow only what makes sense. Keep the amounts small.

The ADVISOR leans back in the chair.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Do these things and the score goes up by itself. It happens without you watching it.

The CLIENT nods slowly.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Now about those zero percent offers. I follow one rule. Save the full price first.

The ADVISOR holds up one finger.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Then check if the payments fit your budget. Both things must be true.

The CLIENT looks up from the notebook.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Other people refuse these deals completely. You need to pick your own rule. But pick something.

The ADVISOR stands and walks to the window.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Just don't choose based on your score. That path leads nowhere good.

The CLIENT closes the notebook.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
The real danger is buying things you don't need. The zero percent rate makes you feel rich.

The ADVISOR turns back from the window.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
You're not getting free money. You're just moving the payment date around. The window closes fast.

The CLIENT stands up.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Read every word of the contract. They hide traps in there.

The ADVISOR walks the CLIENT to the door.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Miss the final payment and they charge you for everything. All the interest appears at once, back to day one.

They reach the door. The ADVISOR opens it.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
You're starting out now. That's good. Building wealth takes years. Time is your best tool.

The CLIENT steps into the hallway.

ADVISOR (CONT'D)
One last thing. Ignore your credit score.

The door closes.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::cbaa1dc4-0458-47d8-b3a6-f6f1b4b4:
INT. PRAGUE CINEMA - NIGHT

A man walks down the aisle and sits. The lights dim. The film starts on screen.

EXT. PARIS STREET - DAY (ON SCREEN)

Soldiers march past old buildings. A woman in costume appears.

INT. CINEMA - NIGHT

The man shifts in his seat. He frowns at the screen.

EXT. FRENCH COUNTRYSIDE - DAY (ON SCREEN)

Adjani's character shoots a fat man. The man falls dead. She runs away from the body.

INT. CINEMA - NIGHT

The viewer leans back. He crosses his arms.

EXT. DIFFERENT LOCATION - DAY (ON SCREEN)

Adjani stands before Depardieu. She opens her mouth to confess.

INT. CINEMA - NIGHT

The man rolls his eyes.

EXT. SAME LOCATION - DAY (ON SCREEN)

Adjani tells Depardieu she killed the fat man. Violins start playing. The music swells loud and sad.

INT. CINEMA - NIGHT

The viewer shakes his head. He looks annoyed.

EXT. PANTHEON PARIS - MORNING (ON SCREEN)

German tanks roll into the empty square. The army takes over the city.

INT. CINEMA - NIGHT

The man nods slightly. He seems less angry now.

EXT. BRIDGE BORDEAUX - DAY (ON SCREEN)

Refugees crowd onto the bridge. They put down bags and blankets. Children cry. People settle into small camps.

INT. CINEMA - NIGHT

The viewer watches this scene with interest. Then Lemoine appears on screen and speaks his lines badly.

INT. CINEMA - NIGHT (LATER)

The man grimaces at the acting.

EXT. VARIOUS LOCATIONS - DAY (ON SCREEN)

More expensive scenes play out. Crowds fill the frame. The camera moves over detailed sets.

INT. CINEMA - NIGHT (LATER)

The credits roll. The man stands up. He walks out to the lobby. He pulls out his phone. He opens a website. He types a review. He gives the film one out of ten. He hits submit. He puts the phone away. He steps outside into the Prague night. He walks home through the old streets.
script_events.coling::dc1c93ce-9792-4a14-bd29-c025f261:
INT. MOVIE THEATER - PRAGUE - NIGHT

A person sits alone in the dark theater. The credits roll.

EXT. PRAGUE STREET - NIGHT

The person walks out into the cold air. They stop under a streetlight.

INT. APARTMENT - NIGHT

The person sits at a computer. They open a website. They begin typing.

FLASHBACK - EXT. PRAGUE STREET - EARLIER THAT DAY

The person walks past a movie poster on the wall. The poster shows actors in old heroic poses. The person keeps walking.

INT. APARTMENT - CONTINUOUS

The person types more words. They pause. They remember something else.

FLASHBACK - INT. MOVIE THEATER - EARLIER

The person buys a ticket. The clerk hands it over. The person enters the theater.

INT. APARTMENT - CONTINUOUS

The person writes about the language of the film. They mention their mother. They add a sentence about Prague. They type the names of three people they admire.

The person starts a new paragraph. They describe a character. The character does something stupid on screen.

FLASHBACK - INT. MOVIE THEATER - EARLIER

Adjani appears on screen. She talks to Depardieu. She confesses to a murder. She says she killed a fat man.

Music swells loud. Violins play. The person in the audience frowns.

INT. APARTMENT - CONTINUOUS

The person types faster now. They mention another film. They write the title. They compare the two movies.

The person scrolls up. They read what others wrote before. They see praise for an actor named Lemoine. They shake their head.

FLASHBACK - INT. MOVIE THEATER - EARLIER

Lemoine acts badly on screen. He delivers his lines wrong. The person watches in disbelief.

The scene changes. The Pantheon appears in morning light. German soldiers march into Paris. The person leans forward slightly.

Another scene begins. Refugees crowd onto a bridge. The bridge is in Bordeaux. The camera moves across their faces.

INT. APARTMENT - CONTINUOUS

The person finishes typing. They write a final number. They hit the button. The comment posts online.
script_events.coling::fedf3b3b-fd89-4a69-bc59-0ff4e485:
INT. SMALL MOVIE THEATER - NIGHT

A person sits in the half-empty theater. The credits roll on screen.

EXT. THEATER LOBBY - NIGHT

The person steps outside and pulls out a phone.

INT. COFFEE SHOP - NIGHT

The person sits down with a laptop and opens it. Fingers start typing.

ON SCREEN - BLOG POST

Words appear: "I think I'll be the only one who's saying this but yes, I was a lil bored during the film."

The person pauses and sips coffee.

More words appear: "Not to say that this is a bad movie, in fact it's a very good attempt at portraying emotions - dilemma, sorrow, love."

The person looks up at the ceiling and thinks.

Typing resumes: "I felt that something's not quite right, maybe it's just me."

A friend walks in and waves.

The person waves back but keeps typing: "I'm not drawn to the characters enough."

The friend orders at the counter.

More text fills the screen: "This is a simple story, about ordinary people, ordinary lives."

The friend sits down at another table.

The person types faster now: "The director tries to relate a simple guy's life, and how he copes with the news of his illness by laughing it away every time."

A waitress brings more coffee.

The person drinks and continues: "Oh ya his laughter was kinda cute at first but gradually it gets to me, such a deep hearty roar for a gentle man!"

The friend gets up to leave and waves goodbye.

The person nods and keeps writing: "I didn't feel the impact that most readers felt."

Outside the window, rain starts falling.

The typing continues: "I was more drawn to the trivial scenarios like spitting of watermelon seeds with his sis."

The person yawns and stretches.

More words: "The granny who came back for another shot - this is kinda melancholic."

The coffee cup empties.
script_events.coling::a3c20aed-e22b-4f5a-ac3a-784b5d94:
INT. LIVING ROOM - NIGHT

A man sits in a worn chair. He stares at the television screen. The glow lights his face.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
This soap poisons everything it touches.

On screen, characters shout at each other in a pub. One man shoves another. A woman throws a drink.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
For twenty years this show has rotted British society from the inside.

The man leans forward. He watches a fight break out on screen.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
It celebrates oafs and thugs and crooks and fools.

A woman enters the room. She sits down beside him. They both watch.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
People say the show mirrors life.

The characters on screen kiss violently. They stumble into a bedroom.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
But which life does it mirror?

The man picks up a beer. He drinks. He sets the bottle down hard.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
Middle-class writers took courses in universities. They invented poor people from their imagination.

On screen, a character steals money from a cash register. Another character threatens him with a knife.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
They showed their work to other middle-class people. Everyone nodded and smiled.

The woman on the couch crosses her arms. She frowns just like the characters on screen.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
Then something changed in the real world.

The man stands up. He yells at the woman. She yells back. They sound exactly like the television.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
Real people began to copy the fake people. Life started to mirror the show instead.

More people enter the room. They all talk in harsh voices. They threaten each other over small things.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
Other shows copied this formula. They filled themselves with ugly angry characters.

The writers sit in a distant expensive restaurant. They laugh and drink wine. They sign contracts.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
The writers grew rich. They moved to beautiful neighborhoods.

Back in the living room, the people slump in their chairs. The television flickers. No one moves to turn it off.

NARRATOR (V.O.)
You chose this window. You built this prison yourself.
script_events.coling::019875e1-f507-4de8-a2a7-1f1dffeb:
INT. SCREENING ROOM - NIGHT

The lights dim. A film begins to play on the screen.

EXT. SPACE - IO'S SURFACE - DAY

A spacecraft approaches the moon. An alarm suddenly blares inside the cabin.

INT. SPACECRAFT - CONTINUOUS

The crew rushes to their stations. They check readings and shout warnings to each other.

EXT. SPACE - SATURN'S RINGS - LATER

The ship moves toward the glowing rings. A panel on the hull breaks loose and spins away.

INT. SPACECRAFT - CONTINUOUS

Red lights flash across the control room. The captain grabs the radio and calls for help.

EXT. SPACE - NEAR A COMET - LATER

The vessel drifts close to the icy rock. A small fire erupts in one of the engines.

INT. SPACECRAFT - CONTINUOUS

Crew members grab extinguishers and spray foam everywhere. Smoke fills the cabin.

INT. SCREENING ROOM - NIGHT

A viewer shifts in their seat and frowns.

EXT. SPACE - ASTEROID FIELD - LATER

The ship weaves between floating rocks. One astronaut argues with another about the route.

INT. SPACECRAFT - CONTINUOUS

The argument grows louder. Someone slams a fist on a console.

INT. SCREENING ROOM - NIGHT

The viewer sighs and crosses their arms.

EXT. SPACE - DEEP VOID - LATER

The mission continues for months. The crew grows tired and makes small errors.

INT. SPACECRAFT - CONTINUOUS

One astronaut nearly opens the wrong hatch. Another catches the mistake just in time.

EXT. SPACE - RETURN JOURNEY - LATER

The ship turns back toward Earth. The crew sits in silence.

INT. SCREENING ROOM - NIGHT

The credits start to roll. The viewer stands and walks toward the exit.

INT. THEATER LOBBY - NIGHT

The viewer stops and speaks to a friend. They say the science felt real and true. They mention the human problems seemed authentic too. But they wish the film had shown the crew after landing. They wanted to see how space changed their bodies over time. The friend nods and they leave together.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::c986a4de-fede-44ef-b275-ef763424:
INT. PRINCIPAL'S OFFICE - DAY

A STUDENT stands before the PRINCIPAL's desk and starts to speak.

STUDENT
Kids should bring phones to school.

The PRINCIPAL leans back in her chair.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
We can use them at lunch and free time.

The student holds up one finger.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
We turn them off in class.

The PRINCIPAL picks up a pen.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
First reason. Kids get on their phones at lunch.

The student pulls out her own phone as an example.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
They stop looking at each other.

She sets the phone on the desk.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Fewer fights break out that way.

The PRINCIPAL writes a note.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Less drama happens when kids stare at screens.

The student walks to the window.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Teachers get a break too.

She turns back around.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Second reason. More kids show up to school.

The PRINCIPAL looks up from her notes.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
They know phones are allowed.

The student counts on her fingers.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Most kids skip because phones get taken.

She holds up three fingers.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Some kids lose their phone three times.

The student sits down in the chair.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
They fear their parents finding out.

The PRINCIPAL sets down her pen.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Parents learn their kid texted in class.

The student looks at the floor.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Mom and dad take the phone away.

She looks back up.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
They wait for grades to improve.

The PRINCIPAL stands and walks to the window.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
You should think about this plan.

The student joins her at the window.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Teachers stop worrying about lunch fights.

They both look out at the schoolyard.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Staff can rest from all the trouble.

Kids walk past outside.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Teachers here need that rest.

The PRINCIPAL nods slowly.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
