This happens when we use phones at lunch.

The student steps back from the window.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Everyone gets relief from drama.

She moves toward the door.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Staff want it and students want it.

The PRINCIPAL returns to her desk.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
All middle schools deal with this.

The student opens the door.

STUDENT (CONT'D)
Many people think about it.

She exits and closes the door behind her.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::b53b4239-d0ed-4e79-b84e-c3496abd:
INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

A PRESENTER stands at the front. She clicks a remote.

PRESENTER
The article drops on the table.

A ENGINEER picks it up and reads the title aloud.

ENGINEER
Driverless cars are coming.

The presenter nods and walks to the window.

PRESENTER
The technology sounds cool at first.

A SAFETY OFFICER enters the room holding a tablet.

SAFETY OFFICER
Then the questions start.

The engineer sets down the article and stands.

ENGINEER
A car could malfunction on the highway.

The safety officer taps her tablet and a crash video plays.

SAFETY OFFICER
The driver gets hurt in the accident.

The presenter turns back from the window.

PRESENTER
The passenger sits idle for miles.

The engineer mimes closing his eyes.

ENGINEER
He dozes off behind the wheel.

A DESIGNER bursts through the door with blueprints.

DESIGNER
We add entertainment to the dashboard.

She spreads the papers across the table.

DESIGNER
A heads up display appears on the windshield.

The safety officer leans over to examine the plans.

SAFETY OFFICER
The system detects danger ahead.

The designer points to a sensor diagram.

DESIGNER
The display shuts off instantly.

The presenter walks to the table and picks up a coffee mug.

PRESENTER
A commuter runs late for work.

The engineer opens a lunch bag.

ENGINEER
She eats breakfast in the passenger seat.

The safety officer mimes brushing hair.

SAFETY OFFICER
Another person fixes their hair during the drive.

The designer pulls out her phone.

DESIGNER
A business call comes in without a bluetooth device.

The presenter sets down her mug.

PRESENTER
The driver can talk hands free now.

The engineer's expression darkens.

ENGINEER
Weekend arrives and someone goes to a bar.

The safety officer shakes her head.

SAFETY OFFICER
The person gets drunk and stumbles to the car.

The designer crosses her arms.

DESIGNER
He assumes the car will handle everything.

The engineer slams his hand on the table.

ENGINEER
The system fails on the route home.

The safety officer looks up sharply.

SAFETY OFFICER
The car crashes into a guardrail.

The presenter walks to the door.

PRESENTER
Police arrive at the scene.

The designer gathers her blueprints.

DESIGNER
They blame the drunk passenger.

The safety officer closes her tablet.

SAFETY OFFICER
He goes to jail that night.

The engineer sits down heavily.

ENGINEER
Those are the trade offs we face.

The presenter opens the door and exits. The others follow her out.
script_events.coling::c5dd6ecd-4882-4b86-be71-efecfae7:
INT. BEDROOM - MORNING

A woman holds up a dress.

WOMAN
What do you think I should wear tomorrow?

She tosses it on the bed and grabs a blouse.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
What do you think of this outfit?

She picks up a necklace from the dresser.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Would this necklace look good with these shoes?

Her friend enters the room.

FRIEND
You ask me this stuff every day.

The woman sits down on the bed.

WOMAN
Most people want more than one opinion.

A researcher walks into frame holding a clipboard.

RESEARCHER
Studies show that more than half of Americans ask for a second opinion before they do something.

INT. SHOE STORE - DAY

The woman tries on red heels.

WOMAN
Should I get these fancy expensive shoes?

FRIEND
No.

The woman waves over a sales clerk.

WOMAN
What do you think?

The clerk nods.

CLERK
They look great.

A professor enters the store.

PROFESSOR
Harvard did a study on this exact behavior.

He points at the woman.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Fashion keeps changing and people need constant reassurance.

INT. CLOTHING STORE - DAY

The woman pulls an oversized shirt off a rack.

WOMAN
I like this one.

FRIEND
Me too.

Her father walks past them.

WOMAN
Dad, do you like it?

FATHER
No. I hate oversized ugly shirts.

The woman puts it back.

WOMAN
See? Asking for a second opinion helped me.

A psychologist appears next to them.

PSYCHOLOGIST
Feedback shapes your mind to make the correct choice.

A man storms through the store.

MAN
I refuse to listen to anyone.

He grabs the ugly shirt.

MAN (CONT'D)
I will buy what I want.

Another researcher steps forward.

RESEARCHER TWO
George Mason University found that some people ignore negative feedback completely.

The man leaves the store.

RESEARCHER TWO (CONT'D)
They choose the opposite of what they were told.

INT. LABORATORY - DAY

A scientist stands at a whiteboard.

SCIENTIST
Human brains evolved to think we are always right.

He draws a diagram.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
This makes people unable to respect other opinions.

An FBI agent enters.

FBI AGENT
Even serial killers asked multiple people if they should kill their first victim.

The agent opens a file.

FBI AGENT (CONT'D)
Everyone said no.

He closes the file.

FBI AGENT (CONT'D)
The killer did it anyway.

INT. CLINIC - DAY

A doctor sits at a desk.

DOCTOR
The Virginia Department of Health did research on people who never ask for opinions.

A patient walks in slowly.

DOCTOR (CONT'D)
Those with depression and anxiety were ten times less likely to ask for advice.

The patient sits down.

PATIENT
I overthink everything. I feel shy and embarrassed.

The doctor writes notes.

DOCTOR
They expect only negative feedback so they stop asking.

The patient starts crying.

PATIENT
I feel trapped. No one can help me.

A counselor enters.

COUNSELOR
Depression is rising because people fear being judged.

The patient stands up.

PATIENT
I am scared of appearing stupid.

INT. UNIVERSITY OFFICE - DAY

A professor walks to a window.

PROFESSOR TWO
Virginia Tech discovered something interesting.

A student knocks and enters.

STUDENT
I need advice.

An older man follows the student inside.

PROFESSOR TWO
People who ask for advice every day usually ask someone older.

The older man sits down.

OLDER MAN
We have more knowledge and wisdom.

INT. BEDROOM - EVENING

The woman returns with shopping bags.

WOMAN
Looking for feedback is always best if you want good advice.

She unpacks new clothes.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Whether it be a school project or office work or trying on different clothes, there is always room for improvement.

Her friend helps her hang things up.

FRIEND
So ask multiple people for advice and feedback.

The woman smiles.
script_events.coling::f2d66835-0de6-4a50-b3da-a170f060:
INT. HIGH SCHOOL CLASSROOM - DAY

A teacher stands at the front of the room holding a stack of papers.

TEACHER
Summer starts next week.

Students lean forward in their seats.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
You will complete a project over the break.

A student raises her hand.

STUDENT 1
Who picks the topic?

TEACHER
I design it. Not you.

The teacher walks down the aisle and places papers on each desk.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The project covers what we study in September.

A boy flips through the pages.

STUDENT 2
This looks hard.

TEACHER
It prepares you for the fall curriculum.

The teacher returns to the front and writes on the board.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
You will arrive in August already familiar with the material.

A girl in the back row nods slowly.

STUDENT 3
So we get a head start.

TEACHER
Exactly. You enter the class with background knowledge.

The teacher erases the board and writes a number.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
This project counts as your first grade.

Students sit up straighter.

STUDENT 1
You mean it goes in the grade book?

TEACHER
Yes. Before the first test even happens.

A student grins.

STUDENT 2
I could start the year with an A.

TEACHER
If you complete it well.

The teacher sits on the edge of the desk.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
That early grade protects you later.

STUDENT 3
What if I struggle in October?

TEACHER
This grade cushions your average.

The teacher stands and walks to the window.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
I keep the work simple.

Students exchange glances.

STUDENT 1
How simple?

TEACHER
I know you travel during summer. I know you see friends.

The teacher turns back to face the class.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The project takes only a few hours total.

A student exhales with relief.

STUDENT 2
That sounds manageable.

TEACHER
I want you thinking, not stressing.

The teacher picks up a marker.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Some colleagues let students choose their own projects.

STUDENT 3
Why not us?

TEACHER
Students pick topics that are too easy.

The teacher draws a diagram on the board.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
They avoid challenge when given the choice.

STUDENT 1
So you prevent that.

TEACHER
I set the difficulty at the right level.

The bell rings. Students gather their belongings.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Complete this and you benefit all year.

Students file toward the door.

STUDENT 2
When is it due?

TEACHER
The day you return in August.

The last student exits. The teacher collects the extra papers from the desk.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
They will thank me later.

The teacher places the papers in a folder and closes it.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::1eb5e451-a672-4645-8dea-c413ad11:
INT. UNIVERSITY LAB - DAY

PROFESSOR HUANG stands beside a large computer screen.

HUANG
We built this system last year.

A student's face appears on the monitor.

HUANG (CONT'D)
Now the software scans her features.

Numbers flash across the display.

HUANG (CONT'D)
The machine just detected happiness.

The student on screen frowns.

HUANG (CONT'D)
Now it reads sadness instead.

A SECURITY GUARD enters the room.

GUARD
Schools want to buy this device.

HUANG
Banks called us yesterday too.

GUARD
Government offices sent requests this morning.

A technician types commands into the keyboard.

TECHNICIAN
I am installing cameras at the front entrance.

HUANG
Those cameras will scan every visitor.

GUARD
The system flags anyone who seems dangerous.

TECHNICIAN
We stop that person before they enter.

HUANG
Mass shootings drop when we use this tool.

The screen goes black suddenly.

TECHNICIAN
The computer just crashed.

GUARD
Machines break down without warning.

HUANG
We fix bugs as they occur.

A BUSINESS EXECUTIVE walks through the door.

EXECUTIVE
My company tested your invention last week.

HUANG
What did your customers do?

EXECUTIVE
They looked at our new products on shelves.

TECHNICIAN
The system read their reactions in real time.

EXECUTIVE
We learned which items they liked best.

HUANG
Then you changed your marketing plan.

EXECUTIVE
Sales went up the following month.

A STUDENT pulls out her phone.

STUDENT
My phone already scans my face to unlock.

HUANG
Next year it will read your mood too.

STUDENT
The phone will suggest activities to cheer me up.

TECHNICIAN
We need five more years of testing first.

GUARD
Some facilities already run secret trials.

The executive leaves the lab.

A TEENAGER appears on the video screen via chat.

TEENAGER
I told my friend I felt fine today.

HUANG
But the system detected something else.

TEENAGER
The software knew I was lying to her.

STUDENT
My friend saw the alert on her device.

TEENAGER
She called me right away to talk.

STUDENT
I admitted I needed help badly.

HUANG
The technology saved a life that day.

The guard walks to the window.

GUARD
Suicides fall when people get support early.

TECHNICIAN
We prevent tragedies before they happen.

HUANG
Society becomes safer for everyone.

A GROUP OF SUPPORTERS gathers outside.

STUDENT
Those people want this system everywhere.

GUARD
They carry signs demanding action now.

HUANG
Citizens have the right to speak up.

TECHNICIAN
They believe this tool protects their families.

The protesters chant loudly.

STUDENT
They want a better country for their children.

HUANG
We will keep working to improve lives.

The computer screen lights up again.

TECHNICIAN
The system just came back online.

HUANG
Tomorrow we start the next phase.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::c0381ae0-3b9c-40a4-bc53-f4a76564:
INT. RESEARCH LAB - DAY

A scientist places a paper on the desk. The paper extends work from Lenc and Vedaldi's 2015 study.

The first page shows that CNN representations at the FC7 layer respond to transformations in predictable ways.

A colleague enters the room and reads over the scientist's shoulder.

COLLEAGUE
They trained more than thirty networks.

The scientist nods. Each network uses different forms of jitter.

COLLEAGUE (CONT'D)
But what does it all mean?

The scientist shrugs. The main message remains unclear.

A graduate student walks in holding a coffee mug. She sets it down on the table.

GRADUATE STUDENT
They tested a different layer than the 2015 paper did.

The colleague flips to the next page. The findings confirm that jitter creates invariance, which everyone already knew.

The scientist circles a section about representation distances with red pen.

SCIENTIST
Look at this problem here.

The graduate student leans closer. The authors only examined the FC7 layer.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
That layer sits right before FC8.

The colleague points to a diagram. FC8 projects directly to class likelihoods.

GRADUATE STUDENT
FC8 is just linear projection.

The scientist underlines another passage. The equivalence map merely re-projects FC8 weights from one network to another.

The colleague stands and walks to a whiteboard. He draws several network layers.

COLLEAGUE
They should have tested more layers.

The graduate student opens her laptop. She types notes about the missing classification error data.

GRADUATE STUDENT
Where are the testing dataset results?

The scientist flips ahead several pages. No classification error appears anywhere.

SCIENTIST
We need that to know if representations are actually compatible.

The colleague erases part of his diagram and redraws it.

A professor enters carrying a stack of papers. She drops them on the desk with a thud.

PROFESSOR
What about the K-NN experiment?

The scientist finds that section. The methodology remains unclear.

GRADUATE STUDENT
Did they measure per test example?

The colleague returns to his seat. Nobody answers the graduate student's question.

PROFESSOR
Did they train the equivalence map first?

The scientist shakes his head. The paper does not specify.

The graduate student highlights text on her screen. Networks trained on similar jitter should show more compatibility.

COLLEAGUE
The proposed method fails on some tasks.

The professor picks up the paper and reads. Lambda one and lambda two have tiny values.

PROFESSOR
The loss just becomes simple data jitter.

The scientist writes notes in the margin. The loss adds together original and transformed image losses.

GRADUATE STUDENT
Maybe FC7 was the wrong choice.

The colleague closes his notebook. The paper shows interesting FC7 results but draws few new conclusions.

The professor walks to the door.

PROFESSOR
I cannot recommend acceptance.

The scientist gathers the pages together. The equivalence experiments contain too many problems.

The graduate student saves her notes. The finetuning approach needs more work.

COLLEAGUE
They could refine the experiments.

The professor pauses in the doorway.

PROFESSOR
Make it more investigative.

The scientist places the paper in a folder. That might create a real contribution.

The graduate student notices the angles on pages one and five lack units.

GRADUATE STUDENT
Are these degrees?

The colleague finds an error on page three. The text says M_g gets maximized, but actually the loss over M_g does.

The scientist reads footnote two on page four. Halving activations is not really dropout.

The professor returns and points to Figure 3a and 3b on page seven.

PROFESSOR
White diagonal elements mislead readers.

The scientist agrees. Distance between identical representations should show as zero.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::07106895-c293-4117-be28-f7598533:
INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

A REVIEWER sits at a desk. Papers spread before them.

REVIEWER
I read your paper. Good work.

The Reviewer picks up a pen.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The information bottleneck principle catches my interest.

The Reviewer opens a notebook.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Deep neural networks gain something from this approach.

The Reviewer writes a note.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Your paper trains deep networks with IB for the first time.

The Reviewer pauses. Sets down the pen.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The original papers only talked about the concept.

The Reviewer flips to another page.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
I will mention independent work later.

The Reviewer nods.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Your variational lowerbound derivation comes through clearly.

The Reviewer underlines a section.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
People unfamiliar with variational inference can follow it.

The Reviewer turns another page.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The IB principle explanation also works well.

The Reviewer examines a graph.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Your experimental results show promise.

The Reviewer frowns now.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The model presentation confuses me though.

The Reviewer circles a paragraph.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
In variational inference, p usually means the model.

The Reviewer draws an arrow.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The letter q represents the inference engine.

The Reviewer taps the page.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
This separation keeps inference independent from modeling.

The Reviewer shakes their head.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Your VIB assumes p of x and y as underlying data distribution.

The Reviewer makes another mark.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
You approximate it with empirical distribution.

The Reviewer writes in the margin.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
So the actual model becomes q of y given z times p of z given x.

The Reviewer flips forward.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Then page eight presents p of y given x as predictive distribution.

The Reviewer looks up.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Predictive in what sense exactly?

The Reviewer writes a question.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
I guess you meant the integral of q of y given z times p of z given x.

The Reviewer crosses something out.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
But this creates a contradiction between your two definitions.

The Reviewer turns to a new section.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
You connect VIB to variational auto-encoder nicely.

The Reviewer reads further.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The warm-up training by tuning beta interests me.

The Reviewer stops reading.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The loss function formula matches VAE when beta equals one.

The Reviewer leans back.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Yet the underlying models differ completely.

The Reviewer points at the text.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
In VIB, r of z approximates p of z variationally.

The Reviewer makes a note.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
So r of z is not a model component.

The Reviewer compares two equations.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
In VAE, it serves as the prior distribution.

The Reviewer writes more.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The modeling procedure actually defines it there.

The Reviewer continues writing.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Similarly, p of z given x belongs in the VIB model.

The Reviewer underlines again.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
In VAE that becomes the approximate posterior.

The Reviewer adds a comment.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
You can choose it independently in VAE.

The Reviewer closes the notebook.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The modeling procedure presentation lacks clarity overall.

The Reviewer picks up the paper.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
I hope revision makes these points clearer.

The Reviewer sets it down.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The current presentation troubles me as a Bayesian.

The Reviewer opens to the VAE section.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
script_events.coling::745b25d5-34c6-4c43-a690-6414f205:
INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

A researcher stands at a podium and clicks to the first slide.

RESEARCHER
We built a system that picks training sentences using a CNN classifier.

The slide shows a comparison table.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
We tested it against language models from earlier studies.

An audience member raises her hand.

AUDIENCE MEMBER
Did you compare it to bilingual selection methods?

The researcher pauses and looks down at his notes.

RESEARCHER
We did not test cross-entropy differences from both languages.

He advances to the next slide showing the CNN architecture.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
At first I wondered why we chose a CNN over an RNN.

A diagram appears on screen.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Then I realized certain parts of a sentence matter more than others. The CNN finds those parts.

Another audience member leans forward.

SECOND AUDIENCE MEMBER
Did you test whether bag-of-words works better than sequence representation?

The researcher shakes his head.

RESEARCHER
We described both options but ran no experiment to compare them.

He clicks to a text-heavy slide.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
The write-up explains the one-hot encoding and the pre-trained embeddings in detail.

THIRD AUDIENCE MEMBER
A diagram would help more than all those words.

The researcher nods and moves to the results section.

RESEARCHER
The experiments back up our claims.

He stops and frowns.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
One concern arose about how we chose the number of sentences. We used a validation set.

FOURTH AUDIENCE MEMBER
Which validation data exactly?

The researcher shuffles his papers.

RESEARCHER
The paper does not specify that. We also did not explain how we picked the CNN settings.

FIFTH AUDIENCE MEMBER
How much do results change with different settings?

RESEARCHER
We have not measured that sensitivity.

He points to a table on the screen.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Table two compares approaches but uses different sentence counts for each method.

AUDIENCE MEMBER
Figure one suggests your method wins even with matched counts.

The researcher agrees and continues.

RESEARCHER
Someone suggested we test the method with more in-domain data beyond the development set.

He clicks forward.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Another idea was to show example sentences that each method selected.

A new slide appears with citations.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Axelrod replaced words with part-of-speech tags in his work. We could compare that against word embeddings.

SIXTH AUDIENCE MEMBER
Your source-plus-target scoring resembles the Lewis-Moore selection approach.

RESEARCHER
You are right. We should cite that work near line four thirty-five.

He closes his presentation folder.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Finally, we might extend the CNN to learn weights for combining source and target scores in the bilingual setting.

The lights come up.
script_events.coling::4e7728dc-010d-47cb-95f2-16525a71:
INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

A researcher stands at a podium. She holds up a paper.

RESEARCHER
This submission takes character models and keeps words in the context.

She flips to the next page.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Kim published this same idea back in two thousand fifteen.

A colleague in the front row raises his hand.

COLLEAGUE
Jozefowicz did it too, one year later.

The researcher nods and makes a note.

RESEARCHER
Both teams already used RNNs and LSTMs for their work.

She walks to a whiteboard and writes a list.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Jozefowicz compared different character methods in detail.

She circles one item on the board.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
This paper skips that discussion entirely.

A door opens. Another reviewer enters the room.

NEW REVIEWER
The novelty here applies only to machine translation.

The researcher turns back to face the group.

RESEARCHER
The authors rerank N-best lists to solve the problem.

She pauses and frowns.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
They never explain how reranking handles unknown words in translation.

The colleague stands up from his seat.

COLLEAGUE
Section two point three makes exaggerated claims about vocabulary.

He reads from his notes.

COLLEAGUE (CONT'D)
They say vocabulary becomes obsolete with their method.

The new reviewer shakes her head.

NEW REVIEWER
Later they doubt perplexity works without explicit vocabulary.

The researcher writes more comments on the board.

RESEARCHER
Frequent words still matter for good modeling performance.

She references a paper number.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Archive sixteen zero nine point zero eight one four four proves this point.

The colleague sits back down.

COLLEAGUE
Section two point three claims the objective needs finite vocabulary.

The new reviewer stands and approaches the board.

NEW REVIEWER
That statement only holds true for full word forms.

She adds a correction to the list.

NEW REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Subwords and characters can cover infinite vocabularies implicitly.

The researcher underlines a section heading.

RESEARCHER
The authors must qualify their statement about this limitation.

She turns to a new page in her notes.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Section two point four never clarifies the character embedding output.

The colleague pulls out a red pen.

COLLEAGUE
The description there lacks sufficient detail and precision.

The new reviewer points to another section.

NEW REVIEWER
Section three point four describes NCE configuration choices.

She taps the page with her finger.

NEW REVIEWER (CONT'D)
The authors never explain how they picked these parameters.

The researcher adds this to her list of concerns.

RESEARCHER
Section four point one ignores Kim's similar conclusions.

The colleague flips through reference papers.

COLLEAGUE
Kim suggested improvements the authors should discuss here.

The new reviewer finds another citation.

NEW REVIEWER
Shaik calculated perplexity for unknown words back in twenty thirteen.

The researcher checks section four point two.

RESEARCHER
The authors claim perplexity cannot work for unknown words.

She closes the paper and sets it down.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Table four omits the full training vocabulary size.

The colleague starts listing grammar errors.

COLLEAGUE
Page two has a plural error with input layers.

The new reviewer squints at a figure.

NEW REVIEWER
Figure one uses fonts that are far too small.

The researcher finds more typos.

RESEARCHER
Page three says note instead of denote for WE.

She continues down her list of corrections.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Section two point three drops an S from parameters.

The colleague marks another mistake.

COLLEAGUE
Page five needs an article before factored way.

The new reviewer circles two more errors.

NEW REVIEWER
Page five writes a before n-best when an is correct.

The researcher reaches the final comment.

RESEARCHER
Section four point two ends with an incomplete sentence fragment.

She looks up at the group.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
The verb and article both go missing there.
script_events.coling::60e5cc06-240c-4ed3-80bd-353d0ba8:
INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

A SCIENTIST stands at a whiteboard covered with diagrams of solar panels.

SCIENTIST
Solar power is a miracle of modern science.

He draws a dollar sign on the board.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
One tiny problem shows up though. It costs more than other forms of power.

An ACCOUNTANT enters the room carrying a stack of reports.

ACCOUNTANT
Many people claim installing solar matches the price of building new power plants.

The Scientist nods but then shakes his head.

SCIENTIST
That works on a very large scale. You won't build your own power plant at home.

He walks to a laptop and opens a spreadsheet.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Look at one solar panel. Check how much power it makes on average. Do the math.

A GOVERNMENT OFFICIAL rushes in waving a document.

OFFICIAL
Someone believes the government could invest money and shut down nuclear plants.

The Accountant drops her reports on the table.

ACCOUNTANT
False assumptions are at work here. The government subsidizes solar purchases in California in a huge way already.

The Official sits down heavily in a chair.

OFFICIAL
So they are investing some money right now.

The Scientist points to a map on the wall.

SCIENTIST
The government does not operate nuclear plants. Private corporations run those facilities.

He circles several locations on the map.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The government regulates them only.

The Accountant picks up a calculator and punches numbers.

ACCOUNTANT
Construction costs the most for nuclear plants. Disposal of nuclear material adds more expense. Running the plant itself costs less.

The Official stands up again.

OFFICIAL
Shutting down a working plant would waste money then.

The Scientist walks to the window and looks out at solar panels on a nearby roof.

SCIENTIST
I love solar power for all kinds of reasons. It works at point of use. That means very little loss happens during long distance transmission.

He turns back to face the others.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
It makes practically zero emissions. It stays silent.

The Accountant joins him at the window.

ACCOUNTANT
That matters a lot to some people.

The Scientist gestures at the panels outside.

SCIENTIST
It provides the greatest benefit when need peaks in summer during daytime.

The Official walks over to them.

OFFICIAL
Solar might work best for running air conditioning. Summer brings strong sun and strong need for cooling at once.

The Accountant points at the roof panels.

ACCOUNTANT
The panels provide shade for the building too.

Everyone nods in agreement.

SCIENTIST
Still, a pure cost analysis favors coal or natural gas for electricity.

He closes his laptop with a snap.
script_events.coling::a0b0f9d5-62dc-4996-9de4-5e5f9b3b:
INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

A researcher stands at a podium and holds up a paper.

RESEARCHER
This paper shows Edward. It runs on TensorFlow and Python. It does probabilistic programming.

The researcher clicks a remote. A slide appears on screen.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
The library contains many inference methods. Users can access them easily.

An audience member raises a hand.

AUDIENCE MEMBER
What about the experiments?

RESEARCHER
The paper reviews techniques. It focuses on representation learning. Then it runs two tests.

The researcher advances to the next slide. It shows graphs.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
The first test uses variational inference. But the code is missing.

Someone in the back row stands up.

BACK ROW PERSON
Can we reproduce your results?

RESEARCHER
No link exists to the full code.

The researcher moves to another slide. It displays timing numbers.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
The second test runs HMC on a GPU. It goes fast.

A skeptical reviewer crosses her arms.

REVIEWER
You claim Stan uses hand optimization. That seems wrong.

RESEARCHER
Stan's code is general. It does not target this model or hardware.

The reviewer shakes her head.

REVIEWER
Your implementation is good. Stop making false claims.

The researcher looks down at his notes.

REVIEWER (CONT'D)
Run Stan on one core first. Then show your parallel speedup separately. Add the GPU gains after that.

The researcher nods slowly.

RESEARCHER
Those numbers would help readers. They could predict performance on other machines.

An editor in the front row flips through pages.

EDITOR
The writing is clear. The examples help.

The editor pauses and frowns.

EDITOR (CONT'D)
But some parts are missing from the code snippets.

RESEARCHER
We could provide a notebook. Jupyter would work. Even HTML would be better than PDF.

The editor writes something down.

A professor raises a concern.

PROFESSOR
Your group published Tran et al. last year. It covered similar topics.

RESEARCHER
That paper took a different angle.

PROFESSOR
Where did it appear? Was it published or just submitted?

The researcher does not answer. An uncomfortable silence fills the room.

A student in the middle row speaks up.

STUDENT
Edward will change the field. Bayesian learning will advance. Deep learning will benefit too.

The researcher smiles briefly. Then a critic stands.

CRITIC
Section two claims Stan is not Turing complete. Edward supposedly is.

RESEARCHER
We distinguish specialized languages from general ones.

CRITIC
Stan is Turing complete too. And you provide no proof for Edward.

The researcher closes his folder. The lights come up. People begin to leave.
script_events.coling::108b67b9-1113-4b28-81da-e218ced4:
INT. SMALL BUSINESS OFFICE - DAY

A BUSINESS ADVISOR sits across from a NEW ENTREPRENEUR at a desk.

BUSINESS ADVISOR
First you pick your structure.

The Advisor slides a chart across the table.

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
With a sole proprietorship, all profits flow straight into your pocket.

NEW ENTREPRENEUR
Sounds good.

BUSINESS ADVISOR
Then a lawsuit hits and you lose your house.

The Entrepreneur pulls back.

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
So you form a single member LLC instead.

A document appears on screen labeled "LLC FORMATION."

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Now the company takes the hit, not you personally.

NEW ENTREPRENEUR
Better.

BUSINESS ADVISOR
But self employment tax still drains fifteen percent right off the top.

The Entrepreneur winces.

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Add a partner and you split everything by ownership share.

A second person enters the frame and shakes hands with the Entrepreneur.

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
That tax problem stays though.

NEW ENTREPRENEUR
How do I fix it?

BUSINESS ADVISOR
File an S election with the IRS.

The Advisor stamps a form.

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Now you pay yourself a salary first.

NEW ENTREPRENEUR
And that helps?

BUSINESS ADVISOR
The salary skips the self employment tax entirely.

The Entrepreneur smiles.

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Extra profits pass through based on your ownership slice.

NEW ENTREPRENEUR
What about a C corp?

BUSINESS ADVISOR
The government taxes the company profits once.

He holds up one finger.

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Then they tax your dividends again.

He holds up a second finger.

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Small business owners avoid that structure.

The Entrepreneur nods and stands to leave.

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Or skip all this and start a mega church instead.

The Entrepreneur stops at the door.

BUSINESS ADVISOR (CONT'D)
Go on TV and ask for seed money.

NEW ENTREPRENEUR
That works?

BUSINESS ADVISOR
People send cash and you pay zero tax.

The Entrepreneur walks out shaking his head.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::31049c2c-a6a8-44a9-acaa-b8e3b123:
INT. COFFEE SHOP - DAY

A man types on his laptop. His fingers hit the keys hard.

EXT. STREET - DAY

A woman walks past a tall muscular man on the sidewalk. She keeps her head down and says nothing.

INT. BEDROOM - NIGHT

A teenage boy sits at his computer. He opens a video site and clicks on a video.

The video shows a girl playing a game. The boy types a mean comment and hits send.

INT. LIVING ROOM - DAY

The same girl reads the comment on her phone. Her face falls. She sets the phone down and walks away.

EXT. PARKING LOT - DAY

A woman gets into her car. She closes the door and locks it.

INT. CAR - CONTINUOUS

The woman pulls out of her spot. Another car cuts in front of her.

She slams her hand on the horn. The sound blares. She raises her middle finger at the other car.

EXT. INTERSECTION - DAY

The other car turns left and drives away. The woman drives straight and disappears in the opposite direction.

INT. SECOND CAR - DAY

A mother grips the steering wheel. Her hands shake. She wipes her eyes with one hand.

Her phone sits in the cup holder. A bill notice shows on the screen.

INT. COFFEE SHOP - EVENING

The man from earlier closes his laptop. He stands and leaves.

EXT. SIDEWALK - EVENING

The muscular man walks past the coffee shop. The first man steps outside and nearly bumps into him.

The first man says sorry and steps aside quickly. The muscular man nods and keeps walking.

INT. BEDROOM - NIGHT

The teenage girl sits on her bed. She picks up her phone again. She opens the app and reads more comments. She turns off the phone and lies down.
script_events.coling::ef4cca12-c45c-4b1b-9c67-8db766ad:
INT. AMSTERDAM MERCHANT'S OFFICE - DAY

A MERCHANT sits at his desk. He picks up a letter and reads it.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
Rich ladies in town want cumin now.

He sets the letter down. He opens a ledger and runs his finger down a column of numbers.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The spice costs almost nothing in India.

He closes the ledger and stands up. He walks to the window and looks out at the harbor.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
A ship takes nine months to get there and back.

A SHIPWRIGHT walks past outside carrying lumber. The Merchant turns from the window.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The ship costs a fortune to buy.

He sits back down. He writes numbers on paper with a quill.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The captain demands wages for the whole voyage.

He adds more numbers. He shakes his head.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The crew all want their pay too.

He crosses out the numbers. He throws the quill down.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The boat might sink in a storm.

He picks up a different paper. He stares at it.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The cumin could rot in the hold.

He crumples the paper. He stands and paces.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
A bank would charge terrible interest.

He stops pacing. He sits back down heavily.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The interest would eat all the profit.

He puts his head in his hands.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
If the ship sank, I would lose everything.

He looks up suddenly.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The lender would throw me in prison.

He stands again. He walks to a cabinet and opens it.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
Maybe the lender would just kill me instead.

He takes out a bottle and pours a drink. He drinks it.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
I could pay for one tenth of the cost myself.

He sets the glass down. He smiles.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
I have nine friends with money.

He grabs his coat. He runs out the door.

EXT. AMSTERDAM STREET - DAY

The Merchant walks quickly. He enters a tavern.

INT. TAVERN - DAY

Nine FRIENDS sit at a large table. The Merchant joins them.

MERCHANT
We each pay one tenth.

The friends nod. They shake hands with each other.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
We all buy stock in the voyage.

One friend pulls out a purse. He counts coins onto the table.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
Each of us gets one tenth of the shares.

The other friends add their coins. The pile grows tall.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
We hire the ship with this money.

The Merchant scoops the coins into a bag.

EXT. HARBOR - DAY

A CAPTAIN stands on deck. The Merchant hands him the bag of coins.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
We pay the captain and crew their wages.

The ship raises its sails. It moves away from the dock.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The ship leaves for India.

EXT. OPEN SEA - DAY

The ship crosses blue water under clear skies.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
Nine months pass on the ocean.

INT. AMSTERDAM MERCHANT'S OFFICE - DAY

The Merchant sits at his desk again. A MESSENGER enters.

MESSENGER
Your ship returned this morning.

The Merchant jumps up. He runs out.

EXT. HARBOR - DAY

The ship sits at dock. Workers unload barrels from the hold.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The hold contains mountains of cumin.

The Merchant opens a barrel. He smells the spice and grins.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
We sell it for huge profit.

INT. TAVERN - NIGHT

The ten friends sit together. They divide gold coins into ten piles.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
Each friend takes one tenth of the earnings.

They raise glasses and cheer.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The ladies buy their cumin for less than before.

EXT. SHIPYARD - DAY

Shipwrights hammer nails into a new vessel.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The builders get work making more ships.

EXT. HARBOR - DAY

The Captain counts coins. His crew stands behind him.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The sailors all earn their living.

EXT. INDIAN MARKET - DAY

An INDIAN TRADER sells cumin to a Dutch buyer.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The trader in India gains a steady customer.

INT. AMSTERDAM MERCHANT'S OFFICE - DAY

The Merchant examines a new ledger. The numbers are all large.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
Everyone ends up richer than they started.

He writes the word STOCK at the top of the page.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
None of this happens without stocks.

He dips his quill and keeps writing.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
Capital moves from idle hands to useful work.

He turns the page and starts a new column.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
Risk spreads across many people instead of one.

He sets down the quill. He leans back in his chair.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
No single person faces total ruin anymore.

He picks up a modern newspaper that appears on his desk.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The American market today has lost its way.

He reads an article and frowns.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
It stopped moving capital to productive uses.

He throws the paper down.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
The market became the goal instead of the tool.

He stands and walks to the window again.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
But the basic idea remains brilliant.

EXT. MODERN CITY - DAY (VISION)

Trains rush past. Cars fill highways. People talk on phones.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
Stocks built our railroads and cars.

Factories produce goods. Farms harvest crops.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
They gave us computers and phones and cheap food.

Doctors work in hospitals. Medicine fills shelves.

MERCHANT (V.O.)
They created medicine and all modern things we need.

The Merchant turns from the window. He smiles.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::564547e8-c996-4ee6-8beb-abfe8062:
INT. PHYSICS CLASSROOM - DAY

A TEACHER stands at the board. She claps her hands once.

TEACHER
The energy stays the same no matter where you clap.

She writes on the board.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
On earth the collision sends energy to three places.

She lists them. Sound. Hand damage. Heat.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Some other things happen but we can ignore them.

She picks up chalk and starts writing numbers.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Each hand weighs five hundred grams.

She adds more figures.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
They move at two meters per second.

She solves the equation.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The formula gives us four joules total.

A STUDENT raises her hand.

STUDENT
Do the hands get hurt?

TEACHER
A microscope would show some cells break but not many.

She turns back to the board.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Heat takes most of the energy.

She opens a book and points to a graph.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
This shows a clap lasts twenty milliseconds.

She flips to another page.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
This table lists sound power for different sources.

She taps an entry.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
An alarm clock makes a good comparison.

She writes more numbers.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Even if we miss by a hundred times it still works.

She draws a wave on the board.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
We combine the wave shape with the power numbers.

She finishes her calculation.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
A clap releases two millionths of a joule as sound.

She circles two numbers.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Four joules went in. Two millionths came out as sound.

She divides them.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Sound gets only point zero zero zero zero five percent.

The student raises her hand again.

STUDENT
Where does the rest go?

TEACHER
Heat and hand damage split it somehow.

She shrugs.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
I will not guess the exact split.

She walks to the window and points up.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
In space zero percent becomes sound.

She claps again but makes no noise with her mouth.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
That tiny sound portion just becomes more heat instead.

She returns to the board.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The sound energy was already so small compared to heat.

She underlines her conclusion.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The clap works the same way except you hear nothing.
script_events.coling::8e0f7cff-07ca-48c6-b381-34b577d1:
INT. RESEARCH LAB - DAY

A baby sits in a high chair. She opens her mouth wide. A long "aaaaaa" sound comes out. 

The researcher leans forward and makes a note on her clipboard.

The baby closes her lips. She pushes air through them. A "mmmm" emerges.

The researcher writes again. She turns to her assistant.

RESEARCHER
The mouth works like a switch. Open gives us vowels. Closed gives us consonants.

The assistant nods and picks up a marker. He draws two symbols on the whiteboard: a zero and a one.

ASSISTANT
Binary code for speech.

The baby tries another combination. Her mouth closes then opens fast. Out comes "ma."

The researcher smiles and claps her hands.

A second baby joins them in another chair. This one makes a "pa" sound without prompting.

The assistant adds notes to a chart on the wall.

ASSISTANT
The closed sounds trade places. B becomes D becomes P. The pattern stays the same.

A third baby arrives in a stroller. The parent wheels him close. He babbles "baba" over and over.

The researcher stands and walks to a world map pinned to the board. She places red dots on different countries.

RESEARCHER
Babies invented the words. Adults kept them. We let children name their own parents.

The assistant brings over a stack of books. He opens one to a marked page.

ASSISTANT
It happened with other words too. Poo. Wee. The simple ones.

The researcher flips to another section. She points to a list of Hindi terms written in both scripts and English letters.

RESEARCHER
Grandparents got the same treatment. Daadaa for paternal grandfather. Daadii for paternal grandmother. Naanaa for maternal grandfather. Naanii for maternal grandmother.

The first baby claps her hands. All three babies start babbling at once. The sounds fill the room and blend together.

The researcher closes her book and listens.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::97ce3bac-5618-4fcb-8600-bcf08ed8:
INT. WINE SHOP - DAY

A CUSTOMER stands before rows of bottles. She picks up two similar reds and stares at the labels.

CUSTOMER
How am I supposed to know which one tastes better?

She sets them down. A CLERK approaches from behind the counter.

CLERK
You need to learn what types you prefer first.

The Customer nods and walks to a tasting table in the corner. The Clerk pours three small samples into separate glasses.

CLERK (CONT'D)
Try each one and see what happens.

The Customer lifts the first glass and sips. She makes a face.

CUSTOMER
This costs money though.

The Clerk shrugs and gestures at the bottles around them.

CLERK
That's how it works.

A CHILD enters the shop and reaches for a bottle on a low shelf. The Clerk rushes over and blocks him.

CLERK (CONT'D)
You can't buy this. The law says no.

The Child leaves. The Customer returns to her samples. The Clerk pulls out a chart and taps it.

CLERK (CONT'D)
Wines get divided by where grapes grow and what type they are.

The Customer leans in to read the chart. It lists red types: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir, Merlot, Syrah, Zinfandel. Below that appear white types: Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Gris, Riesling, Gewurztraminer.

CUSTOMER
Some of these have two names.

CLERK
Syrah becomes Shiraz sometimes. Pinot Gris becomes Pinot Grigio.

The Customer drinks her second sample. Her mouth puckers slightly.

CUSTOMER
This one dries out my tongue.

CLERK
That means it has tannins in it.

The Customer picks up the third glass and swirls it.

CLERK (CONT'D)
Cabernet Sauvignon gives you that dry feeling a lot.

She samples the white wine next. Her face brightens.

CUSTOMER
This one tastes sharp.

CLERK
That's acid you're sensing.

The Customer takes another sip and pauses.

CUSTOMER
And this one has sugar.

The Clerk nods and opens a bottle from the shelf. He pours a fresh sample.

CLERK
Smell this one first.

The Customer sniffs the glass deeply.

CUSTOMER
It smells like wood.

CLERK
That's oak you're getting.

The Customer sets down her glass and looks around at all the bottles.

CUSTOMER
Which one should I actually buy?

CLERK
No wine works for everyone.

The Customer picks up a cheap jug from the bottom shelf.

CUSTOMER
What if I like this more than that fancy Bordeaux up there?

She points at an expensive bottle on the top shelf.

CLERK
Then buy the jug.

The Customer hesitates and puts the jug back.

CUSTOMER
I still don't know what I want.

The Clerk walks to a different section and pulls down a bottle.

CLERK
Tell me roughly what you're after. I'll find something in your range.

The Customer follows him to the register.
script_events.coling::ae050f0f-463e-4780-8638-108ef778:
INT. LECTURE HALL - DAY

A PROFESSOR stands at a podium. Students sit in rows.

PROFESSOR
Alexander won for many reasons.

He walks to a map on the wall.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
First, he faced fewer enemies than we once believed.

A STUDENT raises her hand.

STUDENT
What do the modern historians say?

PROFESSOR
Arrian claimed six hundred thousand Persians showed up. Modern experts reject that number.

He picks up a piece of chalk.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Moving more than one hundred thousand soldiers into battle was nearly impossible back then.

He writes "25,000" on the board.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Hans Delbrück thinks only twenty five thousand Persians fought there.

A different STUDENT flips through a book.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Most scholars, like Engels and Green, put the total at one hundred thousand or less at Issus. That included eleven thousand cavalry, ten thousand Persian Immortals, and ten thousand Greek mercenaries. Warry counts one hundred eight thousand total.

The Professor sets down the chalk.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Second, the Macedonians brought better gear to the fight. Only the Greek mercenaries on the Persian side could match them.

A student takes notes.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
The Persians relied heavily on peltasts. Even so, both armies fielded roughly the same number of close combat infantry.

He points to a diagram.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Third, Companion cavalry dominated the world then. Persian horsemen could not compete.

Another student nods.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Fourth, Alexander used the hammer and anvil. One force holds the enemy in place while another crashes into their rear, causing massive destruction and panic.

He taps the diagram.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
This tactic inflicts terrible physical and mental damage. Most battle deaths happen during retreat. Numbers mean nothing without discipline, which armies need above all else.

The bell rings. Students gather their books.
script_events.coling::f249dac3-f3a2-4db9-9758-e18c9f8f:
INT. SMALL TOWN - DAY

A crowd fills the street. Everyone walks toward apartment buildings. Some residents stop and point at empty lots across town.

EXT. CONSTRUCTION SITE - DAY

Builders arrive with trucks. They unload lumber and tools. The first foundation gets poured.

EXT. SALES OFFICE - DAY

A line forms outside. The door opens. People rush inside and grab applications.

INT. SALES OFFICE - CONTINUOUS

Buyers wave cash and checks. The agent raises the price on a board. More hands go up.

EXT. HOUSE NUMBER ONE - DAY

A family carries boxes through the front door. They smile and shake hands with the builder.

EXT. HOUSE NUMBER TWO - LATER

Another family moves in. The agent posts a new price sheet. The numbers climb higher.

EXT. CONSTRUCTION SITE - WEEKS LATER

The builders finish the last house. They pack their tools. No one waits at the sales office anymore.

INT. SALES OFFICE - DAY

The agent erases the old price. He writes a lower number. Still no buyers enter.

INT. HOUSE NUMBER ONE - DAY

The first family opens their mortgage statement. Their faces fall. They pick up the phone.

EXT. APARTMENT BUILDING - DAY

The family loads a moving truck. They drive away from their house. A FOR SALE sign goes up in the yard.

EXT. NEIGHBORHOOD - MONTAGE

More signs appear on every lawn. The agent drops prices again. Houses sit empty.

EXT. SALES OFFICE - MONTHS LATER

A few people walk up slowly. The agent shows them inside. They sign papers at the new low price.

INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

A chart goes up on the wall. One line shoots up then crashes down. An economist points at the peak and then the valley. People in suits nod and take notes. The cycle diagram gets circled in red marker.
script_events.coling::f4f3b137-0da5-4cc5-a8e0-08f5a284:
INT. COMPUTER LAB - DAY

A teacher stands at a whiteboard. She draws a wire.

TEACHER
A signal enters the wire.

She marks a point on the diagram.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
It moves forward. The voltage rises.

She sketches a wave form climbing upward.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The wave takes time to pass through the cable. Light speed gets cut to point six four in copper.

A student raises his hand. The teacher nods at him.

STUDENT
So one meter needs five nanoseconds?

TEACHER
Yes. Now bits start flowing. One hundred million bits per second go into the wire.

She writes numbers on the board. Her chalk taps the surface.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
One thousand nanoseconds hold one hundred bits. Ten nanoseconds hold one bit.

The student leans forward in his seat.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
A two meter cable contains two bits at once. A one hundred meter cable holds fifty bits.

She draws a long line representing the cable. She marks dots along it.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The signal differs at each point. Encoding adds more bits in practice.

She pulls up an image on the projector. Waveforms appear on screen.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
This shows a real ethernet signal. The shape curves and bends.

She clicks to the next slide. Multiple traces overlap.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
This diagram stacks many signals together. We call it an eye.

The student squints at the screen.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The system reads three zones. Top means one thing. Middle means another. Bottom means a third.

She points to black gaps in the pattern.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
These holes must stay open. Noise shrinks them.

The gaps look small and ragged.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The eyes close down. Detection becomes hard. They vanish and the signal dies.

She turns back to face the class.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The cable must behave in specific ways. Wire spacing matters. Wire thickness matters. Materials along the path matter.

A second student speaks up from the back.

SECOND STUDENT
What about interference?

TEACHER
Other signals leak between the pairs. The wires get twisted at different rates. This cancels the interference out.

She draws twisted pairs on the board.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Standards define the parameters. Hardware expects these values.

She opens a video file. Barbed wire fills the screen.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Someone ran ethernet through barbed wire once. It worked.

The video plays. Data flows through the fence wire.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The barbed wire pairs run close and parallel. The pairs separate far from each other.

She pauses the video.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
This configuration mimics cat five cable. The geometry creates the right effect.

The bell rings. Students gather their bags.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
If the pair wires had angled away or the pairs had bunched together the signal would have failed.

The students file out. The teacher erases the board.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::817b2dbf-699e-4bec-825a-2bbdf598:
INT. CYBERSECURITY LAB - DAY

A NETWORK ADMIN sits at a desk. A screen shows traffic flowing through a network.

An alert pops up on the monitor.

The admin clicks a button. The system blocks the bad traffic.

A new attack arrives. The system does not recognize it.

The attack gets through. Red warnings fill the screen.

The admin stands and walks to a whiteboard.

She writes the word SIGMA at the top.

A RESEARCHER enters the room carrying a laptop.

The researcher opens the laptop and starts typing.

Code appears on the screen. A program begins to run.

The program creates fake attacks. These attacks look real but come from the computer itself.

The fake attacks hit the detection system.

Some attacks get through. The system fails to stop them.

The researcher saves the attacks that got through.

He feeds them back into the system as training data.

The system learns from these new examples.

The researcher runs the program again.

More fake attacks emerge. The system blocks most of them now.

A few still get through.

The researcher saves these and adds them to the training set.

The admin returns with coffee. She sits down.

The system trains again on the expanded data.

The researcher launches a third round of fake attacks.

This time the system catches nearly all of them.

The detection rate climbs higher on a graph.

The admin nods and makes a note.

The researcher runs one final test.

The system now stops every attack thrown at it.

The graph reaches one hundred percent.

The admin and researcher shake hands.

They save the improved system to a file.

The researcher closes his laptop.

The admin returns to monitoring the network.

New real attacks arrive at the network edge.

The strengthened system blocks them all.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::0a6f4d1d-1792-4bfc-a4cf-9fcf0636:
INT. UNIVERSITY LAB - DAY

A researcher draws a graph on a whiteboard with dots and arrows that branch and merge.

RESEARCHER
Trees show how species evolve, but sometimes branches join back together.

She adds numbers to the drawing.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
We count the merges by adding up incoming arrows, then subtracting nodes and adding one.

A student enters carrying three diagrams.

STUDENT
Can we build one network that fits all these trees and uses the fewest merges?

The researcher nods and opens her laptop.

RESEARCHER
I wrote a program that solves this for three trees.

She types and a timer appears on screen.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
The speed depends on how many merges we need, multiplied by some fixed number, then multiplied by a simple calculation based on tree size.

The student sits down.

STUDENT
Someone already made a program for two trees that runs in a specific time.

The researcher stands and walks to a filing cabinet.

RESEARCHER
But nobody managed to create one for more than three trees with similar speed until now.

She pulls out old papers.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
The two-tree version uses something called agreement forests to run faster.

The student flips through the papers.

STUDENT
Earlier attempts for multiple trees just tested every possible network shape.

The researcher returns to the whiteboard and erases part of it.

RESEARCHER
Those methods were too slow because they lacked that fixed multiplier property.

She draws a new diagram showing forest sections.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Agreement forests work differently when we have more than two trees.

The student looks confused.

STUDENT
So even finding the right forest doesn't tell us how to build the network?

The researcher circles parts of her drawing.

RESEARCHER
Exactly, so I proved new rules that let us rebuild the network without testing every shape.

She writes an equation.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
These rules work for any number of input trees except for one crucial step.

The student leans forward.

STUDENT
What step?

RESEARCHER
Matching network dots to tree dots, which reduces guesswork during construction.

She closes her notebook.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Someone needs to prove this matching works for four or more trees, which remains unsolved.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::0c653e8b-8157-47f3-bdaa-142023fb:
INT. RESEARCH LAB - DAY

A researcher walks to a whiteboard and writes down a simple equation.

The equation shows that a number in binary form cannot be less than zero.

A colleague enters the room and sits at a desk.

The first researcher explains this connects to major unsolved problems in math.

A third person arrives with coffee and sets it on the table.

The team begins work on proving that solving this takes a very long time.

One researcher opens a laptop and types.

The proof depends on an old guess by two scientists named Shub and Smale.

That guess says computing factorials is hard in a certain way.

A phone rings and someone answers it briefly.

The team discusses a proof system called IPS that was created by Grochow and Pitassi.

One researcher stands and paces near the window.

They discover that short proofs of their equation would link two different proof methods.

A student knocks and enters with printouts of papers.

The researchers spread the papers across the desk.

Their work extends ideas from an earlier paper by Forbes and others.

Someone draws a diagram on the whiteboard with colored markers.

The earlier work found limits for weaker versions of IPS.

A researcher erases part of the board and rewrites a formula.

The new results show their equation captures something important about proof systems.

One person leaves to get lunch for the group.

The remaining researchers write that semi-algebraic reasoning beats algebraic reasoning for strong systems.

Food arrives and they eat while continuing to talk.

They list their first main result on a fresh board.

The Shub-Smale guess implies their equation needs huge proofs in IPS over rational numbers.

Someone spills water and wipes it up quickly.

The equation uses powers of two and variables that are zero or one.

A researcher adds that a related conjecture also gives similar limits.

Another team member nods and makes notes in a journal.

They state no one had found such limits before for IPS.

A clock on the wall shows two hours have passed.

They note the limits also did not exist for simpler systems like Frege.

Someone points out their equation is not just a direct translation from logic.

A researcher circles a key phrase on the board.

This means limits on their equation do not automatically give limits for Frege.

The team moves to discuss their second main result.

One person writes a new heading about algebraic versus semi-algebraic proofs.

They show that short proofs of their equation are necessary for full simulation.

A researcher highlights this condition in yellow marker.

For strong systems this condition also becomes sufficient.

The team introduces a new proof system they call CPS.

Someone writes CPS in large letters.

This system simulates all known semi-algebraic methods and most other concrete systems.

A researcher explains CPS works like IPS but for inequalities over real numbers.

They prove IPS equals CPS in power exactly when IPS can refute their equation efficiently.

The team sits back as the proof concludes on the board.
script_events.coling::a098aa01-9d81-40a6-8321-ca3d4a88:
INT. RESEARCH LAB - DAY

A team gathers around a table covered with data plots.

LEAD SCIENTIST
We need to cluster this data set.

She points to a massive graph on the screen.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Graph-Laplacians will help us do that.

A junior researcher opens a laptop.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
I will start the spectral embedding now.

The computer begins processing.

LEAD SCIENTIST
The embedding gives us fewer dimensions to work with.

Numbers scroll across the monitor.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
K-means can handle the reduced data better.

The lead scientist frowns at the progress bar.

LEAD SCIENTIST
But the cost is still too high for large sets.

She walks to a whiteboard and writes an equation.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
Computing the eigendecomposition takes a huge Krylov subspace.

The junior researcher nods and adds another concern.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
We also still have all the original data points after embedding.

The lead scientist circles a number on the board.

LEAD SCIENTIST
That ruins our efficiency gains.

She erases part of the equation.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
K-means relaxations scale badly with data size.

The junior researcher pulls up a failed clustering result.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
They get stuck in local minima too.

The lead scientist sits down and opens a notebook.

LEAD SCIENTIST
Their success depends on the starting guess we pick.

She sketches a new diagram.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
We will shift our attention to a subset instead.

The junior researcher leans forward.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
Which subset do you mean?

The lead scientist taps the diagram.

LEAD SCIENTIST
A target subset of graph vertices only.

She begins writing code on her laptop.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
I am developing two new algorithms right now.

The code compiles successfully.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
These algorithms create a low-dimensional representation of the graph.

She runs the first algorithm.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
They preserve global distances between target nodes.

The junior researcher examines the output.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
The target subset clustering matches the full spectral clustering.

The lead scientist starts the second algorithm.

LEAD SCIENTIST
A reduced-order model of the graph-Laplacian makes this possible.

Results appear on screen.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
It approximates the diffusion transfer function accurately.

She filters the inputs and outputs.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
We restrict everything to the target subset.

The junior researcher checks the Krylov dimension.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
The required subspace dimension dropped dramatically.

The lead scientist runs k-means on the subset.

LEAD SCIENTIST
Conventional algorithms work in their most robust regime now.

She pulls up synthetic test data.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
We verified this with numerical experiments.

The junior researcher loads real data next.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
Both synthetic and real data confirm it.

The lead scientist opens a transfer function file.

LEAD SCIENTIST
Our ROM approach works in a data-driven way.

She gestures at a massive network diagram.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
This becomes the only option for extremely large graphs we cannot access directly.

The junior researcher lists applications on the board.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
We can use these algorithms for representative subset clustering alone.

The lead scientist adds another use case.

LEAD SCIENTIST
They also work for quality control checks.

She writes a third application.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
They reduce problem size enough to enable sophisticated algorithms.

The junior researcher mentions an example.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
Like SDP-based k-means instead of Lloyd's algorithm.

The lead scientist closes her laptop.

LEAD SCIENTIST
They can become building blocks for a multi-level approach.

She files the notebook away.

LEAD SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
That divide-and-conquer algorithm will handle the full graph.

The junior researcher saves all the results.

JUNIOR RESEARCHER
We will report that method in our next article.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::d9b96a87-ee9b-46e9-995f-edfccd85:
INT. RESEARCH LAB - DAY

A TEAM enters the room and sits at a long table.

LEAD ENGINEER
We have a task. We must build codes for storage systems.

She draws on the board. The codes will have n nodes and k data units.

MATHEMATICIAN
Any t nodes can fail at once.

LEAD ENGINEER
Each one gets fixed using only r nearby nodes.

The team writes down the rules. The values r, k, n, and t must all be positive whole numbers.

MATHEMATICIAN
We need r to be less than k, and k less than n.

LEAD ENGINEER
Also t cannot exceed n minus k.

A JUNIOR MEMBER stands and walks to the window.

JUNIOR MEMBER
How do we fix multiple breaks?

LEAD ENGINEER
We fix them one after another in a line.

She points to each failed node in turn on the diagram.

MATHEMATICIAN
The first new node uses only the live nodes around it.

LEAD ENGINEER
The second new node uses live nodes and also the first new node we just fixed.

The junior member nods and returns to his seat.

JUNIOR MEMBER
Do the new nodes hold exact copies?

MATHEMATICIAN
No. They hold different data that still works.

LEAD ENGINEER
We call this functional repair.

She erases part of the board and starts a new section.

LEAD ENGINEER (CONT'D)
Our codes form the most general class. Other teams have made special cases of what we do here.

The mathematician opens a folder and spreads papers across the table.

MATHEMATICIAN
Our goal is to make the rate as high as we can.

LEAD ENGINEER
We found a lower limit on n when t equals two.

She writes a formula. The team leans forward to study it.

MATHEMATICIAN
This extends an old result from another paper.

LEAD ENGINEER
We also found a limit when t equals three.

MATHEMATICIAN
That one beats the previous best limit.

The junior member picks up a marker and adds notes to the board.

JUNIOR MEMBER
Can we hit these limits?

LEAD ENGINEER
Yes. We built codes that reach them exactly.

MATHEMATICIAN
This proves our limits are tight.

The lead engineer circles several numbers.

LEAD ENGINEER
It also shows functional codes and exact codes need the same length for some choices.

JUNIOR MEMBER
What field do we use?

MATHEMATICIAN
Binary. Just zeros and ones.

LEAD ENGINEER
So real systems can use them.

The team gathers their notes and stands to leave.
script_events.coling::6b54ef51-f42e-4ac2-840e-6b536faa:
INT. EUROPEAN COMMISSION BUILDING - DAY

A COMMISSIONER stands at a podium and signs a new bill into law.

INT. PARLIAMENT CHAMBER - DAY

Members of Parliament receive the bill and begin marking changes on paper.

INT. COUNCIL MEETING ROOM - DAY

Council members vote to block the bill with a show of hands.

INT. COMMISSIONER'S OFFICE - DAY

The Commissioner tears up the rejected bill and drops it in a bin.

INT. SMALL COUNTRY DELEGATION ROOM - DAY

Ten representatives from a small nation cast their votes on a screen.

INT. LARGE COUNTRY DELEGATION ROOM - DAY

One hundred representatives from a large nation cast their votes on the same screen.

INT. VOTE COUNTING CENTER - DAY

A technician calculates that both groups carry equal weight in the final tally.

INT. PARLIAMENT FLOOR - CONTINUOUS

A Member of Parliament tries to propose a new law but security escorts her away from the microphone.

INT. HISTORY ARCHIVE ROOM - DAY

Old photographs show unelected assembly members sitting in the first Parliament sessions.

INT. PARLIAMENT CHAMBER - 1979 - DAY

Citizens enter voting booths for the first direct elections.

INT. MODERN PARLIAMENT CHAMBER - DAY

The Speaker grants Parliament members new permissions to amend legislation.

EXT. CITY SQUARE - DAY

A citizen hands out flyers promoting her political views to passersby.

INT. PETITION OFFICE - DAY

Workers stack boxes containing one million signatures on a desk.

INT. COMMISSION REVIEW ROOM - DAY

Commissioners read the petition and add it to their agenda.

INT. PARLIAMENT RECEPTION AREA - DAY

A citizen submits a complaint form about a policy that affects her business.

INT. ELECTION HEADQUARTERS - DAY

Officials prepare ballots for the five year Parliament elections.

INT. VOTING STATION - DAY

A voter marks her choice using a proportional representation ballot.

INT. PARLIAMENT SEATING CHART OFFICE - DAY

An administrator assigns seven hundred fifty seats to the new Members.

INT. PARLIAMENT CHAMBER - DAY

Members from small countries occupy more seats per capita than members from large countries.

INT. CONSERVATIVE PARTY MEETING ROOM - DAY

The European People's Party celebrates winning the most seats.

INT. SOCIALIST PARTY MEETING ROOM - DAY

The Party of European Socialists plans their opposition strategy.

INT. COURT OF JUSTICE - DAY

A judge rules that member states must fund their own political parties.

INT. INQUIRY HEARING ROOM - DAY

Parliament members question officials about administrative failures.

INT. OMBUDSMAN OFFICE - DAY

The Ombudsman opens an investigation file before any trial begins.

INT. QUESTION PERIOD CHAMBER - DAY

A Parliament member demands the Commission answer her written questions.

INT. CENSURE VOTE CHAMBER - 1999 - DAY

Two thirds of Parliament votes to censure the entire Santer Commission.

INT. CONSULTATION MEETING ROOM - DAY

The Commission listens to Parliament advice on a new proposal.

INT. LEGISLATIVE DRAFTING ROOM - DAY

A Parliament member writes a bill but cannot submit it without Commission approval.

INT. FINAL VOTE CHAMBER - DAY

The Council and Commission pass the law while Parliament watches.

EXT. PARLIAMENT STEPS - DUSK

A citizen protester holds a sign reading "Power to the People."

INT. EMPTY PARLIAMENT CHAMBER - NIGHT

The lights go dark on the empty seats.
script_events.coling::049da962-b4ab-4271-80d7-6c08dd71:
INT. LECTURE HALL - DAY

MARTIN LUTHER stands at a podium. Students fill wooden benches.

LUTHER
Mary remained a virgin her entire life. She bore God himself.

A YOUNG MONK raises his hand.

YOUNG MONK
What about the Immaculate Conception?

LUTHER
I accept it fully.

Years pass. Luther's hair grays. He sits at a desk writing.

LUTHER (V.O.)
I have reconsidered. The Church has not defined this doctrine yet.

He crosses out a line in his manuscript.

LUTHER (V.O.)
But Mary lived without sin. That much is certain.

INT. CHURCH - MORNING

Luther walks past a banner for the Feast of the Assumption. He stops.

LUTHER
The Bible says nothing of this.

He takes the banner down.

INT. STUDY - NIGHT

Luther opens a book. A COLLEAGUE enters.

COLLEAGUE
Do the saints live after death?

LUTHER
Yes. Mary and all the faithful continue.

INT. CLASSROOM - DAY

Luther paces before students. His robes are different now.

LUTHER
I have preached about Mary for decades. Sometimes with simple faith. Sometimes with complex arguments.

A student writes notes.

LUTHER
My views connect to Christ. Everything flows from him to our worship.

INT. CATHEDRAL - DAY

Luther watches Catholics pray before a statue of Mary. He frowns.

LUTHER (V.O.)
The Papists have crossed a line. They confuse admiration with worship.

He turns away from the statue.

INT. TOWN SQUARE - DAY

A PRIEST sells indulgences. People pray to saint medallions.

LUTHER
This is idolatry. You pray to the dead as if they were God.

INT. WITTENBERG CHURCH - DAY

Luther, now elderly, climbs into the pulpit. Parishioners wait below.

LUTHER
I will speak once more about Mary.

He opens his Bible. One month later, he dies.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::0b4651e6-8f56-467b-81ae-810fa781:
INT. TECH COMPANY OFFICE - DAY

A programmer sits at a desk and types code on her screen.

PROGRAMMER
This scheme checks if a message is real.

She clicks a button. A green box appears on the monitor.

PROGRAMMER (CONT'D)
The check passes. Now I know who sent this and that no one changed it.

She stands and walks to a whiteboard. She draws two boxes with an arrow between them.

PROGRAMMER (CONT'D)
We use this for software updates and bank transfers and contracts.

A coworker enters the room and stops beside her.

COWORKER
Does it work for legal documents?

The programmer nods and picks up a marker.

PROGRAMMER
Some countries accept it in court. Canada does. So does Brazil and India and Mexico and Turkey.

She writes a list of country names on the board.

PROGRAMMER (CONT'D)
The European Union accepts it too.

The coworker sits down at the table.

COWORKER
How does it actually work?

PROGRAMMER
It uses two different keys. One key signs the message. The other key checks it.

She draws two keys on the board with different shapes.

PROGRAMMER (CONT'D)
Someone sends a message through the internet. The signature proves who sent it.

The coworker leans forward.

COWORKER
Can someone fake it?

PROGRAMMER
A handwritten signature is easy to copy. This one is much harder.

She erases part of the board and writes new text.

PROGRAMMER (CONT'D)
The system must be set up right or it fails.

COWORKER
What if someone denies they sent something?

PROGRAMMER
The signature proves they did. They cannot lie about it if their key stays secret.

She adds a clock symbol to the drawing.

PROGRAMMER (CONT'D)
Some systems add a time stamp. Then the signature stays valid even if the key leaks later.

The coworker stands and walks to the door.

COWORKER
What can you sign?

PROGRAMMER
Anything digital. Emails. Contracts. Any message that a computer can read.

She closes her laptop and follows him out.
script_events.coling::203e204e-a867-4d1d-97e8-bdd789e6:
INT. COMPUTER LAB - DAY

A researcher sits at a desk and types code into a computer.

RESEARCHER
We built a system that takes spoken words and turns them into text on the screen.

The computer displays a microphone icon. The researcher speaks into a headset.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
The computer listens and writes down what I say.

Text appears on the monitor as she talks. A colleague enters the room.

COLLEAGUE
How does it work?

RESEARCHER
Three fields came together. Computer science provided the base. Linguistics added language rules. Engineering made the hardware run.

The colleague picks up a manual from the desk.

COLLEAGUE
What about going the other way?

RESEARCHER
That exists too. Text becomes speech instead.

She opens a new program window. A dialog box appears.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
Some systems need training first. A person reads sample text aloud. The computer studies that voice. Then it knows that speaker better.

The colleague sits down at a second terminal.

COLLEAGUE
What if you skip the training?

RESEARCHER
Those are speaker-independent systems. They work for anyone right away.

The researcher clicks through a series of demos on her screen.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
People use this for many tasks. You can dial a phone by voice. You can route calls. You can control lights and appliances at home. You can search for words in recordings. You can enter data like credit card numbers. Doctors dictate reports. Some programs identify who is speaking. Others type out emails. Pilots control aircraft this way.

The colleague leans forward.

COLLEAGUE
Is recognizing the speaker different from recognizing the words?

RESEARCHER
Yes. Speaker identification finds out who is talking. That helps the system if it trained on that voice. Security systems use it to verify identity.

She pulls up a timeline chart on the wall monitor.

RESEARCHER (CONT'D)
This technology has a long past. Many breakthroughs happened over the years. Recently deep learning changed everything. Big data helped too. Academic papers multiplied. Industries adopted the methods. Companies now deploy these systems everywhere.

The colleague nods and both turn back to their screens.
script_events.coling::9be05dd7-05a8-4b0e-a617-ae611f4d:
INT. LABORATORY - DAY

A PROFESSOR stands at a blackboard. She writes "CONTROL THEORY" in chalk.

PROFESSOR
This field studies how to make machines behave the way we want them to.

An ENGINEER enters the room carrying a box of tools.

ENGINEER
We build systems that move toward a goal without delay or error.

The Professor draws a simple loop on the board.

PROFESSOR
A controller watches a process variable.

She adds an arrow.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Then it checks the set point.

The Engineer opens his toolbox and removes a gauge.

ENGINEER
The controller finds the gap between what is and what should be.

PROFESSOR
We call that gap the error signal.

She writes "SP-PV" on the board.

ENGINEER
The system uses this signal to fix itself.

He adjusts the gauge in his hands.

PROFESSOR
The process variable moves closer to the set point.

A STUDENT walks in and sits down.

STUDENT
What else do we look at?

PROFESSOR
We check if the system can be controlled at all.

ENGINEER
We also test if we can observe what happens inside.

The Professor erases part of the board and draws boxes connected by lines.

PROFESSOR
Engineers draw block diagrams to show these relationships.

STUDENT
What goes in those boxes?

ENGINEER
Transfer functions. They connect input to output using equations.

The Professor picks up a book from her desk.

PROFESSOR
Maxwell described governors in the eighteen hundreds.

She opens the book and points to a page.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Routh advanced the field in eighteen seventy four.

ENGINEER
Sturm and Hurwitz added stability rules in eighteen ninety five.

The Student takes notes.

PROFESSOR
Minorsky developed PID control starting in nineteen twenty two.

The Engineer sets down his gauge and picks up a circuit board.

ENGINEER
Factories use this theory to automate production lines.

STUDENT
Where else does it apply?

PROFESSOR
Aircraft systems rely on these principles.

The Engineer connects wires to the circuit board.

ENGINEER
Communications networks need control theory too.

PROFESSOR
Robotics emerged as a new field from this work.

The Student closes his notebook.

STUDENT
Does it only work for machines?

PROFESSOR
No. Feedback appears in biology.

ENGINEER
Computer systems use these ideas.

PROFESSOR
Sociologists apply control theory to groups.

The Engineer tests the circuit board with a meter.

ENGINEER
