Operations research depends on feedback models.

PROFESSOR
Wherever feedback exists, this theory helps.

The three of them look at the board together as the lights fade.
script_events.coling::5293d27b-2991-4ca1-93ab-e336d0eb:
INT. PHARMACEUTICAL RESEARCH LAB - DAY

A SCIENTIST enters the lab and walks to a computer workstation.

She opens a file showing a protein structure rotating on screen.

The protein target floats in three dimensions as she studies it.

She sketches a small molecule on paper that might fit the protein's shape.

Her COLLEAGUE arrives and looks over her shoulder at the drawing.

They discuss how the molecule's charge could match the protein's surface.

The scientist types commands and a model of the molecule appears next to the protein.

The two shapes move together on screen and lock into place.

The colleague nods and points at the binding site where they connect.

The scientist clicks a button and the computer calculates binding strength.

Numbers flash on screen showing how tight the connection is.

She prints the results and walks them to her SUPERVISOR's office.

The supervisor reads the report and frowns at the data.

He explains that binding strength alone does not make a safe drug.

The scientist returns to her desk looking concerned.

She pulls up a new program that tests other properties of the molecule.

The program runs and shows how the body might absorb the compound.

Another test reveals how fast the liver breaks it down.

A third analysis predicts possible harmful effects on organs.

The colleague joins her again and they review all the new results together.

Several properties look poor and they mark those in red.

The scientist modifies the molecule's structure and runs all tests again.

This time more results turn green on the display.

She saves this version and adds it to a list of candidates.

The supervisor returns and asks how many candidates they have now.

The scientist counts twelve molecules that passed the early screens.

He selects three for the next round of lab tests.

A TECHNICIAN enters carrying a tray of test tubes and cell samples.

She takes the three molecule designs and begins preparing actual compounds.

The scientist watches as the technician mixes chemicals at the bench.

Small vials fill with clear liquid containing the new drug candidates.

The technician labels each vial and places them in the incubator.

Everyone waits as the first real experiment begins.
script_events.coling::d2400f57-c1e4-49a6-aaa9-1c92f181:
INT. RESEARCH LAB - DAY

A scientist sits at a computer and loads a data set onto the screen.

She runs the first statistical test. The result shows no pattern.

She tries a second test with different variables. Again, nothing appears.

She continues testing. The tenth attempt produces a significant result.

She prints only that tenth result and puts it in a folder.

Her colleague enters the room and asks what she found.

She shows him the single positive result. She does not mention the nine failures.

He nods and leaves to write up the findings.

The scientist opens a new data set. She begins searching for correlations between random variables.

She tests hundreds of combinations. Most show nothing.

One combination finally displays a correlation. She saves it.

She moves to a different part of the data. She splits cases into groups.

The first grouping shows no difference. She tries another split.

The third grouping reveals a difference in means. She highlights it.

She closes the file. She has three findings to report.

Each finding appears significant at the five percent level.

She does not record how many tests she ran in total.

The colleague returns with a draft. He describes their discovery as important.

Neither of them mentions the probability. With so many tests, false results become certain.

The data contained random noise. The noise created spurious patterns.

They mistook noise for truth.

The colleague submits the paper to a journal. Reviewers read it.

The reviewers see only the reported tests. They do not know about the hidden tests.

The paper gets accepted. It gets published.

Other researchers read the paper. They believe the findings.

They try to replicate the results. Their attempts fail.

The original findings were false positives. The dredging process guaranteed some tests would appear significant.

The scientist opens another data set. She starts testing again.
script_events.coling::5e64f27a-ba00-4d66-8985-34fc48e8:
INT. FAMILY HOME - DAY

A teenage girl sits on her bed. She closes her eyes and wishes for something different.

She opens her mouth to speak but stops herself. She bites her lip and stays quiet.

Her mother walks past the door without looking in.

The girl picks up a pillow and screams into it. Tears fall down her face.

She throws the pillow across the room. It hits the wall and drops to the floor.

She stands up and wipes her eyes. Her face goes blank and still.

Her mother calls from downstairs. The girl walks to the top of the stairs.

She answers in a flat voice with no feeling in it.

Her mother yells something mean. The girl does not react at all.

She turns and goes back to her room. She picks up dirty clothes from the floor.

She carries the laundry downstairs before anyone tells her to do it.

Her mother looks surprised. The girl puts the clothes in the washer and starts it.

She asks if she can go to the library. Her mother says yes without arguing.

The girl walks to her friend's house first. Her friend's mother opens the door and smiles.

They sit at the kitchen table. The friend's mother talks about school and listens when the girl speaks.

The girl asks a question about college. The friend's mother gives her a helpful answer.

The girl writes the information in a notebook. She thanks the woman and leaves.

She walks to the library and finds books about families. She sits and reads for an hour.

She learns new words for what happens at home. She copies passages into her notebook.

She checks out three books and walks home. Her mother is waiting in the kitchen.

Her mother accuses her of stealing money. The girl has not taken anything.

She says she did not take it in the same flat voice. Her mother keeps yelling.

The girl does not cry or yell back. She just stands there and waits.

Her mother finally stops talking. The girl goes upstairs to her room.

She opens one of the library books and reads more. She highlights a sentence about breaking patterns.

Her friend texts and asks her to come over for dinner. The girl texts back yes.

She tells her mother she is going out. Her mother complains but allows it.

The girl walks back to her friend's house. The friend's mother sets an extra place at the table.

They eat together and talk about normal things. The girl smiles for the first time all day.
script_events.coling::8df379b4-a387-496d-947d-b224f86b:
INT. RANGER STATION - DAY

A RANGER pins two photos on the wall.

RANGER
Black bears need one plan. Grizzlies need another.

EXT. FOREST TRAIL - DAY

A hiker stops. A CUB appears ahead. The MOTHER BEAR steps between them.

INT. RANGER STATION - CONTINUOUS

The Ranger taps the first photo.

RANGER
Black bears come in black, brown, and cinnamon. Their ears point up.

She moves her finger down the bear's back.

RANGER (CONT'D)
No hump here.

EXT. MOUNTAIN SLOPE - DAY

A grizzly walks past. Sunlight hits its blonde fur.

INT. RANGER STATION - CONTINUOUS

The Ranger touches the second photo.

RANGER
Grizzlies show brown, blonde, or silver coats. This hump rises on the back. The face curves inward like a dish. The ears form circles.

She spreads her arms wide.

RANGER (CONT'D)
Full grown, they tower over black bears.

EXT. BERRY PATCH - DAY

A grizzly lifts its nose. It turns toward a scent half a mile away.

INT. RANGER STATION - CONTINUOUS

RANGER
Their noses catch smells from incredible distances. Summer arrives and they eat. Fall comes and they eat more.

She picks up a red canister.

RANGER (CONT'D)
Bear spray shoots pepper in a cone shape. It reaches thirty feet out. A bear charges and you aim.

EXT. CAMPSITE - DAY

A hiker clips the canister to her belt. She feels for the trigger without looking.

EXT. TRAIL - DAY

A bear runs toward her. She counts the distance. Forty feet. She pulls the trigger. The spray shoots out.

INT. RANGER STATION - CONTINUOUS

RANGER
Never spray your tent or your pack. The pepper is too strong.

EXT. DIFFERENT TRAIL - DAY

Two hikers walk and talk loudly. Their voices echo.

RANGER (V.O.)
Human voices travel far. Bears hear them and turn away.

A third hiker joins them.

RANGER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
Groups scare bears more than solo hikers do.

EXT. MEADOW - DAY

A bear runs. It passes a man in seconds.

RANGER (V.O.)
They hit thirty-five miles per hour. You cannot outrun them.

The bear climbs a tree.

RANGER (V.O.) (CONT'D)
Trees offer no safety.

EXT. CAMPSITE - NIGHT

A hiker seals food in a container. Wind blows her scent toward the woods. A bear in the distance turns away.

EXT. TRAIL ENCOUNTER - DAY

A hiker sees a bear. She plants her feet. She shouts. She looks at the ground.

The bear rises on its back legs. The hiker stays still.

A small black bear rushes forward. The hiker swings her fists.

EXT. ANOTHER TRAIL - DAY

A grizzly charges. A man drops and curls up. He locks his hands behind his neck. The bear sniffs him. It walks away.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::4979d6d3-5de1-40a4-9a75-cfd7fc60:
INT. DOCTOR'S OFFICE - DAY

A PATIENT sits across from DR. MARTINEZ at a desk.

DR. MARTINEZ
Call me before you take your pills that morning.

The patient nods and writes this down.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
If you have diabetes, phone me about your insulin too.

The patient looks up from the notepad.

PATIENT
I had asthma as a kid.

Dr. Martinez leans forward.

DR. MARTINEZ
Then we need to take extra steps during the test.

The patient shifts in the chair.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Stop taking aspirin one week before.

PATIENT
When can I start again?

DR. MARTINEZ
We will talk about that after.

The patient puts down the pen.

PATIENT
I might be pregnant.

Dr. Martinez picks up a file from the desk.

DR. MARTINEZ
Then we must weigh the risks carefully.

The patient touches her stomach.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
The test can find a blocked artery in your heart.

PATIENT
What happens if you find one?

DR. MARTINEZ
We may need to put in a stent right away.

The patient looks worried.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Are you nursing a baby now?

PATIENT
Yes, she is three months old.

Dr. Martinez writes on a prescription pad.

DR. MARTINEZ
Use formula for two days after the test.

PATIENT
Why is that?

DR. MARTINEZ
The dye needs time to leave your body first.

The patient takes the note from the doctor.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
You need blood work done before the test.

PATIENT
Where do I go for that?

Dr. Martinez hands over a lab order form.

DR. MARTINEZ
The lab downstairs can do it today.

The patient stands up.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
They will also do a heart tracing.

The patient sits back down.

PATIENT
I am allergic to iodine.

Dr. Martinez closes the file.

DR. MARTINEZ
Then we cannot use the normal dye.

PATIENT
What can you use instead?

DR. MARTINEZ
There are other options we can try.

The patient relaxes slightly.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Do you react badly to shellfish?

PATIENT
I get hives from shrimp.

Dr. Martinez makes another note.

DR. MARTINEZ
That rules out another type of dye.

The patient picks up the notepad again.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Your test will start at eight in the morning.

PATIENT
Can I eat breakfast?

DR. MARTINEZ
No food after midnight the night before.

The patient writes this down.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
No drinks either, not even water.

PATIENT
What if the test was in the afternoon?

DR. MARTINEZ
Then you would stop eating four hours before.

The patient underlines something on the notepad.

PATIENT
Can I have wine with dinner the night before?

Dr. Martinez shakes his head.

DR. MARTINEZ
Avoid all alcohol for one full day before.

PATIENT
I smoke cigarettes.

DR. MARTINEZ
Stop smoking for that same day.

The patient frowns.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Tobacco can change the test results.

PATIENT
What about my other pills?

Dr. Martinez opens a drawer.

DR. MARTINEZ
Bring all your bottles to the hospital.

The patient pulls a list from her purse.

PATIENT
I take vitamins and herbs too.

DR. MARTINEZ
Bring those as well.

The patient adds to her list.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Tell the nurses if any drug makes you sick.

The patient circles something on the paper.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Treat this like you are having surgery.

PATIENT
Should I leave my rings at home?

DR. MARTINEZ
Yes, and your watch and earrings.

The patient touches her necklace.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Take off your nail polish before you come.

PATIENT
What about my contact lenses?

DR. MARTINEZ
Remove those too.

The patient blinks.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Use the bathroom right before the test starts.

PATIENT
How long does it take?

DR. MARTINEZ
Sometimes several hours.

The patient looks concerned.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
The staff will check you in when you arrive.

PATIENT
Will you be there?

DR. MARTINEZ
I will meet you before we begin.

The patient gathers her things.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
A nurse will give you a gown to change into.

The patient stands.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
After the test you will rest here for six hours.

PATIENT
Can I go home right after?

DR. MARTINEZ
We need to watch you for problems first.

The patient moves toward the door.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Try to stay calm during that time.

PATIENT
Will you give me something to relax?

Dr. Martinez stands up.

DR. MARTINEZ
Yes, a sedative before the test.

PATIENT
Can I drive myself home then?

DR. MARTINEZ
No, the medicine will make that unsafe.

The patient stops at the door.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Bring someone to take you home.

PATIENT
My sister can come.

DR. MARTINEZ
She should stay with you that night.

The patient opens the door.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Rest in bed for the first day.

PATIENT
Will my groin hurt?

DR. MARTINEZ
Yes, some discomfort is normal there.

The patient steps into the hallway.

DR. MARTINEZ (CONT'D)
Stay home from work for three days.

PATIENT
When will I know the results?

Dr. Martinez walks to the door.

DR. MARTINEZ
Call me two days after the test.

PATIENT
What if something is wrong?

DR. MARTINEZ
Then we will discuss your options.

The patient walks away down the hall. Dr. Martinez closes the door.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::8c3cf713-de3f-4e3d-9e94-ba8bcf48:
INT. BIOLOGY CLASSROOM - DAY

A TEACHER holds up a ruler to demonstrate scale.

TEACHER
A trapdoor spider measures between point seven nine and one point two six inches long.

She places her thumb next to the ruler.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
That size sits between your pinky nail and your thumbnail.

She sets down the ruler and picks up a photograph.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The spider appears black or brown with a stout body and thick legs.

She points to markings on the photo.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Some types show pale marks on their skin.

She moves her finger across the image.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Others grow a silky coat of hair.

She draws a line down the middle of the photo with her pen.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The body splits into two parts.

She taps the front section.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The thorax holds the head and legs.

She taps the rear section.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The abdomen sits behind it and shows a lighter shade.

She pulls out a magnifying glass and examines the photo closely.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Six eyes arrange themselves in three groups.

She sets down the magnifying glass.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Most other spiders carry eight eyes instead.

She picks up a second photograph showing a tarantula.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
These spiders share ancestry with tarantulas but lack the heavy hair.

She compares the two photos side by side.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Their bodies remain smaller and shine more.

She rotates the trapdoor spider photo to show the head.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The jaws attach to the front of the head and move up and down.

She picks up a third photo showing a different spider.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Other spider jaws move side to side.

She returns to the first photo and points to a larger spider.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Females grow larger than males.

She shakes her head.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Females almost never leave their burrows, so people rarely spot them.

She circles a smaller spider in the photo.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Any trapdoor spider you see will probably be male.

She writes on the board: MALE TRAITS.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Males have short blunt spinnerets at the tip of the abdomen that make silk.

She adds to the list.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
A double spur appears halfway along each front leg.

She continues writing.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The carapace covering the thorax looks dusty and grows light bristles.

She finishes the list.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The pedipalps near the jaws look like boxing gloves.

A STUDENT raises her hand.

STUDENT
How many types exist?

The teacher opens a thick book.

TEACHER
Numerous varieties exist with different features.

She flips through pages.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Scientists keep discovering more varieties each year.

She closes the book.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Check which varieties live in your region to learn their specific marks.

She walks to a world map on the wall.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Continental drift scattered these spiders across the globe in an odd pattern.

She points to North America.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
They inhabit Canada and the United States from the southeast and pacific areas north to Colorado.

She moves her finger south.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
They live in Guatemala and Mexico.

She points to Asia.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
China, Japan, and Thailand host populations.

She indicates Africa.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
South Africa and Madagascar contain them.

She taps Australia.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Australia has many species.

She steps back from the map.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Warm places like temperate forests and deserts attract them everywhere.

She picks up a soil sample in a jar.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
They dig into grassy areas, hillsides, and dirt banks.

She sets down the jar and picks up a model burrow.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
The burrow reaches three quarters of an inch wide and up to eight inches deep.

She lifts a small hinged door on the model.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
A silk door with a hinge covers the entrance.

She sprinkles tiny sticks and pebbles on the door.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
Sticks, pebbles, and natural stuff camouflage it.

A student squints at the model.

STUDENT
That makes them hard to see.

The teacher nods and points to a second
script_events.coling::22aa3208-6e8c-4005-9386-819f202c:
INT. FAMILY HOME - KITCHEN - EVENING

A teen girl stands by the door and watches her dad walk in from work. He sets down his bag. She waits a moment.

TEEN GIRL
How was your day?

DAD
Pretty good, thanks.

She notes his smile. She decides this is a good time. The family finishes dinner. Everyone clears plates. The girl waits until the dishes are done. Her parents move to the living room. She follows them there.

TEEN GIRL
Can we talk?

Her mom looks up from the couch. Her dad sits in a chair. They both nod. The girl sits down across from them.

TEEN GIRL (CONT'D)
I want to tell you something.

She takes a breath. She starts to explain. Her dad leans forward. Her mom crosses her arms. The girl keeps talking. She tells them about a boy at school. She says she likes him. She says he asked her out. Her parents exchange a look.

The next day after school, the girl finds her mom alone in the kitchen. She asks if they can go for a walk. Her mom agrees. They head outside together. They walk down the street. The girl brings up the topic again. Her mom listens this time without her dad there.

TEEN GIRL
Will you talk to Dad for me?

Her mom thinks about it. She says she will try. They walk back home. The girl feels a bit better now.

That evening, the parents talk in their bedroom. The girl waits downstairs. She hears their voices but not the words. After a while, they come down. They sit with her again.

MOM
We need to know more.

The girl nods. She tells them the boy's name. She describes what he is like. She mentions his grades and his hobbies. Her dad asks if they have gone out yet. The girl pauses. She decides to tell the truth. She says yes, once. Her parents look surprised. Her mom frowns.

DAD
You should have told us first.

TEEN GIRL
I know. I'm sorry.

She promises not to hide things again. Her dad sits back. Her mom softens a little. The girl sees an opening. She asks what worries them most. Her dad says he does not know this boy. Her mom agrees. The girl suggests they meet him. She offers to invite him to dinner. Her parents consider this idea.

The next scene shows the girl at school. She talks to the boy in the hallway. She tells him about her parents. He says he will come to dinner. She feels relieved. They make a plan for Friday night.

Back at home, the girl talks with her parents again. She brings up some ideas. She says she will keep her grades up. She promises to study every night for an hour. Her dad asks what her current grade point average is. She tells him. He says it needs to stay that high. She agrees to this rule.

MOM
You can only go out once a week.

The girl wants to argue but stops herself. She thinks about it. She realizes this is fair for now. She nods her head.

TEEN GIRL
Okay. I can do that.

Her dad adds another rule. She must be home by nine on weeknights. She must be home by eleven on weekends. The girl accepts these terms too. Her mom mentions talking to a counselor at school. The girl feels uncomfortable with this. She asks why. Her mom explains it is about health and safety. The girl agrees to think about it.

During the next talk, the girl feels her frustration build. Her dad repeats the same concern. She wants to yell. Instead, she counts in her head. One, two, three, four, five. She answers in a calm voice. Her mom asks another question. The girl feels tears coming. She counts again. She keeps her voice steady. Her dad notices her effort. His expression changes slightly.

TEEN GIRL
I understand your rules.

She makes sure her tone sounds sincere. Her mom watches her carefully. The girl looks right at her. She does not look away. Her dad speaks again. She nods as he talks. He makes a good point about trust. She smiles a little. She tells him he is right.

DAD
Why is this boy important to you?

The girl answers honestly. She explains her feelings. She asks them questions too. She wants to know what scared them when they were young. Her mom shares a story. Her dad adds his own memory. The conversation shifts. Everyone relaxes a bit more.

Later, her mom brings up another topic. She says they need to discuss physical relationships. The girl feels her face get hot. Her mom continues anyway. She talks about being safe and making good choices. The girl listens even though she feels awkward. Her dad adds a few words too. The girl asks one question. Her mom answers it clearly. The talk ends after a few more minutes.

That night, the girl sits at her desk. She pulls out paper and a pen. She writes down everything they discussed. She lists all the rules. She adds her own thoughts too. She writes about why this matters to her. She folds the letter. She walks to her parents' room. She slides it under their door. She goes back to her room and waits.

The next morning, her mom knocks on her door. She comes in holding the letter. She sits on the bed. She tells the girl she read it. Her dad read it too. They talked about it more. Her mom says they appreciate her honesty. She says the boy can come to dinner Friday. The girl hugs her mom. She feels happy and nervous at once. Her mom hugs her back and then leaves the room. The girl sits down and takes a deep breath. She picks up her phone. She texts the boy the good news. He responds right away. Everything is set now.
script_events.coling::794e6ae3-4244-4f1a-902e-9f1eb584:
INT. WARNER BROS. ANIMATION STUDIO - DAY - 1933

EARL DUVALL sits at a desk and picks up a script titled "Honeymoon Hotel."

He opens the folder and reads the first page.

A secretary enters the room and hands him a production sheet marked 6125.

Duvall signs the paper and passes it back to her.

She walks out through the door.

INT. ANIMATION ROOM - DAY

JACK KING bends over a light table and draws a male bug character.

FRANK TIPPER moves to the next desk and sketches a female insect.

BOB CLAMPETT arrives and pulls out a chair to join them.

PAUL FENNELL steps through the doorway carrying a stack of drawings.

CHUCK JONES looks up from his work and waves at him.

FRANK TASHLIN enters last and sets down his pencil case.

INT. MUSIC ROOM - DAY

BERNARD BROWN sits at a piano and plays the opening bars of "Honeymoon Hotel."

NORMAN SPENCER stands beside him and writes notes on sheet music.

Brown stops playing and adjusts the tempo.

Spencer nods his approval and they continue.

INT. SOUND STAGE - DAY

Brown puts on headphones and tests the recording equipment.

The needle drops and begins to capture the music.

INT. SCREENING ROOM - DAY - FEBRUARY 17, 1934

The lights dim and the projector starts.

Color flickers across the screen for the first time in a Warner Bros. cartoon.

The Cinecolor process bathes the bugs in red and blue tones.

Disney owns the Technicolor rights so Warner cannot use that system.

The male and female bugs check into the hotel on screen.

Flames suddenly engulf the building in the cartoon.

The bugs run from the fire and escape.

The film ends and the lights come back on.

Duvall stands and shakes hands with his team.

The cartoon will appear on the Footlight Parade DVD decades later.

Merrie Melodies will switch to Technicolor after one more Cinecolor experiment.

Looney Tunes will remain black and white until 1943.
script_events.coling::9600c031-1ba2-4882-9aa0-8cb6b07d:
INT. LILLEHAMMER WEHRMACHT CAMP - DAY - MAY 1945

German soldiers mill about the compound as World War II winds down in Europe. Thirty-five intelligence specialists gather their files and equipment inside a barracks.

EXT. STOCKHOLM - NORWEGIAN LEGATION - SAME TIME

Swedish agents from C-byrån receive their orders from superiors. Two Norwegian intelligence officers join them for the mission briefing.

INT. OFFICE OF STRATEGIC SERVICES HEADQUARTERS - WASHINGTON D.C. - DAY

Major General WILLIAM J. DONOVAN signs documents authorizing Operation Claw. He seals the papers in an envelope marked classified.

EXT. SWEDISH-NORWEGIAN BORDER - MAY 9, 1945

The Swedish and Norwegian agents cross into Norway in unmarked vehicles. They carry forged transit papers for the Germans.

INT. LILLEHAMMER CAMP - BARRACKS - DAY

The agents enter and identify the thirty-five signals intelligence experts. The Germans pack their Soviet codebooks and archives into crates.

EXT. CAMP GATES - CONTINUOUS

Guards wave the convoy through without inspection. The vehicles speed toward the Swedish border with their secret cargo.

INT. SWEDISH DEFENSE STAFF HEADQUARTERS - STOCKHOLM - DAY

Major General CARL AUGUST EHRENSVÄRD monitors reports of the operation's progress. Police director HARRY SÖDERMAN arrives to coordinate the next phase.

EXT. SAFE HOUSE - SWEDEN - NIGHT

The German experts unload from trucks at a hidden facility. Swedish guards escort them inside for temporary housing.

INT. NORWEGIAN LEGATION - STOCKHOLM - MI4 OFFICE - DAY

KAI HOLST, a resistance fighter, files intelligence reports at his desk. He notices unusual activity among his colleagues.

EXT. TORSLANDA AIRPORT - GOTHENBURG - JUNE 12, 1945

The thirty-five Germans board American transport planes. Swedish officials watch from a distance as the aircraft taxi down the runway.

INT. TRANSPORT PLANE - CONTINUOUS

The planes lift off and bank south toward Germany. The experts clutch their documentation during the flight.

EXT. WIESBADEN MILITARY CAMP - U.S. OCCUPIED GERMANY - LATER

The aircraft land at an American base. Military police lead the Germans to internment barracks.

INT. INTERROGATION ROOM - WIESBADEN - DAY

American intelligence officers question the first German expert about Soviet military codes. He produces documents from the Eastern Front.

EXT. LILLEHAMMER CAMP - JULY 1945

A British-led search team arrives with Norwegian personnel. They begin inspecting remaining German soldiers for war criminals.

INT. CAMP OFFICE - DAY

The search team discovers records showing key personnel vanished weeks earlier. British officers demand explanations from Norwegian liaison staff.

EXT. CAMP GROUNDS - CONTINUOUS

Kai Holst assists in checking German identity papers. He overhears British officers discussing the missing intelligence specialists.

INT. BARRACKS - LATER

Holst finds evidence of the Swedish operation in abandoned files. He photographs several documents with a small camera.

EXT. STOCKHOLM TRAIN STATION - NEXT DAY

Holst steps off a train from Norway. He carries a briefcase with the photographs inside.

INT. SOVIET EMBASSY - STOCKHOLM - AFTERNOON

Ambassador ALEXANDRA KOLLONTAJ receives a visitor at her office. Her secretary announces an unexpected caller.

EXT. GÄRDET NEIGHBORHOOD - STOCKHOLM - EVENING

Holst walks alone down Rindögatan street. Shadows move in doorways behind him.

INT. APARTMENT BUILDING - RINDÖGATAN 42 - STAIRWELL - NIGHT

Footsteps echo as someone climbs the stairs. A door opens on an upper floor.

EXT. APARTMENT BUILDING - EARLY MORNING - JUNE 1945

Police cars arrive with lights flashing. Officers rush inside the building entrance.

INT. STAIRWELL - TOP FLOOR - CONTINUOUS

Holst lies dead at the top of the stairs. A pistol rests near his hand.

INT. POLICE STATION - INTERROGATION ROOM - DAY

Detectives question witnesses from the building. Nobody reports hearing anything unusual during the night.

INT. MORGUE - STOCKHOLM - LATER

A medical examiner writes suicide on the death certificate. He closes the file without further investigation.

INT. HOLST FAMILY HOME - DAY

Holst's relatives receive the official report. They shake their heads in disbelief at the findings.

INT. RESISTANCE MOVEMENT MEETING HALL - STOCKHOLM - NIGHT

Former colleagues gather to discuss Holst's death. They vote unanimously to reject the suicide conclusion.

INT. UNIVERSITY OFFICE - YEARS LATER

Historian TORE PRYSER examines declassified documents about Operation Claw. He circles Holst's name on a personnel list.

INT. ARCHIVE ROOM - DAY

Pryser discovers connections between Holst and Kollontaj in old surveillance files. He types notes about a possible assassination.

INT. OSS HEADQUARTERS - WASHINGTON - 1945

William T. Carlson and Joseph T. Kloman receive medals for their work. Citations specifically mention their unnamed Swedish operation.

INT. SWEDISH PARLIAMENT BUILDING - STOCKHOLM - FEBRUARY 1946

Government officials vote to dissolve C-byrån immediately. Leaked press reports forced their hand.

INT. NEWSPAPER OFFICE - STOCKHOLM - DAY

Journalists type stories about the secret Swedish-American cooperation. Editors debate how much to publish.

INT. AMERICAN INTELLIGENCE FACILITY - GERMANY - 1946

Analysts work through the Soviet codebook from Lillehammer. They crack several encryption systems using the captured materials.

INT. PENTAGON - COLD WAR ERA

Military planners use intelligence from Operation Claw for strategic assessments. The information proves valuable for decades.

INT. BRITISH NATIONAL ARCHIVES - LONDON - 2019

A researcher requests files about Operation Claw. The archivist stamps them restricted until next year.

INT. SWEDISH INTELLIGENCE HEADQUARTERS - MODERN DAY

Officers review the legacy of Swedish-American cooperation. They trace it back to that first controversial mission.

EXT. RINDÖGATAN 42 - STOCKHOLM - PRESENT DAY

Pedestrians walk past the apartment building where Holst died. A small memorial plaque now marks the location.

INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - HISTORICAL SOCIETY - DAY

Scholars debate whether Holst was murdered or took his own life. New evidence remains classified in multiple countries.
script_events.coling::6ec72689-8b99-420d-9182-0a2fa5a4:
INT. RAILWAY OFFICE - DAY - 1885

A clerk stamps papers. He slides them across a desk. An official picks up the documents and walks out.

EXT. CORFE CASTLE VILLAGE - DAY

The official arrives at a construction site. Workers hammer the final planks on a new station building. A locomotive pulls into view for the first time. Steam rises from its stack. Passengers step down onto the platform. The station opens for business on May 20, 1885.

EXT. COUNTRYSIDE - DAY - 1847

A train rolls west on the main line. It reaches Wareham and stops. The tracks end here. Engineers survey the land beyond, pointing toward Swanage in the distance.

EXT. QUARRY - DAY - EARLY 1800s

Men dig clay from the ground. Horses pull carts loaded with the material. The carts roll along iron rails toward the harbor. Ships wait at the docks. Workers load the clay aboard.

EXT. ANOTHER QUARRY - DAY

Different workers cut marble from the earth. They haul the stone to Swanage port. Cranes lift the marble onto waiting vessels. The ships sail away.

INT. MEETING HALL - DAY - 1881

Railway promoters stand before a committee. They unfold maps on a table. The committee members nod. Someone hands over a signed Act of Parliament. The promoters shake hands and leave.

EXT. HILLY TERRAIN - DAY

Surveyors walk through Corfe Castle gap. They plant stakes in the ground. This route cuts through the spine of the peninsula. Workers begin clearing the path.

EXT. CORFE CASTLE STATION - DAY - 1886

A manager from the London and South Western Railway arrives. He signs transfer documents. The Swanage Railway now belongs to the larger company. The local staff receive new uniforms.

EXT. STATION PLATFORM - DAY - 1954

Railway workers push a converted coach into position beside the platform. A family climbs inside to inspect their holiday accommodation. They unpack their bags. The camping coach business begins.

EXT. SAME LOCATION - DAY - 1960

Workers deliver a different coach. This one was formerly a Pullman car. Inside, a kitchen gleams with new fittings. Two sleeping compartments line one side. A room with single beds occupies the other end.

EXT. STATION - DAY - 1962

A second Pullman coach arrives on a flatbed truck. Workers position it next to the first one. Two families now share the holiday site.

EXT. SWANAGE BEACH - DAY - MID 1900s

Tourists crowd the sand. Hotels fill with guests. More trains arrive at the station carrying visitors. The resort town grows.

EXT. CLAY WORKS - DAY - LATER

The quarry stands empty. Equipment rusts. The last workers leave. Gates close and lock.

EXT. MARBLE QUARRY - DAY

This site also shuts down. Cranes sit idle. No ships wait at the port anymore.

EXT. VILLAGE STREET - DAY - 1967

Cars fill the roads. Families drive past the station without stopping. A British Rail official posts a closure notice on the station door. Villagers gather to read it. They shake their heads.

INT. MEETING ROOM - DAY

Local residents argue with railway officials. They present petitions. The officials refuse to change their decision. People walk out angry.

EXT. STATION PLATFORM - DAY - JANUARY 3, 1972

The last train pulls away. A diesel multiple unit with two cars disappears around the bend. Staff lock the doors. The station falls silent.

INT. COUNCIL CHAMBER - DAY - 1972

Dorset County Council members vote. They approve the purchase of the railway land. Clerks record the transaction in official books.

INT. ANOTHER COUNCIL MEETING - DAY - 1980s

Engineers present plans for a road through the gap. They show drawings of a bypass. Council members debate. They vote against the proposal in 1986. The plans go into a drawer.

EXT. SWANAGE STATION - DAY - 1982

A steam locomotive whistles. Volunteers in period uniforms wave flags. The heritage railway begins operating. Tourists board the train. It departs on its short route.

EXT. CORFE CASTLE STATION - DAY - 1995

Workers repair the old platform. They paint the building. Track crews lay new rails. A steam train approaches from the south on August 12. It stops at the restored station. Passengers get off and explore.

EXT. SAME STATION - DAY - FEBRUARY 1996

Officials cut a ribbon. Photographers take pictures. The formal opening ceremony concludes. A brass band plays.

EXT. MERTON PARK STATION, LONDON - DAY - 2002

Volunteers unbolt an iron footbridge. Cranes lift the structure. Trucks carry it away toward Dorset. The bridge was built in 1893.

EXT. CORFE CASTLE STATION - DAY - 2007

Workers lower the footbridge into place. They bolt the cast-iron columns to new foundations. The wrought iron span connects both platforms. Painters apply fresh coats.

EXT. STATION - DAY - APRIL 2007

David Quarmby arrives. He walks across the new footbridge. He cuts another ribbon. Volunteers cheer. People cross safely without using the old track-level gate.

INT. AWARDS CEREMONY - NIGHT - DECEMBER 2007

An announcer calls names. Philip Wycliffe-Jones and his team walk to the stage. Gwyneth Dunwoody hands them a plaque for the National Railway Heritage Awards. They pose for photographs.

EXT. WAREHAM STATION - DAY - SUMMER 2018

A South Western Railway train departs. It travels the restored connection to Corfe Castle. Passengers look out windows at the scenery. The train continues to Swanage.

EXT. CORFE CASTLE STATION - DAY - SAME PERIOD

Another train arrives from Wareham. This one will continue to Poole. A different service heads toward London Waterloo via Weymouth. West Coast Railway Company operates additional Saturday and Sunday trains.

INT. RAILWAY OFFICE - DAY - JULY 2019

Managers review schedules. They cancel the National Rail services. The last commercial train departs. Only heritage services remain now.

EXT. STATION PLATFORM - DAY - APRIL

Spring visitors arrive. Trains run daily through October. Families board carriages. The locomotive whistles and pulls away toward Swanage.

EXT. SAME STATION - DAY - NOVEMBER

Fewer trains operate now. Only weekend service continues through winter. Passengers bundle against the cold.

INT. GOODS SHED - DAY

Museum volunteers arrange displays. They place artifacts in glass cases. A rail van stands nearby with more exhibits. Visitors pay admission and enter.

INT. MUSEUM - DAY

People examine the narrow gauge locomotive called Secundus. Built in 1874, it sits on display tracks. A guide explains its history at Furzebrook Railway. It worked until 1955.

EXT. BIRMINGHAM - DAY - 2000

Museum staff crate the locomotive. They load it onto a truck. The vehicle drives south toward Dorset. The Birmingham Museum of Science and Industry closes this exhibit.

EXT. NORDEN STATION SITE - DAY - PRESENT

Construction crews build a new museum. The Purbeck Mineral and Mining Museum takes shape. Workers prepare a space for Secundus. The locomotive will move here eventually. Trains pass by carrying tourists who will visit when it opens.
script_events.coling::040c1d28-4583-4101-87e6-0631f517:
INT. CURLING CLUB - DAY - 2005

MATT WOZNIAK, twenty-two, steps onto the ice for the first time with MIKE MCEWEN's new team. JUSTIN RICHTER slides a stone down the sheet. ANDREW MELNUK sweeps hard beside him.

INT. CURLING CLUB - DAY - 2006

Richter packs his gear into a bag. Melnuk shakes hands with McEwen and walks away. GEORDIE HARGREAVES enters through the front door. ADAM GUENTHER follows behind him.

INT. CURLING CLUB - DAY - 2007

The four men sit in silence after a loss. Hargreaves stands up first and leaves. Guenther removes his team jacket and sets it on a bench.

INT. DIFFERENT CURLING CLUB - DAY - 2007

Wozniak shakes hands with DENNI NEUFELD. B.J. NEUFELD, Denni's brother, joins them at the table. McEwen signs a paper that makes them official.

INT. COMPETITION VENUE - DAY - 2008

The scoreboard shows they reached the semi-finals at the Safeway Championship. A buzzer sounds to end their run. The team walks off the ice together.

INT. PLAYERS' CHAMPIONSHIPS VENUE - NIGHT - 2008

Wozniak throws his first stone at a Grand Slam event. The rock curls into the house. They win their first game of the tournament. They win a second game the next morning. An opponent's final stone knocks them out of the competition.

INT. OFFICE - DAY - 2009

A computer screen displays the CCA rankings with McEwen's team at number seven. Someone prints the page. The printer stops.

INT. ARENA - DAY - 2009

The team celebrates making their third Grand Slam playoff. Cameras flash around them.

INT. SAFEWAY CHAMPIONSHIP VENUE - DAY - 2009

The scoreboard shows they finished fourth. Players from another team shake their hands.

INT. OLYMPIC QUALIFIER VENUE - DAY - 2009

JASON GUNNLAUGSON releases his final stone in the semi-final. It settles perfectly. Wozniak's team loses by a single point. They miss qualifying for the Olympic Trials. Reporters surround Gunnlaugson instead.

INT. STEINBACH ARENA - DAY - 2010

The crowd roars for the Neufeld brothers. JEFF STOUGHTON delivers his last rock. It wins him the provincial title. The crowd goes quiet as Stoughton's team celebrates.

INT. WORLD CUP VENUE - DAY - 2010

Wozniak sweeps furiously in the final against Stoughton. McEwen's final stone wins them the World Cup. They hoist their first Grand Slam trophy together.

INT. AWARDS CEREMONY ROOM - NIGHT - 2010

An announcer reads McEwen's team name as a nominee for team of the year. Flash bulbs pop.

INT. CANADIAN OPEN VENUE - DAY - 2011

Stoughton's final stone in the semi-final misses. McEwen's team advances to the final.

INT. CANADIAN OPEN VENUE - LATER - 2011

GLENN HOWARD watches his last stone slide in the extra end. It comes up short. McEwen's team wins their second Grand Slam of the season. Wozniak pumps his fist.

INT. SAFEWAY CHAMPIONSHIP VENUE - DAY - 2011

The team enters as the top seed in Canada. Stoughton makes a perfect final shot. McEwen's team loses the provincial final by one point again.

INT. SAFEWAY CHAMPIONSHIP VENUE - DAY - 2012

ROB FOWLER throws the winning stone in the final. Wozniak stares at the scoreboard showing their third straight provincial final loss. A reporter mentions they tied Kerry Burtnyk's record from the nineties.

INT. SAFEWAY CHAMPIONSHIP VENUE - DAY - 2013

Stoughton beats them in the semi-final this time. They avoid a fourth straight final loss by not reaching it.

INT. SAFEWAY CHAMPIONSHIP VENUE - DAY - 2014

Stoughton defeats them in another final. Wozniak removes his gloves slowly.

INT. SAFEWAY CHAMPIONSHIP VENUE - DAY - 2015

REID CARRUTHERS celebrates winning the final. Wozniak walks off after his fifth provincial final loss in six years.

INT. SAFEWAY CHAMPIONSHIP VENUE - DAY - 2016

MATT DUNSTONE's team beats Carruthers in the semi-final. McEwen's team qualifies for the Brier regardless of their final result. Dunstone wins the final but leaves for World Juniors. McEwen's team receives their Brier berth.

INT. BRIER VENUE - DAY - 2016

Wozniak throws his first stone at a national championship. The crowd noise overwhelms him.

INT. SAFEWAY CHAMPIONSHIP VENUE - DAY - 2017

McEwen beats Carruthers in the final. They defend their provincial title.

INT. BRIER VENUE - DAY - 2017

The team finishes the round robin at nine wins and two losses. BRAD GUSHUE also finishes nine and two. Officials award first place to McEwen based on their head-to-head win.

INT. BRIER VENUE - LATER - 2017

Gushue beats them seven to five in the one-versus-two game. They drop to the semi-final.

INT. BRIER SEMI-FINAL - DAY - 2017

KEVIN KOE trails five to three in the eighth end. Koe steals a point without hammer. He scores two in the tenth end. Koe steals again in the extra end to win. Manitoba drops to the bronze medal game.

INT. BRIER BRONZE MEDAL GAME - DAY - 2017

BRAD JACOBS misses his final stone in the extra end. Wozniak's team wins seven to six. They claim their first Brier medal ever.

INT. VITERRA CHAMPIONSHIP VENUE - DAY - 2018

McEwen throws one stone in the first game. He develops a fever between ends. A doctor examines him in the locker room. McEwen has chickenpox and cannot continue. B.J. Neufeld becomes skip for the next games.

INT. VITERRA CHAMPIONSHIP FINAL - DAY - 2018

McEwen surprises everyone by appearing on the ice. Carruthers wins the final anyway.

INT. WILDCARD GAME VENUE - DAY - 2018

McEwen's team defeats Gunnlaugson to claim the wildcard spot. They earn their Brier berth.

INT. BRIER VENUE - DAY - 2018

The team struggles through the round robin. Carruthers also fails to make the playoffs. Both Manitoba teams go home early.

INT. PRESS CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY - 2018

McEwen announces the team will break up after the season. Reporters write frantically.

INT. ELITE 10 VENUE - NIGHT - 2018

Days after the breakup announcement, McEwen throws the winning stone. They win the Elite 10 undefeated. Officials hand them a check for twenty-eight thousand dollars. It becomes their seventh Grand Slam title together.

INT. MIXED DOUBLES VENUE - DAY - 2019

Wozniak plays with his girlfriend MARLENE ALBRECHT. She calls the line for him.

INT. CURLING CLUB - DAY - 2020

Wozniak fills in as a spare for McEwen's new team. ALEX FORREST announces his retirement from competitive curling.

INT. MEETING ROOM - DAY - 2020

Wozniak sits down with Gunnlaugson's team. They offer him the second position. He accepts.

INT. OFFICE - DAY - 2021

An official cancels the provincial championship due to COVID restrictions. Another official selects Gunnlaugson as the reigning champions to represent Manitoba.

INT. BRIER VENUE - DAY - 2021

Team Gunnlaugson finishes with six wins and six losses. The tournament ends for them.

INT. MORTGAGE OFFICE - DAY

Wozniak sits at a desk working as a mortgage broker for Vertuity Mortgage. A client signs papers across from him.

INT. WOZNIAK'S HOME - EVENING

Albrecht enters the front door. Two children run to greet Wozniak. The family sits together.
script_events.coling::f3328e08-1b91-430d-bea9-e5b836b0:
INT. CAR - NIGHT

A woman stands by the road. The driver sees her.

DRIVER
Wait. You can see me?

WOMAN
Yea.

The woman tilts her head.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
What are you?

DRIVER
Tired.

The driver grins.

DRIVER (CONT'D)
Been driving out here for years but this is the first time I've seen anyone out here on the B roads. No one tries to hitch a ride. Aren't you afraid I'm going to knock you out and tie you up? Aren't you worried I'll dance around you naked with a knife? Isn't that the story people tell?

WOMAN
Are you?

The woman steps closer.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
I'm not afraid. I don't want to stand in the middle of a freezing wood in a sundress on an October evening.

DRIVER
Fair enough.

The driver leans over. She opens the car door. The woman climbs into the passenger seat. She puts her feet up on the dash. The interior light comes on. The driver looks down at the woman's ankles. Bruises cover them. Scar tissue shows where she bled out. This woman is not living. Her boots leave muddy prints on the inside of the car. Those boots should be in an evidence locker. Her body should be in the morgue.

DRIVER (CONT'D)
The boots. Were you camping up here?

WOMAN
Something like that. I've been away from the city too long though. My husband thought we needed to get away.

She looks out the window.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
We had been growing apart. He wanted to reconnect.

DRIVER
Errrr.

The driver shifts in her seat.

DRIVER (CONT'D)
And you're leaving without him?

WOMAN
He left without me!

The woman glares at the driver.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Why do you think I was hitch hiking? He took the car keys.

DRIVER
I guess that makes sense.

The driver drops down a gear. She opens the throttle on the straight. The car speeds up.

WOMAN
So how far out are we?

DRIVER
About twenty minutes outside Oxford. Not long now.

WOMAN
What do you mean not long now?

The woman turns away. She looks out of the windscreen. She stares into the light. A truck appears. The car implodes around them. Shattered glass sprays across the seats. The driver's head spins round with a crack. The engine starts hissing. The truck horn drones on. The truck driver slumps across his wheel.

WOMAN
Hey guy. Hey genius.

The dead woman prods the driver.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
You still with us?

The driver turns her head. Her neck is broken.

DRIVER
You're new to this aren't you.

WOMAN
Huh?

DRIVER
You asked why I could see you. That's the thing. I'm already dead.
script_events.coling::3acbf3b4-cdc2-42b4-9b2c-839dd8bb:
INT. DARK CHAMBER - NIGHT

A MAN kneels on the floor, eyes shut tight, sweat dripping down his face.

He reaches out with his mind toward the demon's first barrier.

His hands shape the air as he bends the chaos into a stable form.

The barrier collapses.

He moves to the next one and breaks it apart.

The third barrier falls under his will.

He pushes deeper into the demon's core.

The final barrier rises before him, thick and complex.

A name pulses inside it.

The demon shrieks.

Images flood the man's vision—his own death in a hundred different ways.

He waves his hand and the images vanish like smoke.

He grabs the first thread of the barrier and pulls it loose.

The second thread unravels in his grip.

The third thread snaps free.

The barrier shudders and begins to glow.

The final threads slide into their natural positions.

A hum fills the chamber, rising in pitch.

The man twists his hand in the air.

He speaks the demon's name out loud.

The demon goes still.

Its thrashing stops completely.

The man opens his eyes.

He stands up slowly.

The demon waits, quiet as a tame animal.

The man steps forward.

He places his hand on empty air as if touching the demon's head.

He whispers instructions.

The demon obeys.

The man walks to a stone tablet leaning against the wall.

He reads the ancient text carved there.

He crosses to a wooden chest in the corner.

He opens it and lifts out a grimoire.

Dust falls from the pages.

He finds the passage about destroying demons.

He closes the book.

He turns back to the demon.

"Silence yourself," he says.

"We have work ahead of us."

"I will become the Scourge of Hell tonight."

The demon bows its head.
script_events.coling::a2ab68ca-fbd4-4698-8f7c-6b33ea5e:
INT. COUNCIL CHAMBER - DAY

HARTIGAN takes a drag from his cigarette. He exhales smoke toward the ceiling. He turns to face ZOR'T, the alien delegate seated across the metal table.

HARTIGAN
So are you guys finally ready to let us in the Intergalactic Council? Have we proven ourselves?

Zor't taps a screen embedded in the table surface. Documents scroll past in alien script.

ZOR'T
Well, you've proven yourselves in several capacities, none of which are sought after in the Council.

He swipes through more files. Each document lingers for three seconds before he moves on.

ZOR'T (CONT'D)
Human innovation seems like it is only driven through conflict and destruction. Your warmongers, that you call "politicians" and "monarchs," instigate mass murder and genocide, and then the destitute members of those societies carry them out. Why do the indigent and poor from your world hate each other so?

Hartigan stubs out his cigarette in a tray. He leans back in his chair.

HARTIGAN
I can not answer for the past. Our ancestors were violent, greedy creatures.

Zor't nods slowly. He closes the documents with a wave of his hand. The screen goes dark.

ZOR'T
Since we established contact, our sensors lead us to believe that an abundant amount of your resources have been redirected to weapon-manufacturing sites. Why is this so?

Hartigan shifts in his seat. His hand moves to his jacket pocket.

HARTIGAN
I know nothing of what you speak. It would go against the decree set forth by the Council. Perhaps you've misread your sensor data.

Zor't stands up from his chair. His face changes color to a deeper shade of blue.

ZOR'T
Mr. Hartigan, we do not misinterpret data. This is not hubris, it is fact.

He walks to the window. Outside, crowds press against barriers. Security forces hold them back.

ZOR'T (CONT'D)
You have diverted an alarming amount of your resources towards weapon manufacturing, at great peril to the poorer among you, who now starve and riot outside this very building.

He turns away from the window. He faces Hartigan directly.

ZOR'T (CONT'D)
We at the Council not only abhor violence, but are incapable altogether of inflicting it. This is a gross misconduct and will be grounds for your denial from the Council, and I will see to it personally.

Hartigan pulls a gun from his jacket. He sets it on the table between them.

HARTIGAN
That's all I needed to hear. Thank you Councillor.

He picks up the gun again. He points it at Zor't's face. His finger slides onto the trigger.

Zor't closes his eyes. His body relaxes. His breathing slows to an even rhythm.

Hartigan pulls the trigger. The gun fires. Zor't falls backward onto the floor.

Hartigan stands up. He walks to the window. The crowds below surge forward. They break through the first barrier.

HARTIGAN (CONT'D)
Now, let's show the Council how violent humans can be to get what we want.

He holsters his gun. He exits through the rear door. Alarms begin to sound throughout the building.
script_events.coling::b27b582c-94a8-4076-8b94-e286cb9f:
INT. CONVENTION CENTER HALLWAY - DAY

MARK STANSON stands at the entrance. Bodies lie on the floor. Blood covers the walls.

A WOMAN walks past. The killers ignore her. She exits through the side door.

One killer turns. It stares at Mark. Its mouth opens.

KILLER
Briannnn?

More killers shuffle toward Mark. He reaches for his gun.

A hand grabs his shoulder from behind. Mark spins around.

MARK
What?! NO MARK. MY NAME IS MARK!

The mob closes in. Mark struggles. His badge tears from his shirt.

The badge hits the floor. It lands face up.

Mark looks down. He reads the name engraved on metal.

INSERT - BADGE

"MARCUS BRIAN STANSON"

BACK TO SCENE

Mark stops fighting. The killers swarm him.

CUT TO:

INT. POLICE STATION - THREE DAYS EARLIER

Mark sits at his desk. He opens a file folder.

JOHNSON drops more files on the desk. He walks away without speaking.

Mark flips through pages. He circles a name. Then another name. Both say Brian.

He pulls out a newspaper. An advertisement catches his eye.

INSERT - NEWSPAPER AD

"CONVENTION FOR PEOPLE NAMED BRIAN - 7TH STREET HOTEL"

BACK TO SCENE

Mark stands. He grabs his coat. He runs out the door.

INT. MARK'S CAR - CONTINUOUS

Mark drives fast. He swerves around traffic. His radio crackles with reports of violence.

DISPATCHER (V.O.)
Multiple assaults reported downtown. Victims unresponsive. Requesting backup.

Mark accelerates. He runs a red light.

EXT. HOTEL - MOMENTS LATER

Mark parks. He jumps out. He hears screaming from inside.

He draws his weapon. He enters the building.

INT. CONVENTION CENTER HALLWAY - CONTINUOUS

Mark sees the carnage. Brians lie everywhere. Some scream. Some crawl. Most are silent.

The woman passes him. She walks calmly toward the exit. The killers let her go.

One killer notices Mark. It speaks his middle name.
script_events.coling::78c59284-8d42-44bc-9994-350a50f2:
INT. COMMITTEE ROOM - DAY

A clerk enters and places a folder on the table.

CLERK
Mr Ashley did not come.

Committee members sit down and open their papers.

IAIN WRIGHT
He sent this letter instead.

Wright slides the document across the table to another member.

MEMBER #1
What does it say?

Wright stands and walks to the window.

WRIGHT
He claims we abuse our procedures.

Member #1 reads the letter aloud to the others.

MEMBER #1
He writes that we want a circus.

The members exchange glances and shake their heads.

CHRIS BRYANT
The House can compel him.

Bryant rises from his chair and moves toward the door.

BRYANT
We have that power.

A BBC report plays on the monitor in the corner.

MEMBER #2
This investigation started everything.

The report shows workers at the Shirebrook warehouse.

WRIGHT
The deadline was March twenty-first.

Wright returns to his seat and picks up a pen.

WRIGHT
He missed it completely.

Member #2 closes the folder and pushes it away.

MEMBER #2
We warned him already.

Wright writes notes on a pad of paper.

WRIGHT
We said we would escalate.

Ashley's response letter appears on screen as Wright reads.

WRIGHT
He calls our stance antagonistic here.

The words scroll past on the display.

ASHLEY (V.O.)
You refuse to visit the warehouse.

Bryant walks back into the room with a file.

BRYANT
I spoke in Commons yesterday.

He drops the file on the table with force.

BRYANT
Ashley runs a sweatshop now.

Member #1 looks up at the calendar on the wall.

MEMBER #1
We meet Tuesday to decide.

Wright gathers his papers and stands.

WRIGHT
No one faced contempt since the fifties.

The members begin to leave one by one.

MEMBER #2
This matter goes forward regardless.

Bryant stops at the door and turns back.

BRYANT
The truth will come out.

The room empties and the lights dim.
script_events.coling::7a28bc6c-3b1e-4ac2-a169-10374ef5:
INT. SMALL APARTMENT - BATHROOM - DAY

KEVIN sits on the toilet. He hears a key turn in the front door lock.

The door swings open in another room.

Kevin leans forward. The toilet seat catches his skin.

Footsteps cross the threshold into the apartment.

Kevin counts the people who own spare keys in his head.

The footsteps reach the hallway.

Kevin realizes the walk belongs to no one he knows.

His stomach cramps. He doubles over.

Saliva fills his mouth.

Kevin swallows hard.

The footsteps enter the kitchen.

A drawer slides open.

Another drawer bangs shut.

Cupboard doors rattle on their hinges.

Kevin thinks about his bottle opener from Norway.

The footsteps move closer to the bedroom.

Kevin forces his shoulders to drop.

The footsteps stop.

Silence spreads through the apartment.

STRANGER (O.S.)
Hello?

Kevin opens his mouth.

KEVIN
Hi.

He grips the edge of the sink.

KEVIN (CONT'D)
Please don't come in here.

The stranger shifts weight from one foot to the other.

STRANGER (O.S.)
I didn't think there was anyone home.

KEVIN
Yeah.

Kevin's stomach twists again.

More saliva pools under his tongue.

STRANGER (O.S.)
Are you okay, man?

The stranger sniffs the air.

STRANGER (CONT'D)
I've never smelled anything like... I mean, I'm sorry.

The stranger takes a breath.

STRANGER (CONT'D)
This isn't how it usually works. Are you dying or something?

KEVIN
Probably.

Kevin wipes sweat from his forehead.

STRANGER (O.S.)
Do you need me to call nine one one? I can do that. After I leave, I mean.

KEVIN
Yeah. I might.

The stranger turns toward the front door.

STRANGER (O.S.)
So uh... good bye? Good luck?

The footsteps retreat down the hallway.

KEVIN
Wait!

The footsteps continue.

KEVIN (CONT'D)
Wait! Wait!

The footsteps pause.

STRANGER (O.S.)
What?

Kevin clutches his stomach with both hands.

KEVIN
Can you leave the bottle opener? Please?

He gasps for air.

KEVIN (CONT'D)
It's just the one thing.

The stranger sets something down on a counter.

STRANGER (O.S.)
Sure. Yeah. No problem, man.

KEVIN
Thanks.

The front door opens.

The stranger steps outside.

The door pulls shut.

The lock clicks into place.

Kevin lurches forward.

Vomit erupts from his mouth into the toilet bowl.

His body heaves a second time.

The bathroom fills with the sound of retching.

Kevin spits into the water below.

He reaches for toilet paper and finds none.

Kevin wipes his mouth with the back of his hand.

He slumps against the wall.

His breathing slows.

The apartment returns to silence.
script_events.coling::669f87a1-c0ae-4677-a33d-a44341fa:
INT. PERTH CLUB OFFICE - DAY

Wright sits at his desk and signs a suspension form for both team-mates. He picks up the phone and calls BBC Scotland. A reporter answers and Wright speaks into the receiver about coming down hard on the players. He hangs up and leans back in his chair.

EXT. FOOTBALL STADIUM - HALF TIME - EARLIER

Referee Don Robertson blows his whistle to end the first half. Wright turns away from the pitch and walks toward the tunnel. He enters the darkness and disappears from view. Foster stands near Swanson on the field. Foster swings his fist and connects with Swanson's face. Swanson stumbles backward and then lifts his leg. Foster slips on the grass and falls. Swanson's boot flies through the air toward the defender.

INT. PRESS ROOM - NIGHT

Wright faces reporters and shakes his head. He tells them he missed the incident completely. A journalist asks what he will do. Wright promises the players will face the hardest legal punishment available. He stands up and leaves the room.

EXT. STADIUM PITCH - SECOND HALF

The teams play with reduced numbers after the red cards. Perth players run harder to compensate for being short. Sarris grabs Davidson's shirt inside the penalty box. Davidson falls but the referee waves play on. Wright shouts from the sideline for a penalty kick. The referee ignores him.

INT. LOCKER ROOM - AFTER MATCH

Wright addresses his remaining players and praises their character. He tells them they deserved at least a point from the match. The players nod but look disappointed. Wright mentions the top six achievement again. The team applauds quietly.

EXT. PITCH - DURING INCIDENT

Crawford runs toward the scuffle between Foster and Swanson. He pushes between them. The referee pulls out a yellow card and shows it to Crawford. Assistant manager Beuzelin charges onto the field from the bench. He yells at the referee. The referee points toward the stands. Beuzelin argues but then walks away.

INT. HAMILTON PRESS ROOM - NIGHT

Canning sits before microphones and discusses the match result. He defends MacKinnon for trying to separate the fighting players. He states his players acted appropriately. A reporter asks about discipline. Canning says he will take no action against his squad.

EXT. STADIUM SCOREBOARD - LATE IN MATCH

The clock shows five minutes remaining. D'Acol receives the ball near the goal. He shoots and scores. The Hamilton bench erupts in celebration. The scoreboard changes to show Hamilton ahead.

INT. CANNING OFFICE - LATER

Canning reviews the league table on his computer. Hamilton now sits in eleventh place with twenty seven points. Inverness remains at the bottom with fewer points. Canning smiles and closes his laptop.
script_events.coling::32e519e5-5c7c-4bcb-a0ea-bfeb2b47:
INT. NATIONAL GALLERY OF ATHENS - DAY

A tour guide stands before a large painting. Visitors gather around her.

TOUR GUIDE
This work shows the start of our modern period.

She points to a canvas depicting a battle scene.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Greece won freedom from the Ottomans in the eighteen twenties.

A young student raises her hand.

STUDENT
What came before that?

TOUR GUIDE
Four hundred years under Turkish rule.

The guide walks to another wall.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
The mainland missed the Renaissance completely.

She stops at a map on the wall.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
But look at these islands here.

Her finger traces the coastline.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Crete and the Ionian group belonged to Venice for long stretches.

The student moves closer to examine the map.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Those islands absorbed European art movements from the fourteen hundreds onward.

An older man in the group nods.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Two schools emerged there with real strength.

She names them on her fingers.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
The Cretan School and the Heptanese School both followed paths similar to western trends.

The group shifts to a new gallery room.

INT. GALLERY - SECOND ROOM - CONTINUOUS

Portraits line the walls here.

TOUR GUIDE
Modern Greek art took shape from several forces.

She gestures broadly.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Our economy was weak after the revolution.

A woman writes notes in a small book.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Many Greeks had scattered across Europe over the centuries.

The guide pauses before a formal portrait.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
A new elite class rose up with money to spend.

She points to the subject of the painting.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
German and French styles influenced our artists most.

The group moves on again.

INT. GALLERY - THIRD ROOM - CONTINUOUS

Romantic landscapes dominate this space.

TOUR GUIDE
The eighteen hundreds brought Romanticism to Greece.

A teenager photographs a painting of mountains.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Our painters borrowed from European colleagues.

She walks slowly past each canvas.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
But they mixed in revolutionary spirit and local geography.

The older man stops to admire a coastal scene.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Ottoman rule had left us with no art schools.

She turns to face the group.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
So young artists had to leave the country to learn.

The student looks up from her phone.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Munich became the main destination for them.

She crosses to a display case with old photographs.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Karl von Piloty ran the academy there.

The guide taps the glass.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
He taught true fresco technique on wet plaster.

A security guard shifts position near the door.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
The style was emotional and theatrical.

She lists topics on her fingers again.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
City life, country life, objects, and nature were the main subjects.

The group follows her to another section.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Many students returned home after their training.

She smiles slightly.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Some stayed in Munich permanently.

The woman with the notebook looks up.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Germans called their city Athens on the Isar river.

She indicates a series of portraits.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Personal friendships formed between Greek and German painters.

The teenager puts away his camera.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
This created what we call the Munich School.

She stops at a large portrait of a bearded man.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Nikolaos Gysis taught at the academy.

The guide's voice fills with pride.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
He became a leading figure among our artists.

She moves to the next painting.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Academic realism dominated at first.

The older man adjusts his glasses.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Genre scenes and portraits of wealthy people sold well.

She gestures at a still life.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Landscapes often showed impressionist touches.

The student raises her hand again.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Near the century's end, Symbolism arrived.

She nods toward a mystical scene.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Art Nouveau and Jugendstil followed soon after.

The guide points to a flowing, decorative work.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Gysis and Aristeas explored these new styles.

She walks to the next gallery entrance.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Modernism appeared in the early nineteen hundreds.

The group enters a fourth room.

INT. GALLERY - FOURTH ROOM - CONTINUOUS

Scenes of daily Greek life cover these walls.

TOUR GUIDE
Munich School artists painted ordinary people.

She indicates a market scene.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Local customs and living conditions interested them greatly.

The woman closes her notebook.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Theodoros Vryzakis specialized in history paintings.

She points to a battle canvas.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
The war of eighteen twenty one inspired him most.

The guide moves along the wall.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Nikiphoros Lytras painted realistic Greek life.

She stops at a domestic scene.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Georgios Jakobides focused on babies and small children.

The teenager leans in to see the details.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
He later became this gallery's first director.

She gestures around the room.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Georgios Roilos was another leading painter then.

The older man nods in recognition.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
His early work stayed close to Munich traditions.

She crosses to a seascape.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Konstantinos Volanakis loved the Greek sea above all.

The guide names several more artists.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Symeon Sabbides studied in Munich too.

She counts on her fingers.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Yannoulis Chalepas worked as a sculptor.

The student writes down the names.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Leonidas Drosis also carved stone.

She mentions modern artists next.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Theofrastos Triantafyllidis went there later.

The group shifts toward the exit.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Jorgos Busianis and Giorgio de Chirico studied in Munich as well.

She pauses at the doorway.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Drosis created ornament for the Academy of Athens.

The guide lists more sculptors rapidly.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Lazaros Sochos, Georgios Vitalis, and Dimitrios Filippotis all worked in the new kingdom.

She adds final names.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Ioannis Kossos, Georgios Bonanos, and Lazaros Fytalis completed that generation.

The group enters a fifth room.

INT. GALLERY - FIFTH ROOM - CONTINUOUS

French influenced works hang here.

TOUR GUIDE
A few painters chose Paris instead of Munich.

She approaches a graceful figure study.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
They followed French academy rules but kept personal visions.

The woman with the notebook opens it again.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Jacob Rizos painted female beauty.

She moves to an eastern scene.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Theodoros Rallis depicted the Orthodox world.

The guide stops at a portrait.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Nikolaos Xydias Typaldos did portraits and genre works.

The teenager photographs this painting.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Impressionism was developing in Paris then.

She shakes her head slightly.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Most Greek painters stayed loyal to academic teaching.

The older man examines a landscape closely.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Only vague hints of impressionism appeared in their work.

She brightens at the next painting.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Périclès Pantazis became our first true impressionist.

The guide explains his journey.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
He left Paris and settled in Belgium.

The student looks up with interest.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
There he joined an avant garde group called Circle de la pâte.

The guide walks to a religious painting.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Many artists drew inspiration from El Greco.

She points to the style of the figures.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
His influence appeared especially in religious themes.

The woman writes another note.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Secular art referenced classical Greek styles.

The guide indicates a Byzantine inspired icon.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Religious art looked back to Byzantine tradition instead.

She mentions the island painters.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Ionian artists played a pioneering role in the seventeen hundreds.

The group listens attentively.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
They had learned from Italian Renaissance workshops.

She continues her explanation.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Baroque studios taught them as well.

The guide summarizes the period.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Nineteenth century artists reconnected with ancient Greek tradition.

She adds the European dimension.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
They also engaged with European studio discoveries.

The older man nods in understanding.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Munich School remained the defining influence.

She points to two major examples.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Vryzakis and Lytras show this period best.

The group moves to a sixth room.

INT. GALLERY - SIXTH ROOM - CONTINUOUS

Twentieth century works fill this space.

TOUR GUIDE
Landscape painting dominated the early nineteen hundreds.

She gestures at bright, colorful scenes.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Painters became fascinated with light and color.

The teenager stops to admire a sunny field.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Munich lost its hold on Greek artists.

The guide walks to a Parisian street scene.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Paris became the new center of attraction.

She points to a portrait.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Demetrios Galanis knew Picasso personally.

The student's eyes widen.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
He won wide recognition in France.

The guide quotes a critic.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Andre Malreaux compared his power to Giotto's.

She indicates the next artist.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
The Académie française gave him lifelong membership.

The woman photographs this information panel.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Nikos Engonopoulos gained international fame later.

She describes his dual talents.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
He created surrealist paintings and poetry both.

The guide moves to the nineteen sixties section.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Dimitris Mytaras emerged in the late sixties.

She names his colleague.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Yiannis Psychopedis worked alongside him.

The older man studies their paintings.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
They connected with European critical realism.

She returns to earlier twentieth century masters.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Impressionism influenced the first half of the century strongly.

The guide stops at two major figures.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Konstantinos Parthenis led this movement.

She indicates the adjacent wall.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Konstantinos Maleas shared his vision.

The teenager takes notes on his phone.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
Nikiphoros Lytras joined Munich avant garde groups.

She explains his significance.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
He was the last link to Munich's great tradition.

The guide describes their evolution.

TOUR GUIDE (CONT'D)
These painters developed in new directions.

She emphasizes continu
script_events.coling::76136b55-6fc5-43fa-b998-384c79a1:
INT. TATE GALLERY OFFICE - DAY

BALSHAW sits at her desk. She leans forward.

BALSHAW
We are about a third of the way down the road.

She stands and walks to the window.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
I worked in Manchester. Now I run the Tate.

A REPORTER enters the room and sits across from her.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
I will change this place in twenty years. Serota changed it in the last twenty.

The reporter writes in a notebook.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
He turned a gallery in Pimlico into a global brand. He built Tate Modern.

She returns to her chair and pulls out a folder.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
He used bricks. I will use people.

She opens the folder and slides a page toward the reporter.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
Look at these numbers. Fifty percent of Britain visits a museum once a year.

The reporter picks up the page.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
That means fifty percent do not. I want them.

She taps the page with her finger.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
Seventy-five percent should love our collection. Every young person should visit Tate and think and play here.

The reporter looks up from the page.

REPORTER
How will you do this?

Balshaw pauses. She looks at her hands.

BALSHAW
We need easier words. Art should bring joy. We should stop using hard terms.

The reporter waits. Balshaw shifts in her seat.

REPORTER
Can you give an example?

Balshaw shakes her head.

BALSHAW
Not right now. But we will explain things better.

She stands again and paces to a shelf lined with books.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
Our staff is too white. The whole sector is. We need more people from different backgrounds.

She pulls a book from the shelf and opens it.

REPORTER
What will you change at Tate itself?

Balshaw closes the book and sets it down.

BALSHAW
We do not need to change anything in particular.

The reporter frowns and underlines something in the notebook.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
I mean what I say. I can do this. I have done it before.

She walks back to the desk and sits.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
But I must act. Serota wrote something when he applied for this job years ago.

The reporter flips to a new page.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
He said he would need to grasp the nettle. That is what I must do too.

She looks directly at the reporter.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
You can follow us online. Facebook. Twitter. Instagram.

The reporter closes the notebook and stands.

BALSHAW (CONT'D)
If you have a story, send an email.

The reporter nods and walks to the door. Balshaw watches. The door opens. The reporter exits. The door closes. Balshaw turns back to the window and stares out at the city.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::54bd7a63-4df1-4ef1-979a-2ae688d3:
INT. NEWPORT RFC BOARDROOM - DAY

STUART DAVIES stands at the front of a packed room holding documents.

STUART DAVIES
The WRU and Dragons boards approved the takeover yesterday.

He places the papers on the table.

STUART DAVIES (CONT'D)
Next month the shareholders vote. We need seventy-five percent.

WILL GODFREY enters through the side door and sits down.

STUART DAVIES (CONT'D)
This moment will decide the future of Newport RFC, the Dragons, and Rodney Parade.

He picks up a red folder.

STUART DAVIES (CONT'D)
Without a deal, Rodney Parade Ltd goes into liquidation.

A SHAREHOLDER in the back row raises her hand.

STUART DAVIES (CONT'D)
We sent you all a document last week.

He opens the folder and pulls out a letter.

STUART DAVIES (CONT'D)
Tony Brown wrote to every shareholder. He supports the deal.

EXT. RODNEY PARADE STADIUM - DAY

Rain pours onto the pitch. Water pools in the center. A GROUNDSKEEPER walks across the field and his boots sink into mud.

GROUNDSKEEPER
(into phone)
The match is off. Too much water.

He hangs up and walks toward the tunnel.

INT. BOARDROOM - DAY

Davies points to a chart on the wall.

STUART DAVIES
Rugby started here in eighteen seventy-seven. The Dragons play here now. Newport RFC plays here. Newport County Football Club plays here too.

Godfrey stands and walks to the window.

WILL GODFREY
The pitch floods every winter. We cancel matches. We postpone others.

He turns back to face the room.

WILL GODFREY (CONT'D)
The WRU offer includes repairs and upgrades.

Davies lifts three printed pages.

STUART DAVIES
Our financial position is not healthy. The documents show you the numbers.

He drops the pages and they scatter.

STUART DAVIES (CONT'D)
A no vote means we call in an administrator. An administrator sells the ground to creditors. Rugby at Rodney Parade ends.

A YOUNGER SHAREHOLDER stands up.

YOUNGER SHAREHOLDER
What happens to the venue?

STUART DAVIES
The ground stops operating. The world knows this place. We worked to protect it.

The younger shareholder sits back down.

STUART DAVIES (CONT'D)
Tonight you must understand the implications. Read the circular. Look at the accounts. See our trading position.

Godfrey picks up a valuation report from the table.

WILL GODFREY
The WRU offered three point seven five million pounds for the ground.

He flips through pages.

WILL GODFREY (CONT'D)
That reflects its value as a sports ground, not a development site.

A woman in the front row leans forward.

WILL GODFREY (CONT'D)
Demand for sporting venues is limited. We established a fair price based on that.

He closes the report.

WILL GODFREY (CONT'D)
The facilities are old. Investors ask if further money will bring returns.

INT. TONY BROWN'S OFFICE - DAY

TONY BROWN, over eighty, sits at his desk writing. He finishes a sentence and looks up.

TONY BROWN
(to camera)
I invested four million pounds in nineteen ninety-seven.

He signs the bottom of the letter.

TONY BROWN (CONT'D)
The club turned that into shares. I left the board. They wrote off my investment.

He stands and walks to a cabinet. He opens a drawer and removes financial statements.

TONY BROWN (CONT'D)
I returned to the board later. Martyn Hazell and I put in five point five million more.

He spreads the statements across his desk.

TONY BROWN (CONT'D)
That money kept the Dragons and Newport afloat.

He sits back down.

TONY BROWN (CONT'D)
Two years of board meetings produced this deal. We held challenging discussions. We made difficult decisions.

He folds the letter and slides it into an envelope.

TONY BROWN (CONT'D)
The current business model stopped working. It will fail completely soon.

He seals the envelope.

TONY BROWN (CONT'D)
Martyn and I are both over eighty now. We want to reduce our responsibilities.
