He addresses the envelope to the shareholders.

TONY BROWN (CONT'D)
We explored many options. We wanted a successful Dragons, a secure Newport RFC, a protected venue, and professional rugby in Gwent at Rodney Parade.

He places a stamp on the envelope.

TONY BROWN (CONT'D)
The WRU became our preferred choice, not our last resort.

He drops the letter in his outbox.

TONY BROWN (CONT'D)
They approach this with good intentions. They can make the Dragons succeed. They will ensure rugby continues at Rodney Parade for everyone.

He closes the drawer and the screen fades.
script_events.coling::7426cf8e-20e5-4e81-bfbb-380b1547:
INT. TEHRAN NEWSROOM - SATURDAY MORNING

Iranians turn on their televisions. The screen shows vote totals from Friday. The numbers confirm that 68 seats changed hands. A woman covers her mouth with her hand.

EXT. TEHRAN STREET - CONTINUOUS

People walk outside and talk to neighbors. A man tells his friend that moderates and reformists now control parliament. The friend nods slowly.

INT. GOVERNMENT BUILDING - DAY

An aide enters an office with papers. He places them on a desk. The papers show that this shift ends 13 years of hardliner control. A minister reads the documents.

EXT. CAMPAIGN OFFICE - DAY

Workers take down posters. Someone mentions that President Hassan Rouhani did not win by a huge margin. Another worker says the result still shocks everyone. They pack boxes.

INT. OLD PARLIAMENT CHAMBER - DAY

Hardliner members gather their belongings. One man recalls how they campaigned against government policies for months. Another slams a drawer shut. They leave the building.

EXT. PARLIAMENT STEPS - DAY

A reporter interviews a departing member. The member says hardliners blocked most government plans for three years. He walks away from the camera.

INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

Men in suits review documents about the nuclear deal. One stands and points at the text. He calls it a betrayal. Others murmur agreement.

INT. FOREIGN MINISTRY - DAY

Foreign Minister Javad Zarif sits at his desk. An assistant brings him tea. The assistant mentions that some members called Zarif a traitor in speeches. Zarif sips his tea without speaking.

INT. PARLIAMENT FLOOR - FLASHBACK

A fundamentalist member waves papers and shouts. He demands impeachment. Other members join the chorus. Zarif watches from a gallery above.

INT. ELECTION CENTER - NIGHT

Workers count ballots. The hardliners who attacked Zarif lose their seats one by one. New names appear on the board. Moderate and reformist candidates replace them.

INT. TEHRAN APARTMENT - NIGHT

A family watches election coverage. The father says the nuclear deal ended sanctions. The mother adds that voters rejected those who opposed the deal. Their daughter smiles.

EXT. REGISTRATION OFFICE - WEEKS EARLIER

Officials cross names off a list. Reformist candidates learn they cannot run. They protest but guards turn them away. The door closes.

INT. STATE TV STUDIO - WEEKS EARLIER

A producer reviews footage. He cuts segments about reformist candidates. He approves segments attacking the nuclear deal. The broadcast airs that evening.

INT. COFFEE SHOP - WEEKS EARLIER

Young people gather around laptops. They post messages on social media. Women share campaign information on their phones. The posts spread quickly.

INT. PRESIDENT ROUHANI'S OFFICE - DAY

Rouhani meets with advisors. One advisor says parliament will now support him more. Another advisor warns that problems remain. Rouhani stands and walks to the window.

INT. BANK HEADQUARTERS - DAY

Iranian businessmen enter a European bank. The manager shakes his head. He says his bank cannot process their transactions yet. The businessmen leave disappointed.

INT. US CONGRESS - DAY

American conservatives draft new legislation. They intend to block parts of the nuclear deal. An aide carries the draft to committee.

INT. ECONOMIC MINISTRY - DAY

Officials review charts showing slow progress. One official says delays will hurt reform plans. Another says hardliners will use this against them. They close their folders.

INT. STRATEGY ROOM - NIGHT

Defeated hardliner members gather around a table. They study calendars and timelines. One traces his finger along dates. They begin planning their next campaign. The clock on the wall ticks forward.
script_events.coling::7b1cbc13-ed47-4ccb-81a7-d64aa32c:
INT. HOTEL LOBBY - NIGHT

A woman walks through the front doors with her boyfriend at 2am. They look exhausted.

A long line of guests snakes through the lobby. The woman and her boyfriend join the end.

They inch forward. A clerk waves them up to the desk.

A second woman pushes past them and steps in front. The clerk nods at her.

The second woman complains loudly about a broken toilet in her room. The clerk types on the computer.

The clerk hands the second woman a new key card. The woman walks away.

The exhausted woman steps up to the desk. The clerk frowns at the screen.

The clerk explains that the king non-smoking room is gone. She offers a king smoking room instead.

The exhausted woman shakes her head. The clerk mentions a double queen non-smoking room.

The exhausted woman accepts it. The clerk prints out a key card and slides it across the counter.

INT. HOTEL ROOM - CONTINUOUS

The woman opens the door. She and her boyfriend enter.

Music blasts through the walls from the street below. The woman winces.

Her boyfriend walks into the bathroom. He calls out that there are no towels.

The woman joins him. Water covers the entire bathroom floor.

Hair floats in the puddles. The woman gags.

Her boyfriend steps back into the bedroom. The carpet squishes under his feet.

He grabs a bathmat and throws it on the wet floor. He drags it around with his foot.

The woman collapses onto one of the beds. Her boyfriend lies down beside her.

They close their eyes.

INT. HOTEL ROOM - LATER

A loud blooping sound fills the room. The woman sits up.

The noise repeats. She climbs out of bed.

She walks to the bathroom. Bubbles rise from the toilet bowl.

Water spills over the rim onto the floor. The woman jumps back.

More water spreads across the tile. It seeps into the carpet.

The woman needs to use the toilet but refuses to sit down. She crosses her legs.

Her boyfriend wakes up and sees the flooding. He grabs their bags.

INT. HOTEL LOBBY - MORNING

The woman slams the key card on the desk. A different clerk picks it up.

The woman describes the flooded room. The clerk opens the cash drawer.

The clerk counts out bills and hands them over. The woman takes the money.

She and her boyfriend walk out the front doors into the daylight.
script_events.coling::56d83b20-4592-4ff6-b3ab-c3299c65:
INT. MOVIE THEATER LOBBY - DAY

A WOMAN storms through the entrance doors.

WOMAN
I'm pissed.

She stops at a counter.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
I drove here early like always.

EXT. MOVIE THEATER - MOMENTS LATER

The Woman steps outside into blazing heat.

WOMAN
They made the line form out here. One hundred ten degrees.

She walks forward and sees the line snake around the building corner.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
It wrapped all the way back.

She passes the elevators.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Past these elevators.

She walks by a row of trees.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Past the trees.

She reaches the front steps where the line ends.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Up across the main steps.

She notices people who have been waiting since early afternoon.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Unemployed folks camped out at two for a seven o'clock show.

She shrugs and joins the line.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Fine. Maybe we won't get in.

More people arrive behind her.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
New people kept showing up.

No staff member turns anyone away.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Nobody sent them home.

She decides to stay.

INT. MOVIE THEATER ENTRANCE - NINETY MINUTES LATER

The Woman finally reaches the door.

WOMAN
They had tickets ready in their hands.

An employee holds a small stack.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
They could have counted us out front.

The employee takes her printed ticket.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
They could have sent everyone else away after an hour.

A second employee stands beside the first, doing nothing.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Three workers collected our home printouts.

A third employee hands out theater passes.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
One gave out passes.

The other two women wipe sweat from their faces.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Two just stood there sweating.

The Woman checks her watch.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Seven o'clock hit.

The line still stretches behind her with no movement.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
No end came.

She turns and walks out.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
We left.

EXT. PARKING LOT - MOMENTS LATER

She reaches her car.

WOMAN
They screwed something up inside.

She opens the door.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
They fell behind schedule.

She gets in and slams the door.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Thanks for wasting my time.
script_events.coling::aa7ddd1b-2f96-496d-ba44-14337121:
INT. HOTEL ROOM - DAY

A couple sits on the bed. The woman picks up her phone. She taps the screen and calls the Grand Spa.

WOMAN
We need two spots today before dinner.

A spa employee responds through the speaker.

SPA EMPLOYEE (V.O.)
We have the last massage time open.

The woman smiles and books it. She hangs up.

INT. HOTEL LOBBY - LATER

The couple rushes through the lobby doors. They check their watches. They are ten minutes late.

INT. GRAND SPA RECEPTION - CONTINUOUS

They approach the desk. The woman signs papers. Her boyfriend pulls out his wallet. He hands over a credit card. The payment goes through.

A staff member appears. She waves them forward. She leads them down a hallway.

INT. SPA LOCKER AREA - CONTINUOUS

The staff member opens a locker. She hands them robes. She walks away.

The couple strips off their clothes. They pull on the robes. They tie the belts quickly.

INT. SPA HALLWAY - MOMENTS LATER

Two massage therapists walk up. They introduce themselves. The couple shakes their hands but forgets the names immediately.

INT. MASSAGE ROOM - CONTINUOUS

The door swings open. The couple enters. Soft light fills the space. Warm air wraps around them.

They lie down on two tables. The therapists begin working. Hands press into shoulders. Knuckles dig into backs. The couple relaxes.

A clock on the wall ticks forward. Forty-nine minutes pass instead of sixty.

The therapists step back. They leave the room. The door closes.

The couple sits up. They change back into their clothes. They open the door.

The therapists stand outside. Each holds a glass of cold water. The couple takes them and drinks.

INT. SPA HALLWAY - CONTINUOUS

The boyfriend turns left toward the men's area. The woman turns right toward the women's section. They separate.

INT. WOMEN'S SPA FACILITY - CONTINUOUS

The woman walks through. She sees a small sauna. She opens a cabinet with basic lotions. She finds a shower with standard soap. She frowns slightly.

An employee mops nearby but says nothing about closing time.

The woman checks her watch. She walks out.

INT. HOTEL HALLWAY - EVENING

The couple meets again. They hold hands.

WOMAN
Better than nothing.

They walk toward the elevators. The doors open. They step inside.
script_events.coling::6c998ea5-d795-44ca-8a25-22424b17:
INT. EL CHORRO RESTAURANT - DAY

A woman enters the dining room and spots her friends already seated at a large table. Eight people gather around bottles of wine. The hostess points her toward the group.

The woman checks her watch. Happy hour ended five minutes ago. Another friend walks through the door behind her. They move toward the table together.

The host from their party stands up. She walks across the room to intercept the waitress. The waitress approaches with menus in hand.

HOST
These are the two ladies I mentioned.

WAITRESS
Happy hour is over.

The woman sits down. She orders a drink from the menu. She adds an appetizer. She looks up at the waitress.

WOMAN
It's only five minutes after. Can you check if our drinks count for happy hour? Our friends are ordering a lot.

WAITRESS
I can't do that.

WOMAN
Can you ask the manager to bypass the system?

The waitress shakes her head. She turns away. She walks back to the kitchen without asking anyone.

The woman leans back in her chair. She remembers another visit to this restaurant. That day she arrived early to meet the same friend.

EXT. EL CHORRO PATIO BAR - DAY (FLASHBACK)

The woman sits at the outdoor bar. She orders a cocktail. Two women sit to her right. Another woman sits to her left.

The two women on the right signal the bartender. They order a shrimp appetizer. The female bartender frowns.

FEMALE BARTENDER
We're out because of lunch. Order something else.

Happy hour just started. The woman on the left raises her hand. She orders a shrimp appetizer from the regular menu. The bartender nods and walks away.

Minutes pass. A server brings shrimp to the woman on the left. The two women on the right notice the plate. They lean forward. The woman in the middle speaks up.

WOMAN
You said you were out of shrimp.

FEMALE BARTENDER
We're out for happy hour.

WOMAN ON RIGHT
How are they different?

FEMALE BARTENDER
Different menus use different shrimp.

The explanation makes no sense. The woman waves to Tim, the male bartender. He walks over. She explains what happened. Tim leaves and returns with the manager.

The manager listens. He walks to the two women on the right. He apologizes. He takes their order. A server brings them shrimp minutes later.

INT. EL CHORRO RESTAURANT - DAY (PRESENT)

The woman opens her laptop at the table. She logs into her work website. She types a message to six hundred real estate agents. She hits send. The message spreads across the network.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::be76162e-6297-4c2c-be8b-8be691cc:
INT. CHEAP PUB - DAY

A woman in tracksuit bottoms walks through the door. She carries no purse for makeup. She goes to the bar and orders a pint. The bartender pours it and takes one pound eighty from her. She sits at a table and drinks. A man approaches the counter and buys a meal for four pounds. He eats and his plate empties. Two people start a game at the first pool table. Another pair begins at the second table right next to them. A cue swings back and hits someone in the spine. That person turns and accidentally jabs another player. This happens again a minute later. The woman finishes her pint and stands. She walks downstairs to the lower level. Television screens cover the walls showing a football match. Music blares from speakers mounted in corners. The song is terrible and no one recognizes it. A man walks to the jukebox and feeds coins into the slot. He selects a different track to stop the noise. The jukebox resets to another awful song when his choice ends. The woman looks around the basement room. The lights are dim because the pub sits underground. Shadows fill the corners and make everything look sad. The furniture is old and no one has replaced it in years. Stains cover the carpet and the walls need paint. She decides she needs the toilet. She finds the bathroom and sees three stalls. A sign hangs on one door saying it is broken. A line of five women waits ahead of her. She joins the queue and stands there. Ten minutes pass while she waits. Her turn finally comes and she enters a stall. The toilet paper holder is empty. She checks the door lock and finds it missing. She uses the toilet anyway because she waited too long to leave now. She exits and washes her hands. She climbs the stairs back to ground level. She walks out the front door into daylight. The street outside looks bright after the darkness inside.
script_events.coling::8340ee01-1f28-4010-adce-4bf3c755:
INT. PLANETARIUM LECTURE HALL - DAY

A PROFESSOR clicks a remote. An old photograph appears on screen.

PROFESSOR
In 1930, astronomers spot Pluto for the first time.

The image shows a tiny blur at the edge of visibility.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
They measure it and think it matches Earth in size.

She advances to the next slide.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Everyone agrees to call it a planet.

The slide changes again. A technician wheels in a larger telescope.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Better instruments arrive in the following decades.

She points at new data appearing on screen.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
The measurements shrink. Now Pluto looks as big as Mars.

Another slide clicks forward.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Then it drops to Mercury size.

A student raises her hand. The professor nods.

STUDENT
What happened in the seventies?

PROFESSOR
Scientists split that single blur into two separate objects.

A diagram shows Pluto and Charon pulling apart.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
One was Pluto. The other was its moon Charon.

She walks to the window and looks out.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
That made Pluto smaller than Mercury. Much smaller.

The student writes notes. The professor returns to the podium.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Forty years passed. Pluto shrank from Earth size down to something like an asteroid.

A door opens. An ASSISTANT enters with coffee.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
People started asking if it deserved planet status.

The assistant sets down the cup and leaves.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Then the 2000s brought new discoveries. Eris appeared. Quaoar turned up. Sedna came next.

She displays three new images.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Some matched Pluto in size. Some might exceed it.

A clock on the wall ticks forward. The professor erases old notes from the board.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Astronomers faced a decision. Keep Pluto and accept dozens of future planets, or create a new category.

She writes "DWARF PLANET" in large letters.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
They chose the second option and invented dwarf planets.

The student closes her notebook.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
This solution works today. Tomorrow might bring trouble.

She points at a dark region of a star map.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
Something bigger than Mercury probably hides out there.

The lights dim slightly.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
It would fail the orbit test and become a dwarf planet despite its size.

She shrugs.

PROFESSOR (CONT'D)
For now, our definition holds.
script_events.coling::e998d6d5-1fb4-40ea-8696-d286397b:
INT. PARIS CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

Secretary of State JOHN KERRY shakes hands with Russian Foreign Minister SERGEY LAVROV. They sit down at a long table.

EXT. TURKISH-SYRIAN BORDER - SAME TIME

Sen JOHN MCCAIN, 76, steps out of a vehicle. He walks across the border into Syria with members of the Syrian Emergency Task Force.

INT. REBEL HEADQUARTERS - SYRIA - LATER

McCain enters a concrete building. General SALIM IDRIS, chief of staff of the Free Syrian Army, stands to greet him. Eighteen other rebel commanders fill the room.

They all sit. Idris leans forward.

IDRIS
We need weapons. Heavy weapons.

McCain nods and takes notes.

IDRIS (CONT'D)
A no-fly zone over our territory. Air strikes on Assad's positions.

EXT. SYRIAN VILLAGE - DAY

Government jets fly overhead. Bombs fall on buildings below.

INT. REBEL HEADQUARTERS - CONTINUOUS

Idris points to a map on the wall.

IDRIS
Hezbollah fighters cross from Lebanon here. They fight for Assad. Strike them too.

McCain studies the map. He asks questions. Idris answers each one.

EXT. SYRIAN BORDER - AFTERNOON

McCain walks back toward Turkey after several hours on the ground. He climbs into the waiting vehicle.

INT. MCCAIN'S OFFICE - WASHINGTON DC - NEXT DAY

Spokesman BRIAN ROGERS answers phone calls from reporters. He confirms the trip happened but gives no other details.

INT. WHITE HOUSE SITUATION ROOM - DAY

President OBAMA sits with advisors. They discuss McCain's visit. An advisor mentions the risk of weapons reaching al-Qaeda sympathizers.

Obama shakes his head.

EXT. NORTHERN SYRIA - WEEKS EARLIER

American Ambassador ROBERT FORD crosses the border from Turkey. He meets with opposition leaders in a safe house. This marks his first return since February 2012 when the embassy closed.

INT. SENATE ARMED SERVICES COMMITTEE ROOM - DAY

McCain stands at a podium. He addresses the committee as its top Republican member.

MCCAIN
Cruise missiles. That is what we should use against Assad's forces.

Some senators nod. Others look away.

EXT. SYRIAN BATTLEFIELD - DAY

Rebel fighters fire old rifles at government positions. They have no anti-aircraft weapons. A helicopter gunship circles above them unopposed.

The death toll since March 2011 reaches seventy thousand people.
script_events.coling::fc690535-1b34-43b1-9671-64ab5dda:
INT. COMPUTER LAB - DAY

A hacker sits at a desk. She types a password into a login box. The screen shows an error. She tries another password. The error appears again.

She opens a program that generates guesses. The program starts to check every possible combination. Numbers scroll down the monitor. Each attempt fails and then the next one begins.

The hacker switches to a different method. Now the program tries to guess the secret key instead. This key was made from the original password through a special process. The guessing continues without stopping.

A teacher enters the room. He explains that this approach can break into almost any protected file. The only exception is data that uses a perfect protection method. He adds that hackers use this when no easier weakness exists in the system.

The hacker stops the program. She points at the screen. Short passwords break quickly, she says. Then she starts a new test with longer passwords. The program slows down dramatically. She switches to a word list instead. The brute method would take years for long ones.

A graph appears on the monitor. It shows how adding more characters makes the task grow harder at a steep rate. The hacker nods.

The teacher walks to another computer. He demonstrates a technique that scrambles the data first. This makes it hard to tell when the correct answer appears. He then shows a setting that forces each guess to take more time.

A clock on the wall moves forward. The teacher writes a number on the board. This number represents how long the attack would need to succeed. The hacker studies it.

The teacher picks up a hammer from a shelf. He sets it down on the desk. Some people call this hammering, he says. He points to a shield icon. That represents anti-hammering protection. The lesson ends.
script_events.coling::a5255a94-63d9-4676-8a73-077823d9:
INT. ICANN OFFICE - DAY

A man in a suit opens a folder on his desk. He picks up a pen and starts writing a letter to the Federal Trade Commission.

EXT. COMPUTER SCREEN - DAY

A cursor clicks on Youtube.sucks. The page loads. Another click opens Bing.sucks. More tabs appear showing Visa.sucks and Bankofamerica.sucks.

INT. CELEBRITY MANAGER'S OFFICE - DAY

A phone rings. The manager answers it. Someone tells him Kevin Spacey needs to pay money. The manager hangs up and dials another number.

EXT. BANK - DAY

A wire transfer goes through. The money leaves Kevin Spacey's account. His name vanishes from the offensive website.

INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - EARLIER

ICANN officials sit around a table on March 30. They approve the new domain. Papers get signed. Everyone shakes hands and leaves.

INT. VOX POPULI OFFICE - DAY

Workers type at computers. They send out emails to trademark holders. The emails demand payment of 2,499 dollars per year.

EXT. STREET - DAY

A woman walks past a billboard. The billboard advertises the new domains. She takes out her phone and searches for information.

INT. MICROSOFT HEADQUARTERS - DAY

Executives gather for a meeting. One man stands and complains about the new policy. Others nod in agreement. They draft a complaint letter.

INT. VERIZON OFFICE - SAME TIME

Lawyers review documents. They add their signature to the complaint. A courier picks up the envelope and exits.

INT. ICANN OFFICE - DAY

The complaint letter arrives. Staff members read it aloud. The room grows tense. Someone suggests they reconsider their approval.

INT. VOX POPULI CEO OFFICE - DAY

John Berard sits behind his desk. A reporter asks him questions. He defends his business model. He insists everything follows the rules.

EXT. GODADDY.COM WAREHOUSE - DAY

Workers process domain registrations. Prices flash on screens showing one dollar per year. Customers complete their purchases and log off.

INT. TAYLOR SWIFT'S LAWYER OFFICE - FLASHBACK

The lawyer opens an invoice. It shows charges for removing her name from adult domains. He writes a check and mails it.

INT. ADVISORY BODY MEETING ROOM - TWO WEEKS AGO

Representatives from major companies convene. They call the scheme predatory. Someone uses the word shakedown. They vote to send ICANN a formal request.

INT. ICANN LEGAL DEPARTMENT - DAY

Lawyers draft a new letter. They mention possible contract breach. They discuss remedies and penalties. The letter gets sealed in an envelope.

EXT. POST OFFICE - DAY

The envelope goes into a mail truck. The truck drives toward Canada. It crosses the border and continues north.

INT. VOX POPULI OFFICE - DAY

Staff members prepare for September. They program the system to accept ten dollar registrations. The public launch date gets circled on a calendar.

INT. CONSUMER AFFAIRS OFFICE - CANADA - DAY

Officials receive the ICANN letter. They open it and begin reading. One official picks up the phone to call American regulators. The investigation starts.
script_events.coling::96b22ae3-8d33-4336-9ebe-8bd2645f:
INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

A man in a suit stands at the front of the room. He holds up a chart showing red numbers.

MAN
Care companies are closing down. They cannot pay their staff anymore.

EXT. HOSPITAL ENTRANCE - DAY

A worker in scrubs walks through the doors. A care home van drives past the hospital.

INT. CARE HOME OFFICE - DAY

A manager sits at her desk. She opens an envelope. The letter inside says the company lost its contract.

MANAGER
We tried to keep going. Now we stop.

INT. COUNCIL CHAMBER - DAY

Council members sit around a long table. One woman stands and speaks.

WOMAN
We need more money from the government. Our care workers earn too little.

A man nods his head. He writes something down on paper.

INT. GOVERNMENT OFFICE - CARDIFF - DAY

An official looks at a computer screen. Numbers appear showing new funding amounts.

OFFICIAL
The national living wage goes up in April. We gave councils extra money to cover it.

EXT. RESIDENTIAL STREET - DAY

A BBC camera crew sets up outside a house. A reporter holds a microphone.

REPORTER
We asked all the councils a question. Thirteen out of twenty one answered us.

INT. BBC STUDIO - DAY

The reporter sits at a desk. She reads from notes.

REPORTER (CONT'D)
Care companies signed contracts then pulled out. This happened many times.

INT. OFFICE - CARE ASSOCIATION - DAY

Colin Angel sits in a chair. He leans forward.

COLIN
Our members are struggling. They might not survive much longer.

He stands up and walks to the window.

COLIN (CONT'D)
The councils pay them too little. Rural areas will lose their care companies first.

EXT. CONWY STREET - DAY

A van with "Cymorth Llaw" written on the side parks outside a building.

INT. CYMORTH LLAW OFFICE - DAY

Ken Hogg sits behind a desk. He closes a folder.

KEN
Conwy offered us fifteen pounds per hour. We said no. That amount was not enough.

He stands and puts on his coat.

KEN (CONT'D)
We did not want to leave. But we had to go. Our bank manager needs to see profit at the end of each year.

INT. CONWY COUNCIL BUILDING - DAY

A council spokesperson faces the camera.

SPOKESPERSON
We support vulnerable people despite our financial problems.

INT. MEETING ROOM - LOCAL GOVERNMENT ASSOCIATION - DAY

Steve Thomas enters and sits down. He opens his briefcase.

STEVE
Councils need more money. Then they can pay carers better wages.

He pulls out documents and spreads them on the table.

STEVE (CONT'D)
Without new funding we face a big problem. Nobody feels proud of what we pay social care workers.

INT. GOVERNMENT CHAMBER - LONDON - DAY

An announcement appears on a screen. The amount reads two billion pounds.

INT. CARDIFF OFFICE - DAY

An official receives a phone call. She writes down the figure of two hundred million pounds.

OFFICIAL
This money came from London. We have not decided how to spend it yet.

INT. GOVERNMENT BUILDING - REBECCA EVANS' OFFICE - DAY

Rebecca Evans sits at her desk. She looks at the camera.

REBECCA
The cabinet will decide where the money goes. We are working on recruitment problems right now.

She picks up a document.

REBECCA (CONT'D)
A registration scheme starts in twenty twenty. This will give workers proper recognition. They look after our most vulnerable people. No job matters more than that.

She puts the document down and picks up another.

REBECCA (CONT'D)
Workers will see career development opportunities. That does not happen now. We already invested money to improve their working conditions.

She signs the document.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::5fd0fd85-ca70-4e53-8dd5-eac22c60:
INT. CONFERENCE ROOM - DAY

An ECONOMIST stands at a whiteboard. Three EXECUTIVES sit at a table.

ECONOMIST
We need to stop messing up for ten minutes.

He draws a circle on the board.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
The problem is uncertainty. It blocks growth.

An EXECUTIVE leans forward.

EXECUTIVE 1
What does that mean for us?

ECONOMIST
No one invests. No one builds. Everyone waits.

He writes "DEBT" in large letters.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
They wait because government debt keeps the crisis alive.

EXECUTIVE 2 opens a folder.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
I study economics but Europe is not my main area. Someone here might know more than me.

He pauses. No one speaks.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
Governments borrowed too much. They gave people more than they could pay for.

He draws an arrow pointing down.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
Government money comes from the economy. The economy shrinks and government income drops.

EXECUTIVE 3 nods slowly.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
The recession hit. Governments were already spending beyond their means. Then their income fell even further.

He adds more arrows.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
Their debt spiraled out of control after that.

EXECUTIVE 1 stands and walks to the window.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
The rational move is cutting spending to reduce debt.

He draws an X through the circle.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
But here comes the catch. The weak countries have economies that hurt too much already.

EXECUTIVE 2 closes the folder.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
The cuts they need would damage their economy worse. Their income would drop again. The debt would not get solved.

He writes "GREECE" on the board.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
Greece cuts spending to zero deficit. Their economy crashes. Their debt increases anyway because income falls.

EXECUTIVE 3 shakes his head.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
Countries need growth to increase revenues. Revenues let them reduce deficits. Lower deficits decrease uncertainty. Less uncertainty brings growth.

He draws a loop.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
Each step requires the previous step. We must find a way to create growth despite rising debt.

EXECUTIVE 1 turns from the window.

EXECUTIVE 1
What solutions exist?

ECONOMIST
The European central bank could allow moderate inflation. Say ten percent.

He writes "10%" on the board.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
Debts become more affordable. Some debts actually shrink.

EXECUTIVE 2 reopens the folder and takes notes.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
Spain pays seven percent on bonds. Ten percent inflation means they pay a negative real rate.

He moves to a new section of the board.

ECONOMIST (CONT'D)
Or they could make banks less volatile. Investment houses too.

EXECUTIVE 3 stands.

EXECUTIVE 3
I understand the idea now.

The Economist sets down his marker.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::47287806-d919-4000-abf1-68414815:
INT. GAME STORE - DAY

A CLERK stands behind the counter. A CUSTOMER enters holding a list.

CUSTOMER
Which Final Fantasy game came first in each timeline?

The Clerk pulls out a chart and spreads it on the counter.

CLERK
Final Fantasy 5 started one continuity.

He taps the chart.

CLERK (CONT'D)
Then Legend of the Crystals arrived as its sequel.

The Customer leans forward.

CLERK (CONT'D)
FF7 launched another timeline.

He slides a box across the counter.

CLERK (CONT'D)
Crisis Core showed up later as the prequel.

The Customer picks up the box.

CLERK (CONT'D)
Dirge of Cerberus followed as a sequel.

He sets down three more boxes.

CLERK (CONT'D)
FF Tactics began its own world.

The Customer nods.

CLERK (CONT'D)
Vagrant Story appeared far in the future of that world.

He points to another box.

CLERK (CONT'D)
FF 12 took place far in the past of the same world.

The Customer reaches for a different game.

CLERK (CONT'D)
We do not discuss FF Tactics Advanced here.

He pushes that box away.

CLERK (CONT'D)
FF 10 opened its continuity.

The Customer grabs it.

CLERK (CONT'D)
FF 10 - 2 came next.

He adds another to the pile.

CLERK (CONT'D)
FF 13 started a three part set.

The Customer counts on his fingers.

CLERK (CONT'D)
FF13 - 2 joined the collection.

He stacks the boxes higher.

CLERK (CONT'D)
FF13 - 3 completed that trilogy.

The Customer looks confused.

CLERK (CONT'D)
All other games stand alone.

He waves his hand over the remaining titles.

CLERK (CONT'D)
I know zero things about any MMO entries.

The Customer picks up an old cartridge.

CUSTOMER
What about the American releases?

The Clerk opens a drawer.

CLERK
The original launched in both Japan and America with the same number.

He pulls out more cartridges.

CLERK (CONT'D)
Japan kept 2 and 3 to themselves.

The Customer examines the labels.

CLERK (CONT'D)
America received 4 as FF2 on the SNES.

He lines up the cartridges.

CLERK (CONT'D)
America missed 5 completely.

The Customer frowns.

CLERK (CONT'D)
America got 6 as FF3.

He taps the final cartridge.

CLERK (CONT'D)
FFVII fixed the whole mess and the numbers matched again.

The Customer gathers his purchases and exits.
script_events.coling::193845c4-6305-4c19-a075-01cc05c9:
INT. BEDROOM - NIGHT

A man sits on the edge of his bed. He looks at the camera.

MAN
You shut down completely.

He lies back on the pillow.

MAN (CONT'D)
Think about the time before your birth.

The lamp clicks off. Darkness fills the room.

MAN (CONT'D)
Death works the same way.

INT. KITCHEN - DAY

A woman pours coffee into a mug. She shakes her head.

WOMAN
Everyone gets this wrong.

She sets the pot down hard.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
Sleep is not unconsciousness.

A second woman enters through the doorway.

SECOND WOMAN
What do you mean?

The first woman turns to face her.

WOMAN
Your brain still responds to sounds.

She snaps her fingers.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
An alarm wakes you up.

She picks up the mug.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
True unconsciousness means nothing gets through.

She takes a sip.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
The real answer involves memory.

She sets the mug down again.

WOMAN (CONT'D)
The memory system goes offline at night.

INT. LIVING ROOM - EVENING

A young boy sits on a couch. He fidgets with his hands.

BOY
Eight hours never feels short to me.

His mother walks past carrying laundry.

BOY (CONT'D)
I always know I slept that long.

He stands up and moves to the window.

BOY (CONT'D)
When I was little I wanted sleep to pass faster.

He presses his hand against the glass.

BOY (CONT'D)
Christmas morning took forever to arrive.

He turns back to the room.

BOY (CONT'D)
People say death is like sleeping.

He sits back down.

BOY (CONT'D)
That never comforts me at all.

He picks up a book from the table.

BOY (CONT'D)
My brain keeps working through the night.

INT. OFFICE - AFTERNOON

A man leans against a desk. He crosses his arms.

MAN TWO
It feels instant for me.

A colleague rolls her chair closer.

MAN TWO (CONT'D)
I close my eyes one moment.

He blinks slowly.

MAN TWO (CONT'D)
Then I open them the next.

He uncrosses his arms.

MAN TWO (CONT'D)
I never catch the moment I fall under.

INT. APARTMENT - MIDDAY

A woman wakes on a couch. She looks around confused.

WOMAN TWO
Short naps mess me up completely.

She checks her phone.

WOMAN TWO (CONT'D)
Thirty minutes can feel like days passed.

She stands slowly.

WOMAN TWO (CONT'D)
I wake up not knowing where I am.

She walks to the kitchen sink.

WOMAN TWO (CONT'D)
A full night never does this to me.

INT. COMPUTER ROOM - NIGHT

A young man types at a keyboard. He stops and looks up.

YOUNG MAN
Reposting only takes eight hours.

He grins.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
But it feels like five minutes.

INT. FACTORY - DAY

A worker watches a machine. He sighs.

WORKER
Five minutes of work feels like eight hours.

INT. LABORATORY - EVENING

A scientist stands at a whiteboard. She writes with a marker.

SCIENTIST
Consciousness shuts down completely during sleep.

She draws a line.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The same thing happens when you die.

She caps the marker.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
The you that exists stops existing.

She erases part of the board.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
A new you starts each morning.

She writes again.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
All versions access the same memories.

She steps back.

SCIENTIST (CONT'D)
This creates an illusion of continuity.

INT. CLASSROOM - AFTERNOON

A teacher points to a diagram on a screen.

TEACHER
Specific brain regions control time perception.

She clicks to the next slide.

TEACHER (CONT'D)
These areas go inactive during sleep.

INT. GROCERY STORE - EVENING

A man places cheese in his cart. He picks up bananas next.

MAN THREE
Foods with certain vitamins change your dreams.

He moves down the aisle.

MAN THREE (CONT'D)
Cheese and bananas work best.

He stops at the checkout.

MAN THREE (CONT'D)
Your sleep will feel much longer.

He pays and leaves the store.

MAN THREE (CONT'D)
You will remember everything you dreamed.

INT. TRAIN CAR - MORNING

An older woman stares out the window. She speaks to herself.

OLDER WOMAN
Time moves faster as you age.

The train lurches forward.

OLDER WOMAN (CONT'D)
Five minutes used to drag on forever.

She checks her watch.

OLDER WOMAN (CONT'D)
Now the microwave finishes before I tie my shoes.

The train stops at a station.

OLDER WOMAN (CONT'D)
My commute ends before I finish one game.

She exits onto the platform.

OLDER WOMAN (CONT'D)
Work passes in an instant now.

She climbs the stairs.

OLDER WOMAN (CONT'D)
Evening arrives before I notice it.

She reaches the street.

OLDER WOMAN (CONT'D)
This pattern terrifies me deeply.

INT. HOSPITAL RECOVERY ROOM - DAY

A patient opens his eyes. A nurse stands nearby.

PATIENT
Full anesthesia erases time completely.

He tries to sit up.

PATIENT (CONT'D)
I have experienced it five times.

The nurse helps him.

PATIENT (CONT'D)
I always wake wondering when surgery will start.

He looks around the room.

PATIENT (CONT'D)
Regular sleep feels different to me.

He settles back.

PATIENT (CONT'D)
Dreams make me aware time has passed.

INT. BEDROOM TWO - MORNING

A man wakes and rubs his face.

MAN FOUR
Alcohol makes sleep feel short.

He swings his legs out of bed.

MAN FOUR (CONT'D)
Otherwise my dreams feel very vivid.

He stands.

MAN FOUR (CONT'D)
I wake up thinking dreams were real.

He walks to the bathroom.

MAN FOUR (CONT'D)
Most of
script_events.coling::4622a5f2-c96d-4ea1-9629-b734e976:
INT. OBSERVATORY CONTROL ROOM - DAY

A monitor displays a map of space. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey has grown to cover a wide area. Empty regions now appear on the screen.

Rojas walks in and sits at a computer. She types commands and the display changes. Her method pulls out galaxies that sit in voids. More than a thousand dots light up in the dark zones.

A colleague enters and leans over her shoulder. He asks what she found. Rojas explains these galaxies live where matter is thin.

The colleague moves to his own desk. He opens a file that shows how bright each void galaxy is. The data spans from very dim to fairly bright objects.

Rojas joins him and they fit a curve to the numbers. The curve takes a particular shape. They write down three values that describe it.

The colleague pulls up a second file. This one holds galaxies from dense walls between voids. He fits another curve to that group.

Rojas compares the two curves on split screens. The wall galaxies shine brighter at their peak. But the slopes at the faint end match closely.

She frowns and opens more files. She sorts the wall galaxies by how packed their neighborhoods are. Only the most crowded regions show a different slope.

The colleague suggests a new comparison. He filters the wall galaxies to keep only the blue ones. He adds another filter for shape and then one more for a spectral line.

Rojas runs the fit again on this subset. The curve now matches the void galaxy curve almost perfectly. The peak shifts just slightly.

She leans back and crosses her arms. The colleague opens a theory paper on his tablet. The predictions show a steeper slope than what they measured.

Rojas shakes her head. The voids must not be full of tiny dim galaxies after all. She saves the results and closes the windows. They both stand and walk toward the door.

FADE OUT.
script_events.coling::ffaf0483-45dd-41b7-ac1d-8a511127:
INT. LIVING ROOM - DAY

DAVE TYLER, 72, sits in an armchair and opens a photo album.

EXT. BACK GARDEN - HIGH WYCOMBE - DAY

Dave walks across his lawn toward a white dome structure.

He reaches the observatory door and pulls it open.

Inside, a telescope points upward through the dome opening.

Dave flips a switch and the dome roof begins to rotate.

He adjusts the telescope mount and aims it at the sun.

A laptop screen beside him flickers on and displays a bright orange disc.

Dark spots appear across the sun's surface as the image focuses.

Dave clicks the mouse and the camera shutter fires.

A massive prominence erupts from the edge of the sun.

Gas streams outward in a long arc above the surface.

Dave leans forward and captures the event with another click.

The sun's corona glows around the edges in the filtered view.

A solar flare brightens suddenly in one region.

Dave types notes into a document on his computer.

The dome continues its slow turn to track the sun's movement.

INT. LIVING ROOM - DAY (1957)

Young Dave, age 14, sits before a television set.

The BBC logo appears and a program title reads SKY AT NIGHT.

A presenter begins speaking about stars and planets.

Dave's eyes widen as he watches the first episode.

EXT. BACK GARDEN - DAY (1968)

Adult Dave carries an old telescope across his yard.

He sets it on a camera tripod and tightens the bolts.

His friend waves goodbye from the garden gate.

Dave peers through the eyepiece and turns the focus knob.

Saturn appears in the view with its rings clearly visible.

He steps back from the telescope in amazement.

His hand trembles as he reaches for the eyepiece again.

EXT. BACK GARDEN - DAY (1977)

Dave hammers nails into wooden frame pieces.

He lifts a curved panel and attaches it to the structure.

The dome takes shape over several hours of work.

He bolts the final section into place at sunset.

INT. OBSERVATORY - NIGHT

Dave installs the telescope on its permanent mount.

He connects cables from the camera to the computer.

The system powers up and runs through a test sequence.

EXT. BACK GARDEN - DAY (PRESENT)

Dave exits the observatory and locks the door behind him.

He walks back toward his house carrying a memory card.

INT. LIVING ROOM - DAY

Dave inserts the card into his computer and files load.

A sunspot image from February fills the monitor.

He selects another file and a prominence from January appears.

Dave prints the best images and adds them to his album.

He closes the book and places it on a shelf.

INT. COFFEE SHOP - DAY

MARK sits at a small table. His friend SARAH walks in.

MARK
Look at this list. Joan Rivers, Donatella Versace, Michael Jackson, Meg Ryan, Suzanne Somers, Mickey Rourke, Lara Flynn Boyle, Melanie Griffith, Janice Dickinson.

SARAH
What about them?

She pulls out a chair and sits down.

MARK
They all got tons of plastic surgery. Most of them tell people what looks good.

SARAH
Joan Rivers was on TV for that.

MARK
She was pretty when she was young. She looked good when she got older too.

SARAH
Then what happened?

MARK
Near the end she looked like a puppet. You know that old Genesis video? Land of Confusion?

Sarah nods.

MARK (CONT'D)
Nobody calls it a mental problem. Everyone acts like it's fine.

SARAH
She died during one of those surgeries.

MARK
Right. Surgery number seven hundred or whatever. She wanted it done.

SARAH
So what's the issue?

MARK
That's the disease talking. An alcoholic wants to drink all the time. A kleptomaniac wants to steal stuff. A homeless guy with problems wants to sleep in the gutter.

Sarah picks up her coffee cup and takes a sip.

MARK (CONT'D)
But nobody stopped her. Nobody said she had a problem. Nobody got her help.

SARAH
People hired her to judge how others looked.

MARK
Exactly. They told her she looked great. They said she should get more work done.

Sarah sets down her cup.

MARK (CONT'D)
This spreads to other women. They see it and think it's normal.

SARAH
You think the people around her made it worse?

MARK
Her friends enabled her. Her doctors told her she needed surgery six hundred and fifty eight. They caused this death.

Sarah leans back in her chair.

MARK (CONT'D)
It's like the doctor who gave Jackson too much of his drug. He overdosed him.

SARAH
What about burn victims?

MARK
That's different. Someone caught in a fire gets seven hundred surgeries to fix the burns. That's medicine working right. That's a miracle.

Sarah crosses her arms.

MARK (CONT'D)
I believe people can choose what they do. But there's a limit.

SARAH
What kind of limit?

MARK
You tell a gambler not to go to Vegas. He lost his house last time.

Sarah uncrosses her arms and leans forward.

SARAH
So you think this is a real disease?

MARK
I do. Am I being too harsh? Is it too soon to talk about this?

SARAH
Maybe people will say you're wrong.

MARK
I don't think I am wrong.

Sarah picks up a napkin and folds it.

MARK (CONT'D)
Some people will say it wasn't even plastic surgery that killed her.

SARAH
What do they think it was?

MARK
I don't know. Some other explanation. But that misses the point.

Sarah puts down the napkin.

MARK (CONT'D)
She was beautiful when she was young. She was beautiful when she got old too.

SARAH
But then she changed.

MARK
She looked like those puppets. From that Genesis video. Land of Confusion.

Sarah stands up.

MARK (CONT'D)
Society doesn't treat this like a mental disease. Everyone says it's normal and fine.

SARAH
She would be alive now if she hadn't gone.

MARK
Surgery seven hundred. She felt she needed it.

Sarah walks toward the door.

MARK (CONT'D)
She was okay with it. That's the disease part. An alcoholic stays drunk all the time and thinks it's fine. A kleptomaniac steals and thinks it's fine. A homeless person sleeps in a gutter and thinks it's fine.

Sarah opens the door. She looks back at Mark. He stares at his list. She walks out. The door closes behind her.

INT. FUNERAL HOME - DAY

A young man walks into the chapel. He stops and scans the rows of mourners. The mourners turn their heads and stare at him. Their faces twist with disgust. The young man steps toward the front. An usher points him to a seat near the altar. He sits down and waits. The funeral director approaches him. The director hands him a folded paper. The young man opens it and reads his father's request. His hands start to shake. He stands up and walks to the podium. The mourners lean forward in their seats. He grips the edges of the podium.

YOUNG MAN
I can see you all know who I am. Your faces tell me that much. I left home years ago. I quit school and ran. I never came back to visit. It was not because I hated him. I just felt nothing when we talked. We sat in rooms together like strangers. Now he wants me to speak here. I have never done this before. We only ever discussed one thing. He told me stories about Vietnam. He was a kid back then trying to earn money. Maybe he wants me to repeat those stories now. I will try.

He looks down at his notes. He crumples the paper. He throws it aside.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
I lived in his house for years. I never learned what beer he drank. I never asked what car he wanted. I never knew if he had hobbies. He grew up without a father. No one taught him to throw or fish. So he did not know how to teach me. He tried in his way. I was too angry to notice.

A woman in the front row dabs her eyes. The young man loosens his tie.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
He talked about his mother once. That was rare for him. He cried when he told me. It was the first time I saw that. The second time was our last meeting. He ran away from his home when he was young. He only saw his mother again at her funeral. He said that was his biggest regret. He wished he had hugged her more. He wanted her advice. He wanted to know how to treat women right.

Tears roll down his cheeks. He wipes them away with his sleeve.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
I just realized something standing here. I did the same things he did. I ran away like he ran away. I skipped her funeral like he skipped hers. No, I mean his mother. Wait, I mean I skipped his funeral in a way by never coming home.

He stops and takes a breath. He starts again.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
I followed his path exactly. Every mistake he made, I made too. 

He steps back from the podium. He walks down the steps. The mourners watch him go. He reaches the chapel door. He pushes it open. Sunlight floods in. He walks outside into the cemetery. He finds the fresh grave. He kneels beside it. He touches the dirt. He stands up and walks toward the parking lot. He stops and turns back. He speaks to the headstone.

YOUNG MAN (CONT'D)
I should have asked what beer you liked, dad. I would pour it here for you now.

He turns away. He walks to his car. He gets in and drives off.

FADE OUT.

Our investigation concerns a two-dimensional tight-binding construction representing a topological crystalline insulator whose protection derives from rotational symmetry. This architecture emerges through layering two Chern insulators bearing opposing Chern numbers, each transforming under conjugate representations within the rotation group—exemplified by $p_\pm$ orbitals. Though superficially resembling the Kane-Mele framework, this configuration notably fails to sustain stable gapless boundary states. Nevertheless, distinctive topological phenomena manifest themselves: quantized fractional charge accumulates at rotational defects (disclinations), while threading elementary magnetic flux induces angular momentum pumping. These responses find their description through mutual Chern-Simons coupling linking the electromagnetic gauge field to an effective gauge field embodying rotational symmetry.

Furthermore, we demonstrate that although the occupied bands resist symmetric Wannier representation, this obstruction dissolves upon incorporating suitable atomic orbitals—a signature of 'fragile' topology. Consequently, the system's response becomes derivable by expressing it as a superposition of atomic orbitals weighted with positive and negative integer coefficients.

Following our analysis of this prototypical example among two-dimensional topological crystalline insulators protected by rotation, we establish a broader principle: all such insulators protected by point group symmetries yet lacking protected boundary states necessarily constitute either atomic insulators or fragile phases. This yields a remarkable conclusion—gapless boundary states arise in non-interacting electron systems if and only if a stable Wannier obstruction persists.

We subsequently employ dimensional reduction, mapping the classification problem for two-dimensional rotationally-protected topological crystalline insulators onto a zero-dimensional analogue. This transformation enables us to obtain the complete non-interacting classification for such insulators, while also revealing how interactions reduce this classification scheme. The baryon acoustic oscillation peak, discerned within the cosmic matter distribution at redshifts extending to approximately 3.5, manifests the persistent expansion of that sonic horizon initially detected through temperature anisotropies pervading the cosmic microwave background. Contemporary observations permit determination of this peak's location with remarkable precision—better than one percent when employing galaxies, and roughly 1.4 to 1.6 percent utilizing Lyman-alpha forests alongside quasar clustering patterns. When combined with the Alcock-Paczyński effect, which emerges from the evolving ratio between angular and spatial/redshift dimensions of presumably spherically-symmetric source distributions across varying distances, this oscillation measurement constitutes among the most potent instruments available for probing the Universe's underlying geometry.

Within this investigation, we harness five distinct peak measurements drawn from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey IV's conclusive data release, spanning mean redshifts of 0.38, 0.51, 0.70, 1.48, and 2.33, to conduct an unmediated comparison between the standard Lambda-CDM paradigm and a prominent alternative framework designated the R_h=ct universe. For thoroughness, we augment the Alcock-Paczyński diagnostic with a volume-averaged distance probe predicated upon constant comoving distance scale r_d. Both analytical approaches remain unencumbered by uncertain parameters, notably the Hubble constant, rendering them exceptionally well-suited for discriminating between competing cosmological models.

Our analysis reveals that the R_h=ct construction garners preferential support from these observations when evaluated exclusively through the Alcock-Paczyński effect, commanding approximately seventy-five percent likelihood against the standard model's twenty-five percent. Conversely, Planck-Lambda-CDM secures advantage over R_h=ct when assessed solely via the volume-averaged distance probe, achieving roughly eighty percent likelihood compared to twenty percent. A synthesis incorporating both diagnostic techniques yields an indeterminate result, conferring comparable statistical support to each cosmological framework. Consequently, this work cannot substantiate claims that baryon acoustic oscillation evidence, considered independently, necessitates an accelerating Universe.

I should acknowledge at the outset my genuine affection for Cowboy Bebop. Its animation and visual design achieve sublimity, its soundtrack stands among the medium's finest achievements, and its action sequences deliver consistent excellence. When these elements converge, the series occasionally transcends its components to become an audiovisual triumph—nowhere more breathtakingly than in its concluding episodes. Yet despite these considerable virtues, the series harbors sufficient flaws that I cannot conscientiously elevate it to masterpiece status, nor rank it among anime's paramount achievements except perhaps as an introductory gateway for newcomers to the form.

My reservations center primarily upon characterization. Spike and Jet, I readily concede, represent compelling creations, yet they constitute merely half the Bebop's central quartet. Ein receives introduction as a "data dog," supposedly possessing hyperintelligence, yet this premise evaporates immediately; thereafter he functions as nothing beyond the crew's ordinary pet, his purported cognitive gifts abandoned entirely. Faye embodies numerous regrettable tendencies in female characterization: she manifests as domineering, avaricious, vain about her appearance, and perpetually requires rescue or impedes the group's efforts rather than contributing meaningfully. Her wardrobe choices exist transparently for audience titillation rather than narrative purpose. Ed oscillates unpredictably between endearing and grating, straddling that precarious boundary, yet receives scant development beyond her inaugural appearance.

The principal antagonist Vicious proves especially disappointing. He possesses minimal interiority or intelligible motivation beyond naked ambition for increased authority. Although the narrative gestures toward his history, it never establishes coherent psychological foundations for his actions. By the series' conclusion, Vicious remains little beyond a malevolent figure draped in dark garments, whose combat prowess challenges Spike sufficiently to complicate marksmanship, functioning primarily as symbolic representation of the criminal syndicate from which Spike fled. Consequently, the five episodes featuring him—Sympathy for the Devil, both Jupiter Jazz installments, and both Real Folk Blues segments—fail to generate the profound impact the narrative clearly intends them to carry.

Beyond these character deficiencies, the episodic quality fluctuates wildly. For a predominantly standalone series containing merely five installments advancing an overarching narrative, such inconsistency proves particularly damaging. Certainly, exceptional episodes exist: Waltz for Venus and Ganymede Elegy demonstrate the heights the series can reach. Yet equally present are thoroughly mediocre offerings such as Bohemian Rhapsody, Speak Like a Child, and Boogie Woogie Feng Shui, which neither advance character nor deliver memorable spectacle.

I find myself seeking understanding here. What dimensions of this celebrated work elude my appreciation? Where should I redirect my attention to perceive the qualities that have secured its reputation? I acknowledge my perspective may suffer from blind spots or misplaced expectations that prevent proper recognition of its achievements.

This represents a sincere inquiry rather than mere contrarianism. The series clearly resonates powerfully with countless viewers who regard it as definitive of the medium's possibilities. I wish to comprehend that perspective more fully, to grasp what my current viewing framework prevents me from recognizing. Perhaps I weigh certain elements too heavily while undervaluing others. Perhaps the very qualities I perceive as weaknesses function differently within the work's aesthetic logic than I currently understand. I remain genuinely open to reconsidering my assessment if provided with perspectives that illuminate what my present interpretation overlooks or misconstrues.

I confess myself genuinely uncertain about this question, though I shall commence by examining the case opposing same-sex marriage for two considerations: first, because I incline less toward this position—which appears considerably more vulnerable and unpopular—and championing a frailer stance about which I harbor fewer convictions allows me to refine my capacity for articulating arguments; second, because I maintain that those advocating for same-sex marriage bear the burden of demonstration (as I shall elucidate), prompting me to begin from the contrary perspective. I ask that you first view a particular video, merely two minutes in duration. The reasoning it presents persuades me that those seeking to reconstitute the defining characteristics of matrimony as an institution must shoulder the evidentiary burden. I harbor no objection to redefinition per se, yet such reconstitution demands compelling justification. When respondents answer the inquiry "Do you consider same-sex marriage advisable?" with "Why not?," they commit the teapot fallacy—attempting to transfer the burden of demonstration to their interlocutor.

I find equality an insufficient argument. Certainly, individuals of divergent sexual orientations merit equivalent entitlements to existence, liberty, autonomy, and the pursuit of fulfillment as our constitutional documents specify. Nevertheless, invoking equality here constitutes a red herring. Matrimony is neither a privilege nor an entitlement requiring uniformity across all relational configurations. Marriage represents an institution constructed around procreation, whereas homosexual relationships—however affectionate and devoted—remain by definition non-procreative. Heterosexual unions may likewise be non-procreative, as with elderly or infertile partners, but the video clarifies why this proves non-analogous: exceptions to a standard do not justify extending definitions to encompass what lies outside that standard, since norms cannot be characterized by their aberrations. This "equality" differs fundamentally from women's suffrage or emancipation from bondage.

The criterion frequently appears as a posed question: "If two individuals love one another, why shouldn't they receive permission to wed?" Matrimonial criteria bear no relation to affection, nor even to romantic attachment specifically. If your standard becomes two persons experiencing romantic or sexual devotion, then consanguineous relationships become permissible. Some contend that incest differs because familial contexts involve power asymmetries and genetic abnormalities. Power imbalances exist within any relationship—heterosexual, homosexual, or consanguineous. No rationale exists for basing matrimonial legislation upon this factor. Furthermore, incestuous partners need not produce offspring, may adopt, or could be infertile or homosexual themselves. One might argue that consanguinity should constitute a legitimate marital form alongside homosexuality. You may attempt defending this position, provided you supply valid reasoning, since the burden of demonstration falls upon you.

The "why should you care?" argument proves invalid. That a proposition harms no one adversely does not authorize arbitrary institutional modification. Even utilitarian frameworks fail to validate this reasoning. Homosexual individuals can maintain fulfilling, enduring romantic and sexual partnerships without denominating them marriage. Reconstituting matrimony for one group's contentment resembles (logically, though not emotionally) capitulating to lobbyist pressure for their satisfaction.

Most arguments favoring same-sex marriage constitute appeals to sentiment or popularity. The phrase "gay rights" was crafted to suggest we maintain detention facilities for such persons. Even "homophobe" was invented to stigmatize opposition. When insufficient competitors exist to populate a complete field within a single classification, organizers frequently merge analogous categories. Athletes with milder cerebral palsy impairments may compete alongside amputees bearing comparable functional limitations, though each remains evaluated exclusively within their designated division. This consolidation occurs routinely in cycling competitions, expediting proceedings while maintaining administrative efficiency.

An athlete whose cerebral palsy affects ambulation would join this final category alongside any competitor whose disability similarly compromises both legs, regardless of underlying pathology.

Programs fail for myriad reasons, though certain patterns recur with predictable frequency. Consider these familiar culprits:

Division by zero: Elementary mathematics teaches us that dividing any quantity by zero yields an undefined result — a fundamental impossibility. When software instructs a computer to perform this forbidden operation, the machine protests, signaling that something impermissible has been attempted. Should the software lack provisions for handling such objections, collapse follows inevitably.

Access violation: Every running application receives permission to manipulate only designated regions of memory; other territories remain strictly forbidden. When software attempts to trespass into prohibited zones, the computer issues a stern rebuke, announcing the transgression. Again, if the application cannot accommodate this reproach gracefully, termination ensues.

Deadlock: Imagine two children, yourself and your companion Billy, engaged with building blocks. You possess the crimson block; Billy clutches the azure one. Desiring an exchange, you propose surrendering your crimson piece only after receiving Billy's azure treasure. Billy, employing identical logic, insists upon receiving your crimson block before relinquishing his azure possession. This impasse persists indefinitely — neither party yields, neither transaction completes, nothing advances. When such paralysis afflicts software, the application freezes entirely, leaving no remedy except forcible termination and fresh initialization.

Unhandled exception: Certain applications incorporate sophisticated error-detection mechanisms. When anomalies surface, one component "throws" an exception — essentially broadcasting an alarm — while another component should "catch" this alert and address it appropriately. If an exception propagates through the entire system without any component intercepting and resolving it, typically a dialog window materializes, announcing that difficulties have escaped proper management, whereupon the application ceases functioning.

These scenarios all stem from "bugs" — defects embedded within the code itself. Bugs represent segments improperly constructed or inadequately prepared for the full spectrum of potential circumstances. Some applications harbor more defects than others. What accounts for this disparity? Perhaps the developers worked under excessive time pressure, or perhaps testing protocols proved insufficiently rigorous. Alternatively, the application's inherent complexity may render comprehensive anticipation of every conceivable scenario extraordinarily difficult.

Consider programs as "methodologies for accomplishing tasks" — a frequently cited illustration involves constructing a peanut butter and jelly sandwich. Your initial attempt might enumerate: obtain bread, obtain peanut butter, obtain jelly, obtain knife, spread peanut butter on one slice, spread jelly on the other slice, press slices together, serve. Should your peanut butter supply become exhausted midway through these instructions, you find yourself stranded without any subsequent steps to follow — that constitutes a crash.

A more elaborate program might describe operating a pizza restaurant — numerous ingredients exist, countless combination possibilities emerge, multiple employees arrive and depart simultaneously, and substantially more complications can materialize. Some difficulties admit solutions; others resist correction entirely. Those problems that cannot be rectified — or that developers prove too indolent to address — manifest as crashes. The comparison illuminates how complexity breeds vulnerability: simple procedures fail in obvious, easily preventable ways, whereas intricate systems harbor countless opportunities for catastrophic breakdown, many lurking undetected until circumstances conspire to expose them during actual operation.

Two distinct queries demand consideration here, though their answers converge upon impossibility:

Regarding a bridge: The Atlantic's magnitude staggers comprehension. Depending upon one's chosen crossing, the span might exceed America's entire continental width. Beyond mere distance, however, lies the compounding challenge of maritime conditions—perpetual moisture and violent tempests inflicting relentless degradation upon concrete and steel, the fundamental materials such construction would require. Meanwhile, surface conditions preclude pontoon-style architecture, for the ceaseless undulation would generate stresses sufficient to fragment any floating causeway. Even supposing these obstacles surmounted, the resulting thoroughfare would traverse such monotonous emptiness that few travelers would willingly endure the tedium, particularly given the impossibility of carrying sufficient fuel for completion. Maintenance presents nightmarish complications, given saltwater's corrosive assault on every component. Concerning a tunnel: Oceanic depths introduce pressures exponentially exceeding anything terrestrial experience provides. Consider the discomfort accompanying modest pool diving, then magnify that sensation ten-thousandfold. Such tremendous forces mean any excavated passage must maintain absolute impermeability, for the slightest breach would trigger catastrophic structural failure, crushing walls inward and drowning occupants instantly. Technical elaboration clarifies the core difficulty: prefabricated sections would require joining within the excavated channel, yet no available methodology could produce seams sufficiently robust against such pressure. Even granting successful completion, would the result prove practical? Consider vehicular range between refuelings, or human endurance limits before exhaustion demands rest. Should emergency arise mid-crossing, response personnel would require hours merely reaching the incident location.

Possibility exists, certainly, even employing contemporary technology. Economic viability, however, remains utterly absent—costs would prove astronomical while benefits remain minimal. Technological advances anticipated throughout coming decades might render the endeavor more feasible, yet current assessment must acknowledge the project's impracticality. The engineering challenges, though formidable, pale beside the economic and logistical absurdities. No rational analysis supports proceeding, regardless of technical capability. The Atlantic's immensity, coupled with the absence of compelling justification, ensures such infrastructure remains confined to speculation rather than serious planning. Future generations might reconsider should circumstances dramatically alter, but present conditions offer no encouragement whatsoever.

Should your institution employ proportional allocation, a six-hundred-dollar remittance would diminish your transaction balance by five hundred and your withdrawal balance by one hundred.

The composite annual percentage rate, consequently, represents nothing more than the sum of each rate multiplied by its corresponding obligation. Here, the calculation yields fifteen percent: point one three five times five thousand, plus point two two five times one thousand, divided by six thousand total. Statisticians term this a weighted mean.

Should the institution instead apply remittances differently—perhaps favoring the cheaper obligation initially, or directing some prescribed portion there while channeling the remainder toward costlier debt—then entering this averaged figure into computational tools becomes problematic. Your effective composite rate will climb progressively as you extinguish the transaction balance while leaving the withdrawal balance intact, or potentially decline under reversed circumstances.

The weighted mean probably approximates reality reasonably well given the scenario you describe, provided the allocation rules don't exclusively retire the cheaper obligation. It therefore constitutes the simplest approach for approximate projections where rough accuracy suffices rather than precision.

An alternative methodology using web-based computational tools involves treating these as distinct obligations or separate accounts. Numerous calculators accommodate multiple balances simultaneously. You can then distribute funds differently between the two "accounts." This permits you to determine, for instance, how many months will elapse before you've eliminated the costlier balance entirely, though perfect correspondence with actual outcomes seems unlikely—unless you locate specialized software incorporating this particular feature, you must either accept modest computational error or perform the arithmetic manually to achieve exactitude.

I have just emerged from a cinema in downtown Prague having witnessed this production. My attendance owed nothing to the poster, whose Hollywood-inflected heroic styling struck me as thoroughly antiquated. Nor did the prestigious cast attract me—such stellar French assemblages typically prove lamentable. Rather, I went simply because Prague offers precious few films in my native French tongue. Additionally, I cherish Adjani, Depardieu, and Rappeneau's magnificent Cyrano. Consequently, I felt compelled to compose these observations, for the prevailing consensus regarding this picture on IMDb strikes me as profoundly mistaken.

I experienced no disappointment, though perhaps not as intended: the production precisely resembles its advertisement. The personages prove exactly as foolish as their appearance suggests. Initially I imagined Adjani might embody deliberate caricature, offering comic relief worth genuine amusement. Alas, no! Consider the moment when she confesses to Depardieu that she murdered the corpulent gentleman slain early in the narrative—suddenly violins swell in ostentatiously maudlin orchestration, presumably meant to evoke tears and reveal depths beneath Adjani's superficial presentation. Perhaps this constituted humor operating at some rarefied tenth dimension, but regrettably my comic sensibilities cannot ascend such altitudes! Should I desire genuinely amusing French cinema concerning the Second World War, I revisit La Grande Vadrouille, which delivers infinitely superior entertainment!

I have also encountered IMDb commentary praising Lemoine's supposedly masterful performance. I must declare I have never witnessed such execrable acting—though admittedly I have never sampled Ed Wood's oeuvre. Nevertheless, the cinematography achieves considerable distinction, featuring numerous expensive, handsomely composed sequences: the Pantheon bathed in morning light as German forces enter Paris, refugees establishing encampments upon a Bordeaux bridge. Rappeneau possesses genuine filmmaking talent, yet he flourishes best when provided superior material. Cyrano presented no challenge in this regard—he bore no responsibility for composing the dialogue!

My assessment: one out of ten.

Permitting students to carry cellular devices into school buildings and utilize them during unstructured intervals—provided they remain deactivated throughout instructional periods—merits serious consideration. Several compelling arguments support this measured approach to technology integration.

First, allowing telephone access during midday meals could substantially diminish interpersonal conflicts. When adolescents engage with their devices, their attention shifts away from potentially volatile social dynamics. This distraction reduces both confrontational incidents and the accompanying emotional turbulence, benefiting not merely the student population but equally the faculty charged with maintaining order and fostering productive learning environments.

Second, such permission might enhance attendance rates. A significant proportion of chronic absenteeism stems from students' reluctance to surrender their devices upon entering campus. Many young people, particularly those facing repeated confiscations, avoid school altogether rather than risk parental discovery of their classroom infractions. These students fear that mothers or fathers, learning of unauthorized texting during lessons rather than attentive participation, will revoke telephone privileges until academic performance improves. By legitimizing usage during appropriate intervals, schools eliminate this attendance barrier.

Third, this policy would alleviate considerable administrative burden. If students exercised their device privileges exclusively during designated free periods and lunch intervals, educators would no longer need to monitor and mediate the interpersonal conflicts that currently consume their energy. Faculty members deserve respite from the exhausting emotional management that characterizes contemporary middle school environments. Granting controlled access to technology could provide precisely that relief.

The cumulative effect would benefit the entire educational community. Both staff and students would experience welcome reprieve from the persistent social turbulence pervading these institutions. When considering that middle schools across the system grapple with similar challenges, the potential for widespread positive impact becomes evident.

This proposal represents neither wholesale capitulation to technological distraction nor rigid prohibition. Rather, it offers balanced accommodation: acknowledging adolescents' connection to their devices while preserving the sanctity of instructional time. Such compromise addresses legitimate concerns from multiple constituencies while potentially transforming the daily atmosphere of educational institutions.

The prospect of autonomous vehicles presents a paradox: technological marvel shadowed by legitimate concern. While these innovations captivate the imagination, their safety remains an open question demanding scrutiny.

Consider first the vulnerabilities inherent in such systems. Mechanical failure poses genuine danger—a malfunction could precipitate collision, inflicting injury upon passengers who have surrendered control. Moreover, the very passivity these vehicles encourage invites drowsiness. When human engagement dissolves, vigilance wanes, and drivers may succumb to sleep. Yet manufacturers have anticipated this hazard. As one proposal suggests, entertainment systems and heads-up displays could occupy passengers during automated operation, then deactivate instantly when circumstances require human intervention, jolting attention back to the road.

The advantages, however, prove equally compelling. Imagine reclaiming those frantic morning minutes: breakfast consumed leisurely while the vehicle navigates traffic, or grooming completed after a hurried shower and hasty dressing. Professional obligations, too, become manageable. Without Bluetooth connectivity, telephone conversations while driving invite both distraction and legal penalty—citations issued for handheld device usage. Autonomous operation eliminates this dilemma, permitting necessary calls without compromising safety or inviting enforcement action.

Yet a darker possibility emerges when convenience breeds irresponsibility. Weekend revelry might tempt individuals to drink excessively, trusting automation to deliver them home unscathed. Should malfunction occur under such circumstances, the resulting collision would carry devastating consequences. Law enforcement arriving at the scene would hold the intoxicated passenger accountable, regardless of automated features. Incarceration would follow, the technology offering neither excuse nor protection.

This tension between promise and peril defines the autonomous vehicle debate. The technology offers undeniable liberation from tedious tasks, transforming commutes into productive intervals. Simultaneously, it introduces novel vulnerabilities—mechanical unreliability, diminished alertness, misplaced confidence in fallible systems. Whether innovation ultimately serves or endangers us depends not merely on engineering sophistication, but on our wisdom in deployment, our honesty about limitations, and our willingness to maintain responsibility even when machines shoulder the burden of operation. The question persists: does convenience justify the gamble?
